title: Spreadsheet So Boring It Hurts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The MBA Guy

transcript.speaker: The MBA Guy
transcript.text: I put together a spreadsheet that might interest you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! It's so boring, it hurts my head!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My brain is trying to escape through my ear!

transcript.speaker: The MBA Guy
transcript.text: I get this a lot.

situation: The MBA Guy hands the Boss a spreadsheet he thinks might interest him. As the Boss reads it, he cries out in pain, then collapses back in his chair with his feet up, claiming his brain is trying to escape through his ear. The MBA Guy calmly says this happens to him often.
punchline: The MBA Guy's spreadsheets are so mind-numbingly dull that they cause physical pain, and he is so used to the reaction that he shrugs it off.
summary: A manager is physically overwhelmed by the sheer tedium of a colleague's spreadsheet, and the colleague is unfazed because it happens all the time.

title: Dogbert's Extravagant Coach Class Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Until the company returns to profitability I will only fly coach.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll book three coach seats in a row so I can stretch out.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One of you will be a sherpa for my bedding.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll bring my own air marshal to punch anyone who talks while I'm napping.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And a videographer so I can see the playback when I wake up.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior view of the office building
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, announces at a meeting that he will sacrifice by flying coach until the company is profitable again. He then lists elaborate demands, including three seats, a sherpa for his bedding, a personal air marshal and a videographer, that make his coach travel far more costly than first class.
punchline: Dogbert's 'sacrifice' of flying coach comes with so many extravagant add-ons that it undermines the cost-cutting gesture entirely.
summary: A CEO pledges to fly economy to save money, then piles on so many luxury extras that the pledge means nothing.

title: Intern Regrets Challenging Rhodes Scholar

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Overqualified temp

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: It's funny that you're a Rhodes Scholar yet you can only find work as a temp.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am only an intern and yet I enjoy the power and prestige of being your superior.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: In retrospect I shouldn't have challenged her to a cage fight.

situation: Asok, an intern, gloats to a temp worker that he outranks her even though she is a Rhodes Scholar. In the last panel he appears bandaged, bruised, wearing an eye patch and with his arm in a sling, telling Dilbert he should not have challenged her to a cage fight.
punchline: Asok's smug taunting of a far more accomplished temp ended in a cage fight that he lost badly, leaving him comically battered.
summary: A boastful intern lords his rank over a brilliant temp and ends up beaten and bandaged after picking a fight with her.

title: Dogbert CEO Threatens MBA With Dropouts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO versus the MBA

transcript.speaker: MBA
transcript.text: My analysis doesn't support your strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My analysis says I can hire three high school dropouts to slap you until it does.

transcript.speaker: MBA
transcript.text: No... please, not dropouts!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They will kick your assumptions.

situation: An MBA-wielding employee tells CEO Dogbert that his analysis does not support Dogbert's strategy. Dogbert replies that he can hire three high school dropouts to slap the employee until the analysis agrees. The terrified employee begs him not to, and Dogbert adds that they will kick his assumptions.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses data-driven analysis by threatening physical intimidation to force the numbers to agree with his strategy, and the final line twists 'kick your ass' into 'kick your assumptions'.
summary: A boss-dog brushes off a skeptical analyst by promising to hire thugs who will beat the findings into line.

title: Janitor Gets Inflated C-Level Title

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Floyd, I'm giving you a C-level title.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll be the Chief Janitorial Officer, in charge of all dirt, germs, dead critters and problematic excretions.

transcript.speaker: Floyd
transcript.text: Is it because I'm so important?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What answer would make you clean up poop faster?

situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, promotes Floyd the janitor to a C-level title, Chief Janitorial Officer, which just means he's responsible for all the filth. Floyd hopefully asks if it's because he's so important, and Dogbert responds by asking what answer would motivate him to clean up poop faster.
punchline: The fancy title is a manipulation tactic, and Dogbert openly admits he'll say whatever flatters Floyd into doing the dirtiest work faster.
summary: A scheming dog boss dresses up a custodian's grubby duties with an executive-sounding title and cynically admits the flattery is just a motivational trick.

title: Training Chickens to Replace Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today we'll discuss ways to improve our workflow process.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As you know, a good process is a substitute for good employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The ultimate goal is to simplify our processes so much...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That we can train chickens to do your jobs in return for pellets.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll begin by discussing our process for funding new projects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Could any part of our process be replaced by, for example, ringing a bell with your beak?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, but only the part that you do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's a wrinkle in the plan.

transcript.speaker: Chicken
transcript.text: Pellet.

setting: Conference room during a workflow meeting
situation: The Boss leads a meeting on improving workflow, declaring that a good process can substitute for good employees and that the goal is to simplify things so much that chickens could do the staff's jobs for pellets. When he asks which part of the funding process a chicken could replace by ringing a bell with its beak, Alice answers that it's only the part he does. In the last panel the Boss admits there's a wrinkle in the plan while a chicken thinks about pellets.
punchline: Alice points out that the only job simple enough for a chicken to do is the Boss's own, turning his insult against the staff back on him.
summary: A manager who dreams of replacing his workers with pellet-fed poultry is told by a sharp-tongued employee that the bird would only be fit to take over his own duties.

title: Fact-Checking Dilbert's Date by Email

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've made a number of inaccurate statements during the course of this date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to break the romantic mood, so I'll send you an e-mail with links that you can review on your own time.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: It sounds like you two are over. Would it hurt my tip if I take a run at her?

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a date at a restaurant and, phone in hand, tells his companion she has made inaccurate statements. He says he will email her links to review later so as not to spoil the romantic mood. A waiter, overhearing, decides the date is finished and asks if it would hurt his tip to hit on her.
punchline: Dilbert's pedantic fact-checking kills the date so completely that even the waiter sees it as over and asks permission to pursue her, with only his tip as a concern.
summary: A man who corrects his date's facts and promises her a follow-up email watches as their waiter decides she is now fair game.

title: Presentation About Avoiding the Presentation

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My cubicle is surrounded by loud idiots who make it impossible for me to concentrate on my work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you create a presentation on why you couldn't do the presentation you're supposed to be doing?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wouldn't it have been just as easy to create the actual presentation?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm hoping to use this one more than once.

situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug presents a slide showing a floor plan with his cubicle labelled 'ME' surrounded by noisy neighbours. The Boss asks whether he made a presentation explaining why he couldn't make the assigned presentation, and he admits he did. When asked why he didn't just make the real one, he says he wants to reuse this excuse presentation repeatedly.
punchline: The employee has put more effort into a reusable excuse presentation than the actual work would have taken, planning to recycle it every time he wants to dodge a task.
summary: A worker builds an elaborate slide deck to justify not doing his assigned slide deck, planning to recycle the excuse indefinitely.

title: Suggestions That Aren't Really Suggestions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you see my suggestions for your presentation?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I rejected them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They aren't optional.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why do you call them suggestions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes I call things the wrong names to improve morale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You should just say what you're thinking. I can handle the truth.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. Make all of the changes I want, you ignorant hump.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And do it now while I mock you with sheep noises.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Baaaa! Baaaa! Baaaa!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe your first way was better.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one will ever love you!

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert if he saw his suggestions for a presentation, and Dilbert says he rejected them. The Boss admits the suggestions were really mandatory and that he mislabels things to boost morale. When Dilbert asks him to speak plainly, the Boss insults him and mocks him with sheep noises, and Dilbert quickly asks him to go back to the polite approach.
punchline: Dilbert demands brutal honesty from his boss, gets abusive insults instead, and realizes the euphemistic management-speak was preferable after all.
summary: After insisting his boss drop the euphemisms, an employee gets a barrage of insults and animal noises and decides the polite deception was better.
themes: be careful what you wish for
keywords: no one will ever love you

title: Dead Squirrel Oven Mitten Eco-Gesture

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company has replaced Styrofoam cups with paper cups to save the planet.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They work just as well if you use a dead squirrel as an oven mitten.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This one still has some fight left in him.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces the company has swapped Styrofoam cups for paper ones to help the environment. Alice, sarcastic about how hot the paper cups get, puts a dead squirrel on her hand to use as an oven mitten. In the last panel the squirrel seems to come back to life and thrashes around while Dilbert and the Boss watch.
punchline: Alice sarcastically points out that the paper cups are too hot to hold, and her grisly squirrel solution turns out to be not quite dead, exposing the absurdity of the green initiative.
summary: A well-meaning eco-friendly cup swap leaves a coworker so burned that she improvises a gruesome, and surprisingly lively, hand protector.

title: Struggling Artist Works for Food

transcript.speaker: Artist
transcript.text: I work here to pay the bills, but I'm actually an artist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. You must be a terrible artist if you have to work here just to eat.

transcript.speaker: Artist
transcript.text: My work isn't commercial.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's not really art if no one likes it.

setting: Conference room table at the office
situation: A coworker in a beret and scarf tells Dilbert and another colleague that he only works at the company to pay bills and is really an artist. Dilbert and the other coworker respond by mocking his artistic ability, pointing out that a successful artist wouldn't need a day job and that art nobody likes isn't really art.
punchline: The self-described artist's excuse that his work isn't commercial is undercut by the coworker's jab that art nobody appreciates doesn't count as art, implying he is simply a bad artist.
summary: A beret-wearing office worker claims to be a true artist, only to have his colleagues ridicule him for needing a day job and having no audience.

title: Side Business On Company Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's slow at work so I created my own internet business called dilbertfiles.com

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So you're stealing company resources?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call myself a CEO.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I think I saw someone who isn't a miscreant.

setting: A cocktail party or social gathering with a bar in the background
situation: Dilbert, holding a martini, tells a woman at a party that he started his own internet business during slow periods at work. She points out that he is using company resources to do it. He shrugs it off by saying he calls himself a CEO, and she responds that she thinks she spotted a business leader who isn't a miscreant.
punchline: Dilbert justifies using his employer's time and resources for his side business by claiming the CEO title, and the woman sarcastically implies that all CEOs are miscreants and she has trouble finding one who isn't.
summary: A man brags about running a website on his employer's time and equivalently excuses it by calling himself an executive, drawing a cutting remark about executives' ethics.

title: Evaluating Cloud Instead of Working

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's implement cloud computing so I have something to talk about at the executive meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell them we're evaluating it. That way neither of us needs to do any real work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like it when you do real work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry. I thought you were leading by example.

situation: The Boss wants to announce a cloud computing initiative purely so he has something to report at the executive meeting. Dilbert suggests claiming they are merely evaluating it, which lets both of them avoid real work. The Boss complains that he likes it when Dilbert works, and Dilbert retorts that he was just following the boss's example.
punchline: Dilbert turns the boss's criticism around by implying the boss never does any real work himself, so Dilbert was only imitating his leadership.
summary: A manager who craves a talking point for upper management gets a sarcastic reminder that his own idleness sets the standard for his employee.

title: Dogbert CEO Demands Ten Billion Years Pay

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Union Representative
transcript.text: The union will agree to deep cuts if you agree to work for one dollar per year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I agree, as long as I get my pay in advance and the mandatory retirement age is waived.

transcript.speaker: Union Representative
transcript.text: Fine.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Call payroll and tell them to cut a check for my next ten billion years of service.

situation: Dogbert, serving as CEO, is offered a deal by a union representative: the union will accept deep cuts if the CEO works for one dollar per year. Dogbert accepts on the condition that his pay is given in advance and that mandatory retirement is waived. He then has an assistant order a paycheck covering ten billion years of service.
punchline: Dogbert exploits the loophole of one dollar per year by demanding advance payment for ten billion years, which turns the supposedly modest salary into an enormous payout.
summary: A CEO takes advantage of a union's symbolic salary demand by prepaying himself for an absurdly long career.

title: Taking a Literal Bullet Interview

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a bullet for the team?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... Sure.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Good. The team is already at the firing range waiting for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stupid weak economy!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zing

setting: A job interview office, then an outdoor desert firing range
situation: Dilbert is interviewing for a job and is asked whether he would take a bullet for the team. He agrees, and the interviewer reveals that the team is already waiting at a firing range. In the last panel Dilbert dodges bullets across the range while thinking about the economy.
punchline: The interviewer takes the 'take a bullet for the team' cliche literally, and Dilbert, desperate for a job in a weak economy, is left running for his life.
summary: A job candidate agrees to a teamwork cliche and ends up literally dodging gunfire on a firing range.
keywords: take a bullet for the team

title: Blind Squirrels and Redundant Assignments

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I gave the same assignment to all the employees who look like you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A blind squirrel is more likely to find a nut if there are a lot of blind squirrels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounded cruel. Allow me to rephrase it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I meant vision-impaired squirrels.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he gave the same assignment to every employee who resembles him. He explains this with a blind squirrel analogy, implying that many unskilled workers will eventually stumble on a solution. Dilbert then 'corrects' the insult by politely rewording it as vision-impaired squirrels.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to soften his insult by swapping 'blind' for 'vision-impaired' does nothing to remove the actual insult, that Dilbert and his lookalikes are lucky incompetents.
summary: A manager assigns identical work to a crowd of employees, compares them to sightless rodents hoping for luck, and then only polishes the wording of the slight.

title: Job Candidate's Endless Family Emergencies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have many relatives?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Yes, I have a huge family.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In any given week, how many of them are dying, graduating, going to jail, or getting married?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Maybe... six.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When would you have time to work?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I have to go. Someone fell out of a tree.

setting: Job interview in an office, across a desk
situation: The Boss interviews a candidate and asks about his relatives. After learning the man has a huge family, he calculates how many family events happen in a typical week and concludes there would be no time left for work. The candidate proves the point by abruptly leaving because a relative fell out of a tree.
punchline: The candidate's family crises are so constant that he confirms the interviewer's concern by walking out mid-interview to deal with another one.
summary: An interviewer worries that a candidate's sprawling family will swallow his work hours, and the man promptly leaves to handle yet another relative's mishap.

title: Garbage Slides Become Company Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your PowerPoint slides impressed the executives so much that they're changing our entire strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Those slides were nothing but a bunch of garbage dressed up to look good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And that's what our new product line will be!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his PowerPoint slides so impressed the executives that the company is overhauling its whole strategy. Dilbert honestly admits the slides were just garbage made to look good. The Boss takes this as a cue to announce that garbage is exactly what the new product line will be.
punchline: The company is staking its strategy and new product line on something Dilbert admits is worthless but well-presented, showing how style over substance drives executive decisions.
summary: A manager happily reveals that a deceptively polished presentation has convinced leadership to build the company's future on junk.

title: Failure Puppet Calendar Takeover

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As usual, my co-workers have filled in every space on my Outlook calendar.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I am only a puppet hurtling toward failure.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey there, Failure Puppet!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hoped it wasn't so obvious.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and thinks that his coworkers have booked every slot on his Outlook calendar, leaving him with no control over his time. He gloomily concludes he is just a puppet hurtling toward failure. A coworker walks by holding a coffee mug and greets him as 'Failure Puppet', showing that his helplessness is plain to everyone.
punchline: Dilbert's private despair about being controlled by others' meeting requests is embarrassingly exposed when a coworker cheerfully uses his gloomy self-description as a nickname.
summary: A man whose schedule has been fully claimed by colleagues sulks privately about being a doomed puppet, only to be greeted by a passing coworker with exactly that label.

title: Wally Picks Criminal Role Models

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally dabbles in crime

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A lot of people think crime is a bad thing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But it all depends on how you pick your role models.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I lean toward governors, bankers, athletes and Sith lords.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel a coldness.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Dilbert that crime is only considered bad depending on who you look up to. He then lists the role models he favors, a group of disgraced public figures and a fictional villain, which leaves Dilbert visibly unsettled.
punchline: Wally's role models are governors, bankers and athletes, implicitly criminals or wrongdoers, alongside Star Wars Sith lords, which chills Dilbert.
summary: Wally casually justifies a life of crime by pointing to the questionable heroes he admires, to his coworker's discomfort.

title: Can't Explain Without a Whiteboard

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm one of those people who can't explain things without a whiteboard, but I'll try.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The... uh... fuh... fuh... wah... um... thingamajig... fuh... fuh... eh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Worst case I've seen.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yee... woo... ee-yi-ee-yi-moo...

situation: A coworker in a meeting announces he can't explain things without a whiteboard, then tries anyway. He flails his arms and descends into stuttering gibberish and finally nonsense sounds. Dilbert calmly observes it's the worst case he has seen.
punchline: The coworker's dependence on a whiteboard is so severe that without one he completely breaks down into incoherent babbling, which Dilbert treats like a medical diagnosis.
summary: A meeting participant without a whiteboard loses the ability to speak coherently and spirals into farm-animal gibberish while a colleague clinically assesses the severity.

title: Fast, Perfect, Prayer Rug Requested

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I don't have enough time to do things right, should I just do nothing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or do you prefer that I miss deadlines, or do shoddy work, or pray for divine intervention?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want everything fast and perfect.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I buy a prayer rug?

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks the Boss what he should do when there isn't enough time to do work properly, offering options like missing deadlines, doing shoddy work, or praying for a miracle. The Boss simply insists he wants everything both fast and perfect. Wally responds by asking to buy a prayer rug.
punchline: Since the Boss refuses to accept any tradeoff between speed and quality, Wally sarcastically concludes that only divine intervention can meet his demands and asks for a company-funded prayer rug.
summary: Faced with a manager who demands impossible results, an employee deadpans that his only remaining option is a miracle and requests the equipment for it.

title: Alice Rejects Boss's Mentoring Session

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I thought it was time for us to have a little mentoring session.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How does this make sense when I'm more capable than you in every important way?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we can skip the part where I say you need to be more confident and speak out at meetings.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Duh.

setting: Office desk during a one-on-one meeting
situation: The Boss proposes a mentoring session with Alice. Alice bluntly points out that she is more capable than he is in every important way. The Boss concedes by offering to skip his usual advice about being more confident and speaking up in meetings, and Alice curtly replies 'Duh.'
punchline: The Boss's mentoring is so predictable and pointless that even he admits Alice is better than him, and she agrees without a hint of modesty.
summary: A manager's attempt to mentor his far more competent employee collapses when she calls out his inferiority and he meekly agrees.

title: Worrying About the Wrong Thing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm worried that I won't get a raise this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You shouldn't worry about that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should worry that you might lose your job in the next round of layoffs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should worry about that???

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... probably not.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It makes more sense to worry about the entire company going out of business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And that's nothing if the global economy collapses.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should worry that the only viable livelihood of the future involves cannibalism.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you still worried about not getting a raise?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not so much.

setting: Office hallway, then outside a building, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he is worried about not getting a raise. The boss escalates the worries step by step: layoffs, the company folding, global economic collapse, and finally a future where cannibalism is the only viable livelihood. By the end Dilbert is a trembling wreck, and Dogbert asks if he is still worried about the raise.
punchline: The boss's catastrophizing makes Dilbert's original concern seem trivial, so he is no longer worried about the raise but is now terrified of everything else.
summary: A manager reassures a worried employee by piling on ever bigger disasters until the original concern no longer seems to matter.

title: Dilbert Preempts Every Excuse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Could you make these changes in the database? It will only take five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ooh, I don't know...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you planning to spend ten minutes explaining why you don't have five minutes to do this task?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or are you so incompetent that a five-minute task will take an hour?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or are you limited by company policy because you're a feckless waste of carbon?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or are you the agreeable but unorganized type who will say yes, lose my note, and forget who asked?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was planning to tell you this doesn't need to be done and refuse to change my position even after you give me good reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Experience is just another word for losing hope.

setting: Office cubicle area, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker to make a quick database change and, before the coworker can answer, cuts him off to list every possible excuse and insult in advance. He finishes by anticipating that he would refuse to listen to any good reasons anyway. In the last panel Dilbert is at home with Dogbert and drinks coffee, musing bitterly about experience.
punchline: Dilbert's long experience with workplace excuses has made him so cynical that he argues both sides of the conversation in advance, concluding that experience is merely lost hope.
summary: After years of dealing with stalling coworkers, a man pre-answers every possible objection to a simple request and admits his own stubbornness too.

title: CEO Dogbert Becomes Corporate Pirate

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm taking a side job as a pirate.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll kidnap employees and authorize huge ransom payments to myself for their return.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you'll return them safely?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a different business model.

situation: Dogbert, serving as CEO at the head of the conference table, tells his executives he is taking a side job as a pirate. He explains that he will kidnap employees and then authorize enormous ransom payments to himself. The Boss asks whether he will at least return the hostages safely, and Dogbert dismisses the idea.
punchline: Dogbert has no intention of returning the kidnapped employees, since safe returns would be an entirely separate business model, and he sees no profit in it.
summary: A canine chief executive reveals a scheme to enrich himself by abducting his own staff and ransoming them to the company, with no promise of their safety.

title: Pills Cure Wings, Cause Halo

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: These pills should get rid of the wings that the last pills gave you as a side effect.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It's an off-label use, but I have a good feeling about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What now?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: At this point, sinning is your best bet.

situation: Dilbert sits shirtless on an exam table with angel wings, a side effect of earlier medication. The doctor gives him new pills to remove the wings, but they leave him with a halo instead. The doctor then advises him to start sinning to get rid of his angelic features.
punchline: The doctor's cure for the pills' side effects is to sin, since the only way to stop looking like an angel is to behave badly.
summary: A patient's medication keeps producing heavenly side effects, and his physician's final remedy is to recommend misbehaving.

title: Catbert Deflects With Gas Leak

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: According to your skills inventory, the only thing you are good at is...

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: ...diverting attention from your own lack of value.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Is it just me, or is there a deadly gas leak in the building?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Erk!

setting: Catbert's HR office, at a desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, reads an employee's skills inventory aloud and is about to say the employee is good at only one thing. The employee finishes the sentence himself, admitting his only skill is diverting attention from his lack of value, then immediately demonstrates it by raising a false alarm about a gas leak, which startles Catbert.
punchline: The employee proves his own skills inventory right by deflecting attention with a bogus emergency in the very act of being evaluated.
summary: A worker facing a harsh skills review proves its verdict true by distracting his evaluator with a made-up gas scare.

title: Elbonian Standards Meeting Kung Fu Mud

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Industry standards meeting in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's adopt my company's specs as the industry standard.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Your specifications are weak, and so is your kung fu.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: From that day on, all standards meetings were held in the mud of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Can't... kick! Stupid... mud!

setting: A conference room in Elbonia where the floor is deep mud
situation: At an industry standards meeting in Elbonia, Dilbert proposes that his company's specifications become the industry standard. An Elbonian attendee insults the specs and his kung fu, then tries to attack but is stuck in the knee-deep mud and cannot kick. The narrator explains that all future standards meetings were held in the mud.
punchline: Holding standards meetings in Elbonian mud neutralizes the threat of physical intimidation, making the dispute over specs far less dangerous.
summary: A threatened martial-arts showdown over technical specs fizzles out when the participants are trapped in thick mud.

title: Wally Bills For Being Called Thief

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, can you take a look at this?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd be delighted. What's your project charge code?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It will only take a minute.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you suggesting that I lie about my time?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's only one minute.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: By that line of reasoning, it's okay to steal, as long as you don't take too much.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Incidentally, I have to charge you for the time it just took to label you a thief.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Forget it! I'll ask someone else!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's call that "overhead."

situation: A coworker asks Wally to take a quick look at a document, and Wally demands a project charge code before helping. When the coworker says it will only take a minute, Wally accuses him of asking him to falsify his time and compares it to stealing. Wally then threatens to bill him for the time spent insulting him, and the coworker storms off, after which Wally decides to log the lost time as overhead.
punchline: Wally dodges work by lecturing about timesheet honesty, then charges the time he spent doing so to the generic 'overhead' category, exploiting the very system he claimed to respect.
summary: A colleague's request for a quick favor is turned away with a sanctimonious ethics lecture that Wally quietly files under company overhead.

title: Retirement Home Brochure for Graybeard

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Hi Graybeard. I brought you a brochure for a great retirement home.

transcript.speaker: Graybeard
transcript.text: I'm only 52. I'm not going to retire just so you can get promoted into my job.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Risky adventure?

situation: A young, ambitious employee hands an older coworker a brochure for a retirement home, hoping to nudge him out. The older man, who is only 52, sees through the scheme and refuses to retire just to open up a promotion. The young employee then tries a different pitch, suggesting a risky adventure instead.
punchline: After being caught trying to push the older coworker into retirement, the young employee tries another way to get him to leave his job by suggesting he go off on a risky adventure, which could get him killed.
summary: A scheming young worker tries to pry a veteran colleague out of his position, first with a retirement brochure and then with a darker alternative.

title: Name Owned By Former Employer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I lost an intellectual property case with my ex-employer. Now they own my name.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It costs me five dollars every time I introduce myself.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I already forgot your name. What was it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I tell you next month? I'm on a budget.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sure, if you think you can find me.

setting: Outdoor walking path in a park
situation: Dilbert walks with a woman and explains that he lost an intellectual property lawsuit against his former employer, who now owns his name and charges him five dollars each time he introduces himself. When she admits she has already forgotten his name, he asks to tell her next month because he is on a budget, and she cheerfully says he will have to find her first.
punchline: Dilbert's name is so expensive to say that he would rather delay introductions, and the woman's reply is a polite brush-off hinting she has no interest in seeing him again.
summary: After losing a legal fight with a past employer, a man must pay a fee every time he says his own name, which kills a first conversation with a stranger.

title: Rigging Bids With a Counting Horse

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: CEO Summit

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Obviously it's illegal for companies to rig bids.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But interestingly, the crime is nearly impossible to prove when nothing is written down.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet Eddie. Pay close attention to how many times he stomps his hoof.

situation: Dogbert, speaking to a CEO at a summit, notes that bid rigging is illegal but nearly impossible to prove if nothing is written down. He then introduces a horse named Eddie and tells the CEO to count how many times the horse stomps his hoof. The horse is a silent, deniable way to communicate a bid.
punchline: The counting horse is a wink-and-nod way to coordinate illegal bid rigging without leaving any written evidence, like a cartoonish version of Clever Hans.
summary: A consultant dog shows a smiling executive how to fix bids with no paper trail by using a hoof-stomping horse as the messenger.

title: Unreachable Stakeholder Makes Deadline Impossible

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Finish this project in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And make sure you get input from all the executive stakeholders.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's impossible.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's call one of the ten stakeholders and I'll show you.

transcript.speaker: Phone
transcript.text: Beep beep

transcript.speaker: Voicemail
transcript.text: This is Ed Bigston's voice mail. I'm not available... ever.

transcript.speaker: Voicemail
transcript.text: I am either on vacation, or sick, or traveling, or in a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Voicemail
transcript.text: I do not check e-mail or return phone calls. Like the horizon, I am more of a concept than a corporeal being.

transcript.speaker: Voicemail
transcript.text: Despair is your only option.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try faxing him.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to finish a project in two weeks while collecting input from ten executive stakeholders. When Dilbert says it's impossible, the Boss calls one stakeholder to prove him wrong. The voicemail greeting reveals the executive is completely unreachable, yet the Boss still suggests a fax.
punchline: Even after hearing proof that the executive is unreachable by any means, the Boss clings to his plan and suggests faxing him as if an outdated communication method will solve the problem.
summary: A manager sets out to prove a deadline is feasible by phoning an executive whose voicemail declares he can never be reached, then answers with a suggestion that ignores the evidence.

title: Marriage Proposal By Spreadsheet

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I crunched the numbers, and it makes sense for us to get married.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I can maintain my lifestyle if you live in the closet and your only hobby is cleaning the house when I'm gone.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: If that doesn't work, I can insure the bejeezus out of you and hope for the best.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The best?

situation: A woman with big hair stands by Dilbert's cubicle and reads from a sheet of paper, announcing that her financial analysis shows marriage to him makes sense. She lays out terms in which he would live in a closet and clean her house, then adds that she could instead insure him heavily and hope for the best. Dilbert, on the phone, only asks what 'the best' means.
punchline: Her 'best' outcome is Dilbert dying so she can collect the life insurance, making the proposal a cold financial calculation with no romance.
summary: A coldly calculating coworker pitches marriage to Dilbert as a financial arrangement and casually reveals that his death would be her backup plan.

title: Elbonians Forced To Feel Giving

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It feels good when you volunteer to help others.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's why I talked some poor Elbonians into mowing our lawn for free. I want them to feel the joy of giving.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: All I'm feeling is tired.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Try doing it faster.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: RRRRR

setting: Outdoors on a walking path and in Dilbert's backyard
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert walk along a path while Dogbert talks about how good volunteering feels. Dogbert explains that he got some Elbonians to mow their lawn for free so they can experience the joy of giving. In the backyard, one exhausted Elbonian pushes the mower while another tells him to work faster.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of letting others experience the joy of volunteering is really just exploiting unpaid labor, and the Elbonians are only tired and bossed around rather than feeling good.
summary: A smug Dogbert brags that he is generously giving poor foreigners the gift of volunteering by having them mow his lawn for nothing.

title: Empty Gift From Bonus Pool

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We pooled our bonus checks and got you this gift.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's empty.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Better luck next year.

situation: Alice, Dilbert and Wally present the Boss with a wrapped gift, saying they pooled their bonus checks to buy it. The Boss opens it and finds it empty. Alice cheerfully tells him better luck next year.
punchline: The employees' bonuses were so small or nonexistent that pooling them bought nothing, and Alice's cheerful 'better luck next year' is a passive-aggressive jab at the Boss over the poor bonuses.
summary: Employees hand their manager a gift that turns out to contain nothing, a pointed jab at how little their bonuses amounted to.

title: Taking Ownership Of The Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll never be able to finish my project on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to take ownership.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I hire more programmers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I reduce the number of features?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... I'm just taking ownership of the failure?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be greedy.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he can't finish his project on time, and the boss tells him to take ownership. Dilbert asks for more programmers and for fewer features, and the boss refuses both. Dilbert concludes that all he's being given is ownership of the failure.
punchline: The boss grants no resources and no scope relief, so 'taking ownership' means accepting blame for a doomed project, and the boss even treats the blame as a prize Dilbert shouldn't hog.
summary: A boss who denies every request for help insists his employee own the inevitable flop, then begrudges him the full credit for it.

title: Newsletter Writer Insults Boss's Parents

transcript.speaker: Newsletter Writer
transcript.text: I've been asked to chronicle your rise to management for the company newsletter.

transcript.speaker: Newsletter Writer
transcript.text: So far, I have the story of how your father was a barrel-shaped moron who married a blind woman.

transcript.speaker: Newsletter Writer
transcript.text: But it could have been the other way around. I'm mostly guessing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Lucky guess.

situation: A woman with a notepad tells the Boss she is writing a company newsletter piece about his rise to management. She reads out her draft, which says his father was a barrel-shaped moron who married a blind woman, then admits she is only guessing. The Boss, holding a coffee mug, confirms it was a lucky guess.
punchline: The Boss is so unremarkable and his family so unflattering that the writer's insulting guesses turn out to be accurate, and he cheerfully admits it.
summary: A newsletter writer guesses at the Boss's family history with insults, and he unwittingly confirms she got it right.

title: Dilbert Works Home Without Pants

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yikes!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't be frightened by my green clothing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be working at home today, thus reducing carbon emissions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My telepresence meetings will only display me from here up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By reducing the amount of material in my garment I can use less soap and water on laundry day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And the extra freedom of movement will allow me to mouse more efficiently.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This has to stop. I'll be back in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you use my shaver?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, and I will trim myself daily until you start dressing right.

setting: Dilbert's home living room and home office
situation: Dilbert greets Dogbert in his underwear and explains it is an eco-friendly choice for working from home, claiming it cuts carbon emissions, laundry water and soap, and helps him use the mouse. Dogbert is horrified and leaves, then returns shaved bare. He retaliates by declaring he'll keep shaving himself until Dilbert dresses properly.
punchline: Dogbert responds to Dilbert's pantsless green-living excuse by shaving himself bald as a deliberate counter-ridicule, matching the awkward sight until Dilbert puts on trousers.
summary: A man justifies working from home in his underwear with environmental reasoning, so his dog shaves himself in protest.

title: Downsizing Best Employees First

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gabe was downsized when his last employer had financial troubles. I was lucky to hire him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because they always downsize their best employees first?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry. I didn't mean to put it in context.

situation: The Boss introduces a new hire, Gabe, and explains that he was laid off from his previous employer because of financial trouble, calling himself lucky to have hired him. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether companies always lay off their best people first, then apologizes for having put the remark in context.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic remark implies that Gabe must have been a poor employee if he was let go, and his mock apology admits he said the insulting part out loud.
summary: A manager brags about hiring a laid-off worker, and Dilbert's dry quip turns the boast into an insult before he pretends to retract it.

title: Closing the Closest Parking Lot

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We can save the most money by downsizing the unhealthiest workers first.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do we know who they are?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We'll close the parking lot that's nearest the building.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Should we help them?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's too late for broccoli.

setting: Boss's office, then a distant parking lot
situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells the Boss that the cheapest way to downsize is to cut the unhealthiest workers first. To identify them, he plans to close the parking lot nearest the building. Two employees walking in from the far lot pass collapsed colleagues lying on the pavement and callously joke about it.
punchline: Forcing out-of-shape workers to walk a long distance from a remote lot will literally collapse or kill them, and the coworkers' reaction that it's too late for broccoli treats the casualties as a bad joke.
summary: Catbert proposes culling unfit employees by moving parking far from the office, and the resulting trail of collapsed workers is met with dark indifference.

title: Dogbert Testifies at Bailout Hearings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bailout hearings

transcript.speaker: Committee Member
transcript.text: Mr. Dogbert, did you fly here in a corporate jet?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, the same jet that took you on a fact-finding trip to Aruba, you wool-coated glob of fat.

transcript.speaker: Committee Member
transcript.text: Bring it on! I can do this all day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I yield my time to the hypocrite from another state.

situation: At a congressional hearing on bailouts, a committee member asks Dogbert, seated alone at the witness table, whether he flew in on a corporate jet. Dogbert says yes and insults the questioner for having taken the same jet on a junket to Aruba. The member shrugs it off and Dogbert hands his time to another politician.
punchline: The politicians grilling Dogbert over corporate jet use have enjoyed the same perks themselves, so the hearing is a contest of hypocrisy and insults.
summary: A grilled witness fires back at a lawmaker by pointing out that the lawmaker also rode the corporate jet to a vacation spot.

title: Dogbert's Imaginary Financial Services Company

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're getting into the financial services game.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That way all of our products can be imaginary.

transcript.speaker: Man at table
transcript.text: Can you give me reliable investment advice?

transcript.speaker: Advisor
transcript.text: Yes, as far as you know.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, announces to his staff that the company is entering financial services. He explains this is so all the company's products can be imaginary. A man at the table then asks for reliable investment advice, and an advisor replies with a deliberately slippery answer.
punchline: Financial products are essentially intangible and unverifiable, so a customer can never tell whether the advice is real, and the advisor's 'as far as you know' admits that he could be lying and you would never find out.
summary: A dog in charge of a company chooses the finance industry because nothing it sells has to actually exist, and its advice is trustworthy only until someone checks.

title: Carol's Only Emotion Is Anger

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I want you to feel emotionally invested in the vision and mission of the company.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My only emotion is anger. You can have as much of it as you want.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I can inspire you with my leadership.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I feel like I'm wearing concrete underpants.

situation: The Boss stands by Carol's cubicle and asks her to feel emotionally invested in the company's vision and mission. Carol deadpans that her only emotion is anger and offers him as much as he wants. When he suggests his leadership might inspire her, she replies that she feels like she's wearing concrete underpants.
punchline: Carol's deadpan insult turns the boss's attempt at inspirational leadership into something heavy, uncomfortable and weighing her down.
summary: A manager's plea for emotional buy-in is met with a secretary's simmering fury and a vividly uncomfortable metaphor for his leadership.

title: Cheap Posters Suggest Eating Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: The new motivational posters are in.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: As you requested, I bought the least expensive ones.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Excuse me while I stretch my wagger.

transcript.speaker: Poster
transcript.text: If all else fails... your coworkers are edible

situation: Dogbert, as CEO, is told by his assistant that the new motivational posters have arrived and that he bought the cheapest ones as requested. Dogbert says he needs to stretch his wagger, implying he is about to wag his tail in delight. In the last panel, Dilbert and Wally stand looking at a poster showing a screaming man that reads 'If all else fails... your coworkers are edible.'
punchline: Because the posters were the cheapest available, their 'motivational' message is a ghoulish suggestion of cannibalism, a cruel joke Dogbert gleefully enjoys.
summary: A canine executive orders bargain-bin inspirational posters and delights in the macabre slogan his employees now have to stare at.

title: Programming a Yacht Toward Pirates

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The lucky sales guy

transcript.speaker: Sales Guy
transcript.text: My sales quotas were set too low. I plan to buy a yacht with my commissions.

transcript.speaker: Sales Guy
transcript.text: Would you mind programming the navigation system so I can get drunk while my boat takes me places?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you researching where all the pirates attack?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's better if you don't know.

situation: A sales guy with a money bag over his head brags to Dilbert that his quotas were set too low and he'll buy a yacht with his commissions. He then asks Dilbert to program the boat's navigation system so he can drink while it takes him places. Later, a coworker catches Dilbert researching where pirates attack.
punchline: Dilbert is quietly plotting to program the lucky sales guy's yacht to sail straight into pirate territory, and he refuses to explain because he wants deniability.
summary: After a smug salesman requests a hands-free yacht route, Dilbert secretly studies the world's most dangerous waters for him.

title: Vacation Temp Wants Your Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a temp to cover your job while you're on vacation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's far more qualified than you, and her stated goal is to replace you. But don't worry.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How am I supposed to not worry about that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yoga?

situation: The Boss tells an employee that he has hired a temp to cover her work during her vacation. He then casually reveals that the temp is more qualified and intends to take her job permanently, and tells her not to worry. She reacts with alarm, and he offers yoga as his solution.
punchline: The boss creates a serious threat to her job security and then offers a glib wellness suggestion instead of any real reassurance.
summary: A manager cheerfully warns a vacationing employee that her replacement is better than her and wants her position, then recommends relaxation exercises.

title: New MBA Recommends Jargon

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I just got my MBA, and I'm here to solve all of your problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our products are junk and we're completely out of capital.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Have you tried jargon?

situation: Asok, a fresh MBA graduate, announces at a meeting that he is here to solve the team's problems. Dilbert explains that the products are junk and the company has no money. Asok's only suggestion is to try using jargon.
punchline: Business school has equipped the new MBA with nothing more useful than buzzwords, so his answer to real, serious problems is to talk fancier.
summary: A freshly credentialed business graduate offers meaningless corporate buzzwords as the cure for a company with bad products and no money.

title: Mordac Denies Laptop, Offers Pizza Box

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: May I use this laptop that no one else is using?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: No, but you can have my old pizza box while you waterboard yourself in your own tears.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I guess that's better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Really? In that case you can't have it.

situation: An employee politely asks Mordac, the head of information services, for permission to use an unused laptop. Mordac refuses and sarcastically offers his old pizza box instead, along with a cruel remark about waterboarding oneself in tears. When the employee meekly accepts the pizza box as better than nothing, Mordac withdraws that offer too.
punchline: Mordac is so determined to deny anyone anything that he takes back even the worthless pizza box the moment the employee shows a flicker of gratitude.
summary: A hopeful worker asks for a spare computer and ends up being denied even the garbage Mordac mockingly offered as a consolation.

title: Buying the Company to Humiliate Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I bought the company that fired you. Now you can interview with me for your old job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You already know everything about me. An interview would have no purpose other than to humiliate me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Since when do things need two purposes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is Tuesday good?

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has bought the company that laid Dilbert off and offers him an interview for his old job. Dilbert objects that Dogbert already knows everything about him, so the interview could only serve to humiliate him. Dogbert shrugs off the objection and asks if Tuesday works.
punchline: Dogbert doesn't deny that humiliation is the point; he only questions why a thing would need more than one purpose, then cheerfully schedules it.
summary: After purchasing the firm that dismissed Dilbert, Dogbert offers him a pointless interview for his former position and breezily admits to enjoying the embarrassment.

title: Silent Gary's Beard Decides Technology

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I invited Silent Gary to help us decide on a technology direction.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We think he's a genius because he has a beard and he never speaks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Gary, do you think we should use open source software for our support platform?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here it comes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's rubbing his beard and giving me creepy eye contact.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I detect a slight hint of disgust. It means Gary hates the idea!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes, it's all so obvious now. This is the worst idea in the history of mankind.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The meeting is over. Silent Gary has spoken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're actually a moron, aren't you?

transcript.speaker: Silent Gary
transcript.text: Don't ruin this for me.

situation: The Boss invites bearded, silent Gary to a meeting to help choose a technology direction, admitting they think he's a genius only because of his beard and silence. The Boss asks about open source software and reads Gary's beard-rubbing and eye contact as disgust, then declares the idea terrible and ends the meeting. Afterward Dilbert confronts Gary, who asks him not to ruin his good thing.
punchline: Silent Gary is undeserving of his reputation as a genius and knows it, so he begs Dilbert not to expose that his authority rests entirely on a beard and silence, which the Boss over-interprets.
summary: A manager treats a quiet bearded man's facial gestures as expert judgment, and the man privately pleads to keep the con going.

title: Dogbert's Snow-Filled Corporate Jet

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gas up the company jet, Flunky. I'm going skiing in Aspen.

transcript.speaker: Flunky
transcript.text: Using the corporate jet for a vacation sends the wrong message.

transcript.speaker: Flunky
transcript.text: And you can't ski in the summer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What message do forty planeloads of snow send?

situation: Dogbert, now the CEO, orders his flunky to fuel the company jet so he can go skiing in Aspen. The flunky objects that using the corporate jet for a vacation looks bad, and also that it's summer so there's no snow. Dogbert responds by asking what message it would send to fly in forty planeloads of snow.
punchline: Dogbert answers a concern about appearances by proposing something far more wasteful and extravagant, showing an executive who abuses company resources with no shame.
summary: A pampered canine chief executive brushes aside warnings about optics by planning to airlift entire jets of snow for his own ski trip.

title: Bank Too Broke For Eviction

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't afford to pay the mortgage this month.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's no reason to worry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I doubt your bank can afford postage to send you an eviction notice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That didn't make me worry less.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How are we set for firearms?

setting: Dilbert's living room, sitting on the couch
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he cannot pay his mortgage this month. Dogbert reassures him by saying the bank is probably too broke to even mail an eviction notice. When Dilbert is not comforted, Dogbert asks whether he has enough firearms.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance is really a jab at the failing banks of the financial crisis, and his follow-up question about firearms darkly implies that things could get violent and desperate.
summary: Dogbert tries to calm a mortgage-strapped Dilbert by joking that the bank is too poor to evict him, then makes things worse by asking about his weapons stockpile.

title: Wally Blames Ted for Missing Socks

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's time to stir the soup.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think Ted is stealing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You know how sometimes you can't find things in your office?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... Yes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That only happens on days when Ted has been in the building.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I think he was wearing a new sock the other day. Have you ever lost a sock?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's been in my house?!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Either that or your wife and Ted have some sort of arrangement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It makes my lack of accomplishments seem unimportant.

setting: Office hallway and doorway outside the Boss's office
situation: Wally announces he wants to stir the soup, then plants the idea in the Boss's head that Ted is a thief. He builds up the suspicion with missing office items and a lost sock, then suggests Ted may be having an affair with the Boss's wife. The enraged Boss storms off to confront Ted, while Wally enjoys the distraction from his own lack of work.
punchline: Wally deliberately stirs up a baseless scandal about Ted so that the Boss's anger at Ted makes Wally's own do-nothing performance look insignificant.
summary: By feeding the Boss escalating rumors about a coworker, a lazy employee gets everyone's attention pointed away from his own slacking.

title: Data Center Without Power Options

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new data center is complete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only wrinkle is that the power company won't give us the kilowatts we need.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: What are our options?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, we can run the servers without air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Until they melt into a toxic blob.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then we can turn the building into a museum that celebrates poor planning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we could all quit our jobs and eat bugs to survive.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Let's go with the toxic blob, but we need to call it something else.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Convergence!

setting: Conference room and office building exterior
situation: Dilbert presents a newly built data center, but the power company won't supply enough electricity to run it. When asked for options, he offers increasingly grim alternatives: overheating the servers into a toxic blob, turning the building into a museum of poor planning, or quitting and eating bugs. The managers pick the toxic blob but want to rebrand it with a buzzword.
punchline: Management is willing to accept an obviously disastrous outcome as long as it can be relabeled with a trendy buzzword like 'convergence'.
summary: Faced with a power-starved data center, managers happily choose a meltdown disaster so long as it gets a fancier name.

title: Pity Listen for a Useless Employee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see my job as giving you the information you need to make the right decision.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I see your job as e-mailing me links to web sites full of stale and incomplete information.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we go back to pretending I'm useful?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Sure. I'll give you a pity listen.

situation: Dilbert explains to a manager that his role is to supply the information needed for good decisions. The manager bluntly replies that Dilbert just emails links to outdated, incomplete websites. Deflated, Dilbert asks to return to the pretense that he is useful, and the manager agrees to offer a pity listen.
punchline: The manager insults Dilbert's contribution so bluntly that Dilbert begs to resume the polite fiction, and the manager grants only a condescending show of attention.
summary: A manager dismisses an engineer's research as worthless link-forwarding, then grudgingly pretends to listen out of sympathy.

title: Treated Like Diseased Livestock Awards

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want suggestions on how we can win one of those "best places to work" awards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could stop treating us like diseased livestock.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop being like that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you were livestock, you'd be eating grass.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My donut is made from wheat flour. Wheat is a grass.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you'd be living in a pen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Also known as a cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Livestock have no freedom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I go home now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Moo.

situation: The Boss asks his team for ideas on winning a "best places to work" award. Dilbert says management should stop treating employees like diseased livestock, which leads to a back-and-forth where the Boss tries to prove they aren't livestock and Dilbert counters each point. The Boss ends by refusing to let Dilbert go home.
punchline: After arguing that employees aren't livestock, the Boss denies Dilbert's request to go home, so Dilbert answers with a sarcastic "Moo," implying the Boss's own behavior proves the livestock comparison.
summary: A manager seeking a workplace award rebuts the claim that staff are treated like cattle, only to confirm it by keeping them penned in.

title: MBA Expert Doubts Own Credentials

transcript.speaker: Management Expert
transcript.text: I have an MBA from a top business school.

transcript.speaker: Management Expert
transcript.text: I'm a management expert because I read case studies about businesses that were in completely different situations.

transcript.speaker: Management Expert
transcript.text: Wait a minute. Why does that suddenly seem ridiculous?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will this take much longer?

situation: A man holding papers, apparently a new MBA-holding manager, stands over Dilbert at his desk and brags about his credentials. He explains that his expertise comes from reading case studies about unrelated businesses, then suddenly realizes how absurd that sounds. Dilbert, still working at his computer, impatiently asks if this will take much longer.
punchline: The MBA holder accidentally recognizes that his claimed management expertise is built on case studies of unrelated companies, which is ridiculous, while Dilbert just wants him to finish talking.
summary: A boastful business-school graduate talks himself into doubting his own qualifications while an unimpressed Dilbert waits for him to leave.

title: Lose-Lose With New Project Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Ellen, your new project manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you do a bad job, Ellen will be on you like a ton of bricks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And if you do a good job, she will feel threatened by your success and make it her mission to destroy you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just tell me I'm going to lose no matter what I do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you can't take the heat, stay out of the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And by kitchen I mean the entire job market.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: And the gene pool.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a bad feeling about this.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: Your anguish nourishes me!

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Ellen, his new project manager, and cheerfully explains that Dilbert will be punished whether he performs badly or well. When Dilbert objects, the Boss and Ellen respond with kitchen-heat clichés, extending the threat to the whole job market and the gene pool. Ellen then gloats that Dilbert's anguish feeds her.
punchline: Dilbert's new manager is openly a sadistic villain who thrives on his suffering, and he is trapped in a no-win situation with no escape, not even through quitting.
summary: A new supervisor is presented as an enemy who will crush her subordinate whether he fails or succeeds, and she relishes his misery.

title: Wally's Fake Eagerness Work-Avoidance Technique

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The successful work-avoider combines a fake eagerness to help with just a hint of likely failure.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, I need load calcs in an hour.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No problem! Unless my computer keeps crashing like it did all morning.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'll ask someone else.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I am begging you to let me help!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wow!

situation: Wally explains to Asok, who is holding a coffee mug, how to dodge work by sounding eager while hinting the task will probably fail. A coworker then asks Wally for load calculations within an hour, and Wally agrees with a warning about his crashing computer. The coworker gives up and goes elsewhere, and Wally loudly begs to be allowed to help while Asok looks on in amazement.
punchline: Wally's pretend enthusiasm is so well crafted that he gets out of the work entirely while appearing to be the most willing helper in the office.
summary: A veteran slacker demonstrates, live, how a show of enthusiasm plus a hint of doom lets him escape an assignment while his young colleague watches in awe.

title: Hiring a Warlord for Economic Forecast

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm hiring you because you're huge and scary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our economic forecast calls for the emergence of warlords in 2010.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you ever pillaged?

transcript.speaker: Interviewee
transcript.text: No, I just go on fake interviews to scope out targets.

setting: The Boss's office, during a job interview
situation: The Boss interviews a large, intimidating candidate and says he is hiring him for his scary appearance, because the company's economic forecast predicts warlords will emerge in 2010. He asks whether the candidate has ever pillaged. The candidate admits he only attends fake interviews to scope out targets to rob.
punchline: The Boss's absurd plan to hire a warlord is matched by a candidate who is actually a predator, using job interviews to case companies he intends to rob.
summary: A boss recruits an intimidating man to prepare for a predicted age of warlords, only to find out the applicant treats interviews as a way to pick out places to plunder.

title: Dogbert's Ponzi Mortgage Bonus Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our new financial product is a hybrid of risky mortgage loans and a Ponzi scheme.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll cover our bad loan losses with our profits from making even worse loans.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll need some wagging room while I tell you how this ties into my bonus structure.

situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, presents a new financial product to executives seated around a conference table. He explains it is a mix of risky mortgages and a Ponzi scheme, where losses on bad loans are covered by profits from even worse loans. He then asks for room to wag his tail as he explains how it boosts his bonus.
punchline: The CEO's scheme is openly fraudulent and self-serving, and his excitement over his own bonus (a wagging tail) shows he cares only about personal payout, mirroring the financial crisis.
summary: A dog in charge of a company cheerfully unveils a doomed lending racket and gets so excited about his own payout that his tail needs space to wag.

title: Elbonia's Recession Cuts Pig Fetching

transcript.speaker: Elbonian man
transcript.text: The big countries are having economic problems. Experts say it will soon affect Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian man
transcript.text: We'll need to cut back on some of our luxury expenses.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian man
transcript.text: You can stop practicing your fetching.

transcript.speaker: Pig
transcript.text: Should I ask why?

setting: Muddy Elbonian village outside a mud hut
situation: An Elbonian man reads a newspaper and tells his companion that a global economic downturn will soon hit Elbonia, so they must trim luxury expenses. He then turns to the family pig, which has been practicing fetching a stick like a pet dog, and tells it to stop. The pig, holding the stick, asks whether it should bother asking why.
punchline: The pig is being kept as a pampered pet rather than livestock, and ending its fetching practice implies the 'luxury expense' being cut cuts the pig's feeding or its life, which the pig darkly suspects.
summary: Hard times in Elbonia mean a pet pig's trick training is no longer affordable, and the pig gloomily senses what comes next.

title: Delegating Strategy Until Failure Arrives

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll execute our strategy in the usual way.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The powerful will delegate to the untalented until failure is achieved.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will that take?
