transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We just finished.

situation: Dogbert, as CEO, tells the Pointy-Haired Boss that the company's strategy is executed by having the powerful delegate to the untalented until failure results. The Boss asks how long that will take, and Dogbert replies that it has already been completed.
punchline: Failure from delegating to incompetent people is so quick and inevitable that the strategy was already executed by the time the Boss asked about it.
summary: A canine chief executive explains his management method of handing work to the incompetent, and it turns out the inevitable collapse has already happened.

title: Therapist Multitasks During Therapy Session

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I multitask during conference calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it wrong to value my own productivity over the inane babbling of others?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Buy bread... pickles... light bulbs...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello?

situation: Dilbert lies on a couch and confesses to his therapist that he multitasks during conference calls. He asks whether it's wrong to value his own productivity over other people's pointless chatter. The therapist, who has been tuning him out and thinking about her shopping list, doesn't respond.
punchline: The therapist does to Dilbert exactly what he admits doing on conference calls, ignoring him to multitask while he talks.
summary: A man confessing his habit of tuning out meetings discovers his own therapist is tuning him out in the same way.

title: Budget Is Whatever You Ask For

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much will it cost to develop our next generation product?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will cost whatever you put in the budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much should I put in the budget?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ask for the biggest number you think will get approved.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we get a lot of money we can build something great.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we don't get much money we can build something lame, and compensate for the lack of quality by lying more vigorously than usual.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll aim low so I don't get yelled at during the executive budget meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I remember a time when this sort of thing would haunt me.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how much the next generation product will cost to develop, and Dilbert says it costs whatever is put in the budget. Dilbert advises asking for the biggest number that will be approved, explaining how the project will go either way, but the Boss decides to ask for a low amount to avoid being yelled at. Dilbert is left reflecting on how this kind of thing used to bother him.
punchline: Dilbert's sound advice is ignored because the Boss prioritizes avoiding criticism over project success, and Dilbert has become so jaded that he no longer cares about the consequences.
summary: A manager picks the safest budget request instead of the smartest one, and his weary engineer realizes he has stopped being bothered by such foolishness.

title: Bonus Depends on Actual Pandemic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I do a great job with the pandemic contingency planning, can I have a bonus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I won't know if you did a great job unless we actually have a pandemic emergency.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... if there IS a pandemic, I might get a bonus?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like where this is heading.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for a bonus if he does a great job on the company's pandemic contingency planning. The Boss replies that he can't judge the quality of the plan unless a real pandemic occurs. Dilbert points out that this means he'd only get paid if a pandemic happens, and the Boss realizes the logic leads somewhere uncomfortable.
punchline: The Boss's own reasoning ties Dilbert's bonus to a real pandemic, giving Dilbert a financial incentive to hope for a disaster.
summary: A manager's insistence on judging a disaster plan only after a real disaster accidentally rewards an employee for wishing one into existence.

title: Inheriting Carl's Deadly Server Job

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to take over Carl's function.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's already gone, but Ted can train you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted was sometimes in the general vicinity when Carl did the function.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Doom

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Try clicking on the red... No, blue... No, red button.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh. Okay. I didn't expect that.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Beep

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Now you either have to erase all of the servers or activate the fire suppression system in the clean room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I click "Cancel"?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: That's what killed Carl.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Anyway, that's all I know. The rest is just common sense.

setting: Office cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to take over the duties of Carl, who is no longer around, and says Ted will train him. Ted's only qualification is having been near Carl while he worked, and his guesswork instructions lead Dilbert into a dangerous choice between erasing all servers or triggering the fire suppression system. Ted casually reveals that clicking Cancel is what killed Carl.
punchline: The knowledge transfer is so poor and the system so dangerous that the previous employee's death is treated as a minor tip, and the trainer ends by claiming the rest is just common sense.
summary: A hapless coworker with no real expertise coaches Dilbert through a lethal software task that already claimed his predecessor.

title: Dogbert's Corpse CEO Placeholder

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm stepping down as CEO because I already milked all of the cash out of this dying cow.

transcript.speaker: Cow
transcript.text: Moo!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My replacement is a dried-up corpse. But don't worry; he's just a placeholder until a new CEO can be found.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The faint breeze is blowing away his head.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should probably hurry.

setting: Company podium during a CEO announcement
situation: Dogbert, acting as outgoing CEO, announces at a podium that he is stepping down after draining the company of its cash. He introduces his successor, a dried-up corpse standing beside him, as a temporary placeholder. By the end, a faint breeze is blowing the corpse's head away as the Boss watches.
punchline: The departing CEO has bled the company dry and leaves a literal corpse in charge, mocking executives who cash out and abandon failing companies while the board scrambles for a successor.
summary: After draining a failing company, its outgoing leader props up a decaying corpse as stand-in boss while it crumbles to dust.

title: Wally's Seven Weeks of Next Week

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, are you done with your project yet?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll be done next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've said, "next week" for seven weeks in a row. What makes you think I'm going to believe it this time?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The first six times?

situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks Wally whether his project is finished, and Wally says it will be done next week. The Boss points out that Wally has said this for seven weeks straight and asks why he should believe it now. Wally replies by noting that the Boss apparently believed it the first six times.
punchline: Wally turns the Boss's challenge around by pointing out that the Boss was gullible enough to accept the same empty promise six times already.
summary: A manager confronts a chronic procrastinator about a project that is perpetually due the following week, and gets a deadpan reply that exposes his own credulity.

title: Insulting Newsletter Profile Interview Request

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: For the company newsletter profile, I need to know how you rose from being an ignorant baboon to an overpaid speed bump.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And make it not boring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not an overpaid speed bump!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My fact-checker will need to see your pay stub.

setting: Office desk, with an exterior shot of the office building in the middle panel
situation: A newsletter writer sits across from The Boss and asks him to explain how he rose from an ignorant baboon to an overpaid speed bump. The Boss angrily protests that he is not an overpaid speed bump. The writer calmly responds that a fact-checker will need to see his pay stub.
punchline: The writer's insult is delivered as a routine interview question, and when the Boss denies being overpaid, she implies his pay stub will prove it.
summary: A reporter preparing a flattering-sounding profile instead insults a manager's competence and salary, then threatens to verify his paycheck.

title: Dilbert Seeks Motherly Advice, Gets Insults

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilmom

transcript.text: How's work, Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My investments are worthless and my odds of finding a suitable mate are nearing zero.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My life has no meaning, no joy and no hope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have any motherly advice?

transcript.speaker: Dilmom
transcript.text: Shake it off, you big wuss.

transcript.speaker: Dilmom
transcript.text: And you can pass that wisdom to the grandchildren you won't be having.

transcript.speaker: Dilmom
transcript.text: You're not good at this.

transcript.speaker: Dilmom
transcript.text: Eat broccoli. Whatever.

setting: Outdoor walk along a path in a hilly neighborhood
situation: Dilbert's mother asks how work is going while the two take a walk. Dilbert unloads a long list of woes about his overworked job, pay cut, worthless investments, poor romantic prospects and meaningless life, then asks her for motherly advice. She responds with insults and a barbed remark about his lack of children, then offers a throwaway tip.
punchline: Dilbert's mother answers his heartfelt despair with a mocking putdown and a half-hearted 'eat broccoli, whatever' instead of any comfort, showing even his own mom thinks he is hopeless.
summary: After Dilbert pours out all his misery on a stroll, his unsympathetic mother tells him to toughen up and mocks his bleak future.

title: Arrogant Coworker With Huge Forehead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired an arrogant guy with a huge forehead. He's on your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great. Everything this guy says will seem more annoying than usual because of his huge forehead!

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: I keep a wine glass with me at all times. I'm a foodie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Case in point!

situation: The Boss introduces a newly hired arrogant coworker with a very large forehead who will be joining Dilbert's project. Dilbert complains that the forehead will make everything the man says even more irritating. The new hire then proves Dilbert right by announcing he carries a wine glass everywhere because he's a foodie.
punchline: The new hire's pretentious boast instantly confirms Dilbert's prediction, with Dilbert's "case in point" showing that the arrogance is just as annoying as feared.
summary: Dilbert dreads working with a pompous new teammate and is immediately vindicated when the man brags about his wine-glass habit.

title: Coworker Turns Into Tree From Recession

transcript.speaker: Tree
transcript.text: The economy scared me so bad that I turned into a tree.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Tree
transcript.text: It's the same principle as a blind person developing better hearing.

transcript.speaker: Tree
transcript.text: When you're stealing cat food from convenience stores, I'll be living large on rainwater.

situation: A coworker sits across a table from Dilbert and announces that fear of the bad economy literally transformed him into a tree. He explains this as an adaptation, like a blind person gaining better hearing. He then boasts that while others are reduced to stealing cat food, he will thrive on rainwater.
punchline: The coworker's absurd self-transformation is presented as a smart survival strategy for a recession, mocking how people scramble to adapt to a collapsing economy while implying everyone else will end up destitute.
summary: A man who became a tree out of economic panic smugly claims his new biology will keep him comfortable while everyone else is reduced to scavenging.

title: Incorporating In Another Dimension

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.text: We're paying too much taxes. Bring me a physicist and a tax attorney.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I want to incorporate in another dimension. Make it happen.

transcript.speaker: Physicist
transcript.text: Somewhere in the multiverse it's already done.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like you. The lawyer guy is fired.

situation: Dogbert, now CEO, summons a physicist and a tax attorney because he thinks the company pays too much tax. He orders them to incorporate the company in another dimension. The physicist answers that it has already happened somewhere in the multiverse, and Dogbert fires the lawyer in favor of the physicist.
punchline: The physicist avoids the impossible task by claiming it's already true in some parallel universe, which pleases Dogbert enough to fire the lawyer who would have had to give a realistic answer.
summary: A scheming canine executive wants to dodge taxes by relocating his company to a different universe, and rewards the scientist who dodges the question with a clever non-answer.

title: Employee Engagement Means Working Harder

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need more of what the management experts call "employee engagement."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know the details, but it has something to do with you idiots working harder for the same pay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is anything different on your end?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I'm supposed to be happier.

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that they need more 'employee engagement,' admitting he doesn't know the details except that it means employees working harder for the same pay. Dilbert asks what will change for management, and the Boss replies that he is supposed to be happier.
punchline: Employee engagement is revealed to be a euphemism where employees give more effort for no extra reward while management is the only one expected to benefit.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits that a trendy workplace buzzword really just means extracting more labor for no extra money, with only himself expected to feel better.

title: Meeting Exists to Remind Boss Hatred

transcript.text: Puce

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cerulean

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ecru

setting: Office meeting area and an exterior view of an office building
situation: At a stand-up meeting, the Boss announces that all status reports must be given as red, yellow, or green. The second panel shows the building with other color names (mauve, puce, cerulean, ecru) pointing at it, hinting at the attendees' silent reactions. The Boss later stands alone with a coffee mug, with Catbert nearby, and muses that meetings serve mainly to remind him how much he hates them.
punchline: The Boss, who calls and enforces these pointless meetings, admits their only real purpose is to remind him how much he hates meetings.
summary: After imposing a color-coded reporting rule, a manager sheepishly concedes that meetings only serve to make him despise them.

title: Boss Forgets Four Questions

transcript.text: ...And those are the four things I need you to ask our VP of Marketing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Got it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should write them down.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll remember.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have a lot on your mind. A little note might be a good idea.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How hard is it to remember three things?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sheesh!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Four things! There are four questions!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right, right. There's the one about the battery, and the other two.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are four questions! Four, four, four!!! And none of them are about a battery!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that day

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Should the new software have a battery?

transcript.speaker: VP of Marketing
transcript.text: How would I know?

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's desk, with an exterior building shot
situation: Dilbert gives the Boss a list of four questions to ask the VP of Marketing. The Boss refuses to write them down, insists he'll remember, and then miscounts them as three. Dilbert yells outside the building in frustration, and later the Boss asks the VP a nonsensical question about a battery.
punchline: The Boss was so sure he didn't need notes that he forgot nearly everything and asks the one irrelevant question Dilbert never gave him, making himself look foolish.
summary: A manager who brushes off advice to take notes botches a simple errand and embarrasses himself in front of an executive.

title: Mountain of Facts, Thimble of Knowledge

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's the mountain of facts that support my recommended technology strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And here's a tiny thimble that holds everything you know about technology. Maybe you could...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Leaders don't like it when you suggest they wear the thimble of knowledge like a little hat.

situation: Dilbert brings the Boss a huge stack of papers supporting his technology strategy recommendation. He then holds up a tiny thimble representing everything the Boss knows about technology and starts to suggest the Boss put it to use. In the last panel, Dilbert is walking away from the office, admitting that leaders resent this kind of suggestion.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic suggestion that the Boss wear his tiny thimble of technology knowledge as a hat reveals how little the Boss knows, and how badly leaders take being told so.
summary: An engineer contrasts a towering pile of evidence with the pitiful scrap of expertise his manager possesses, then ruefully reflects that insulting executives is a poor career move.

title: Inoculating the CEO Against Layoffs

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll be right back after I inoculate our CEO.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you ever decide to reduce our layers of management, Carl is worthless and he thinks your kids look like the director of sales.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That should buy me a few months.

characters: Carl's coworker at the reception desk
setting: Corporate office and the CEO's office
situation: Catbert, the pointy-haired evil HR director, tells a woman at a desk that he'll be right back after he 'inoculates' the CEO. He then visits the CEO and slanders a coworker named Carl while insinuating that the CEO's kids resemble the director of sales. Walking away, he reflects that this will protect his own job for a few months.
punchline: Catbert's 'inoculation' is really a preemptive smear campaign: by planting poisonous gossip about others, he secures his own position when layoffs come.
summary: A scheming HR executive pre-emptively poisons the CEO's opinion of his colleagues so he'll be spared when management layers get cut.

title: Alice Calls Ted a Drama Queen

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'd like you to work with Ted on this project.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ted's a drama queen. Working with him will just slow me down.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Hello? Human resources? Alice is being a bully.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And so it begins.

situation: The Boss asks Alice to partner with Ted on a project. Alice bluntly says Ted is a drama queen who will slow her down. Ted overhears and immediately phones Human Resources to report Alice as a bully, while Alice buries her face in her hands.
punchline: Alice's accusation that Ted is overly dramatic is instantly proven true when he makes a melodramatic bullying complaint to HR over a single remark.
summary: A coworker labelled overly theatrical promptly validates the label by escalating a mild insult into an official grievance.

title: Posting Jobs Already Filled

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're hired, but company policy requires me to post the job opening internally before it's official.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Are you saying your company policy requires you to lie to employees and give them false hope?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: That's cruel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In six months you'll wish you had some false hope too.

situation: The Boss tells a job candidate he is hired, but explains that company policy forces him to post the opening internally first. The candidate points out that this means deceiving current employees with false hope. The Boss cheerfully confirms it and warns the new hire that he will soon wish he had some false hope himself.
punchline: The Boss admits the company's hiring policy is a deliberate deception of employees, then implies working there will be so miserable the new hire will envy those still hoping.
summary: A manager hiring someone on the spot admits that an internal job posting is a sham, then predicts the newcomer will soon be too miserable to feel hopeful.

title: Do It My Way, Then Feel Guilty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, rummage through the piles on my desk and find yourself something to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Afterward, chastise yourself for not doing it the way I would have.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Even if you would have done it wrong?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Especially then. No one likes a show-off.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Asok to dig through the piles on his desk and pick himself a task. He adds that Asok should then scold himself for not doing it the Boss's way. When Asok asks about the case where the Boss's way would be wrong, the Boss says that is exactly when he should feel bad, since no one likes a show-off.
punchline: The Boss demands that Asok feel guilty for not matching his method, and insists this applies even more when the Boss's method is flawed, because outperforming him would be showing off.
summary: A manager hands off his paperwork and insists his underling feel ashamed for not copying his approach, even a mistaken one.

title: Overqualified Temp Seeks Trivial Tasks

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Overqualified temp

transcript.speaker: Overqualified Temp
transcript.text: I have completed all of my menial assignments.

transcript.speaker: Overqualified Temp
transcript.text: Do you have any more trivial tasks to crush my sense of self-worth?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've always wondered how many ceiling tiles are in the men's restroom.

transcript.speaker: Overqualified Temp
transcript.text: Die! Die! Die!

situation: A temp worker tells the boss she has finished all her menial assignments and sarcastically asks for more tasks that will crush her self-worth. The boss obliviously assigns her to count the ceiling tiles in the men's restroom. She silently seethes, with a thought bubble wishing death upon him.
punchline: The boss takes her sarcastic request literally and hands her an even more pointless task, provoking her murderous inner thoughts.
summary: A talented temp bitterly asks for demeaning busywork and her clueless manager happily obliges with something even more absurd.

title: Carol Writes Boss's Insulting Thought

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, send an e-mail to the department with my leadership thought of the day.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: What is it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm busy. Make up something.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: "That which doesn't kill you makes you stronger. So please slap me in my fat, bald head."

setting: Office cubicle area outside Carol's desk
situation: The Boss tells his assistant Carol to email the department his leadership thought of the day. When she asks what it is, he says he is busy and tells her to invent something. Carol then composes a quote that invites everyone to slap the Boss on his fat, bald head.
punchline: Given free rein to write the Boss's message, Carol passive-aggressively turns it into an insult that invites the whole department to slap him.
summary: An assistant seizes the chance to get even when her lazy manager lets her invent his inspirational email.

title: Wally Steals Company Electricity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's on your back?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's a battery.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I recharge it at work with company electricity, then I use it at night to power my home appliances.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If they cut my benefits one more time, I'll make a play for their water too.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert notices Wally carrying a large battery pack strapped to his back while they get coffee. Wally explains that he charges it at the office and uses it to run his appliances at home. He adds that he may start taking the company's water too if his benefits are cut again.
punchline: Wally treats stealing from his employer as fair compensation for benefit cuts, and he is already planning to escalate to taking the water.
summary: A battery on his back lets Wally quietly take his employer's power home, and he hints that the plumbing could be next.

title: Alice Denies Punching Computer

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My computer kept locking up, so I had to let off some steam.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't fix your computer by punching it!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why would I punch my computer? That's crazy.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice?

situation: Alice, carrying a smashed computer monitor, tells the Boss that her computer kept locking up so she had to let off some steam. The Boss scolds her for trying to fix a computer by punching it. Alice then claims she would never punch her own computer, and Asok, confused by the contradiction, says her name.
punchline: Alice cheerfully denies punching her computer while literally holding the broken monitor she just destroyed, contradicting what she said a moment earlier.
summary: A frustrated employee carries her battered monitor yet insists she would never dream of hitting it.

title: Employee Begs to Work Unpaid

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until the economy improves, we are instituting a mandatory week off every quarter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: At least you'll have more time with your families.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Nooo!!! Not my family!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Problems at home?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: May I please work without pay?

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces a mandatory unpaid week off each quarter as a cost-cutting measure and suggests employees will enjoy time with their families. One coworker panics and screams in protest. When the Boss asks if he has problems at home, he begs to be allowed to work for free instead.
punchline: The employee finds home life so unbearable that he would rather work for nothing than spend time with his family, turning the boss's supposed perk into a nightmare.
summary: Told that forced time off will bring him closer to his family, a worker would rather labor for free than go home.

title: Timing Retirement With Global Warming

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Retirement planning in a bad economy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Retirement planning is all about timing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm planning to die from global warming on the same day I run out of money.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's one more advantage of being frail. I figure an hour without sunscreen ought to do the trick.

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Wally and Dilbert stand by the coffee machine holding mugs while Wally explains his retirement strategy. He says he plans to die of global warming just as his money runs out, and adds that his frailty means an hour in the sun without sunscreen should do it. Dilbert listens silently.
punchline: Wally's idea of retirement planning is to time his death to coincide with running out of savings, and he deadpans that his frail body will make it easy.
summary: A coffee-break chat turns dark as a colleague describes engineering his own demise to match his empty retirement fund.

title: Boss Offers Bribe While Confessing Crimes

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: This week I sold company secrets, did some insider trading, and took kickbacks from vendors.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'll give you a taste if you look the other way.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Zip!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's unsettling.

situation: At a meeting table, a bald coworker in a green sweater vest openly boasts to Dilbert and the Boss about selling company secrets, insider trading and taking vendor kickbacks. He then offers them a cut of the proceeds if they look the other way. The Boss instantly spins his chair away to avoid seeing anything, while Dilbert is left disturbed.
punchline: The Boss is so eager to be bribed and stay willfully ignorant that he turns his back instantly, which Dilbert finds unsettling.
summary: A colleague brags about a week of corporate crimes and offers a share of the loot, and the boss swiftly swivels away to avoid seeing it.

title: Honest Advice Gets Wally Beaten Up

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have no project of my own, so I wander the cubicles offering unsolicited advice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Speaking of which, you should put a little extra thought into your cooling system design. It looks monkey-made.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm discovering that honest and helpful are a bad combination.

situation: At a meeting, Wally explains that since he has no project of his own he wanders the cubicles giving unsolicited advice. He then tells a coworker that their cooling system design looks monkey-made. In the last panel he is bandaged and lying on the table with his feet in the air, concluding that being honest and helpful together is a bad idea.
punchline: Wally's blunt, insulting 'advice' gets him beaten up, and he blames the combination of honesty and helpfulness rather than his own rudeness.
summary: After bluntly insulting a coworker's design while roaming the office with nothing to do, a bandaged Wally learns that candor has consequences.

title: Productivity Software Crashes, Wally Wants Pre-Industrial Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My productivity software turned on me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It keeps crashing my computer. But that's okay because I don't need a computer to do my job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you have any assignments that are sort of pre-industrial?

setting: Office, in front of the Boss
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the Boss that his productivity software keeps crashing his computer. He claims this is fine because he doesn't need a computer to do his job. He then asks for assignments that are pre-industrial, so he can avoid technology entirely.
punchline: Wally turns a software failure into an excuse to dodge real work, asking for jobs from before the industrial era that need no equipment at all.
summary: A coffee-clutching employee uses his glitchy software as a pretext to request work that predates machinery altogether.

title: Dogbert's Unemployment Tough Love

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's the worst part about you being unemployed?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it the risk of starvation, the inability to date, or the feeling of being utterly worthless?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far the worst part is this conversation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wait 'til you hear my tough love speech.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside, sitting on rocks
situation: Dilbert, unemployed, sits on a rock outdoors while Dogbert asks him what the worst part of joblessness is. Dogbert lists grim options like starvation, being unable to date, and feeling worthless. Dilbert replies that the conversation itself is the worst part, and Dogbert says his tough love speech is still to come.
punchline: Dogbert's supposedly sympathetic questions are actually insulting, and he threatens that his upcoming 'tough love' speech will be even more unpleasant.
summary: An unemployed Dilbert is badgered by Dogbert's gloomy questions and warned that an even harsher pep talk is coming.

file: 2009/2009-01-02_fear_honesty_panic_reality_worried_first recession_hopes and dreams dashed_yank band aid.gif
title: Recession Advice: Abandon Your Dreams

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: This is my first recession. How worried should I be?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll be fine as long as you don't have any hopes and dreams.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But I still have them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's time to yank off that band-aid.

situation: Asok, a young intern, nervously asks Wally how worried he should be about his first recession. Wally, sipping coffee at his desk, tells him he'll be fine only if he has no hopes and dreams. When Asok admits he still has them, Wally bluntly advises him to get rid of them quickly, like yanking off a band-aid.
punchline: Wally's cynical survival advice is that the way to endure a recession is to kill your own hopes and dreams immediately, and he sees this as a kindness.
summary: A worried young employee seeks reassurance about the economic downturn and instead gets a jaded coworker's instruction to crush his optimism fast.

title: Paper Cups, Green Image

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We replaced our Styrofoam cups with paper cups, but it's not so clear that it helps the planet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We didn't do it to help the planet. We did it to look like the sort of company that cares about that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. In that case it's working great.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as you stop whining.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that switching from Styrofoam to paper cups may not actually help the environment. The Boss admits the change was never about the planet and was meant only to make the company look environmentally responsible. Dilbert sarcastically says it's working, and the Boss says it will keep working only if Dilbert stops complaining.
punchline: The company's green initiative is purely about appearances, and the Boss's own image campaign is only successful as long as employees stop pointing out that it's superficial.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits an eco-friendly office policy exists only to create a good impression, then tells the employee who noticed to stay quiet.

title: Catching Up: Unknowable or Stupid

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If we work day and night, we can match our competitor's features within twelve months.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we catching up to where they will be in a year, which is unknowable, or where they are now, which is stupid?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well played.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got the next one!

situation: The Boss points to a slide showing an arrow from 'Us' to 'Them' and announces that overtime will let the company match a competitor's features in twelve months. Dilbert raises his hand and points out the flaw in the plan: the target is either unknowable or already outdated. Wally compliments the retort and Alice eagerly claims the next chance to challenge the Boss.
punchline: Dilbert exposes the logical flaw in the Boss's catch-up strategy with a perfectly worded dilemma, and his coworkers treat tearing down the Boss's ideas like a game.
summary: A manager's plan to chase a rival's features gets dismantled by a sharp two-option retort, and the team starts competing to deliver the next takedown.

title: Crime Proceeds in Mutual Fund

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I retired from my life of corporate crime and put all of my illicit earnings in a mutual fund.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know the mutual fund is legitimate?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We got all of the money back?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We?

setting: Office lunch table, then Dogbert's office
situation: Wally brags to Dilbert and a coworker over lunch that he has retired from corporate crime and put all his illicit earnings into a mutual fund. Dilbert asks how he knows the fund is legitimate, which makes Wally realise he never checked. In the last panel the Boss reports to Dogbert that they recovered all the money, and Dogbert pointedly questions the word 'we'.
punchline: Dogbert's fund is evidently a scam that fleeces criminals, and Dogbert dismisses the Boss's claim of partnership, implying the stolen money was never going back to Wally.
summary: A retired corporate crook entrusts his ill-gotten gains to a mutual fund that turns out to be run by a scheming dog.

title: Billion Dollar Idea, Billion Years

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Once again, Wally, you have accomplished nothing this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What about that billion dollar cost-saving idea I had?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your idea would only save one dollar per year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Exactly. In a billion years, that's a billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company won't be in business that long.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why not? Do you know something I don't know?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So, what kind of raise are we looking at here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He gave you a billion dollar raise?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's not as good as it sounds.

setting: Boss's office and the office break area
situation: The Boss gives Wally a performance review, criticizing him for accomplishing nothing. Wally defends himself with a cost-saving idea that saves one dollar a year, which he claims adds up to a billion over a billion years. After the Boss points out the company won't last that long, Wally asks about his raise and later tells Dilbert it isn't as good as it sounds.
punchline: Wally apparently got a billion dollar raise, but like his savings idea it pays out at a trivial rate, so the headline number is meaningless.
summary: A lazy employee justifies his worth with a savings plan that only pays off over geological time, then gets a raise with similarly hollow math.
keywords: not as good as it sounds

title: CEO Cuts R&D for Stock Payout

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm nearing retirement, so fire the research and development group.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The cost cutting will goose my stock options so I can cash out before the death spiral.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please don't make the noise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Too late! Cha-ching!

setting: CEO's office in a corporate headquarters
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, orders the research and development group fired because he is close to retiring. He explains that the cost cutting will inflate his stock options so he can cash out before the company declines. The Boss asks him not to make the cash register noise, but Dogbert cheers 'cha-ching' anyway.
punchline: Dogbert openly admits he is gutting the company's future for a personal payout, and gleefully makes the cash register noise the Boss begged him not to make.
summary: A soon-to-retire canine chief executive happily sacrifices his firm's innovation department to boost his own stock windfall before the company collapses.

title: Greatest Generation Versus Bag Generation

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Your age group has destroyed the hopes of my entire generation.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Your parents were the so-called "Greatest Generation." I wonder what your age group will be known as.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: I'll bet it includes the word "bag."

setting: Office, near the Boss's office doorway
situation: A young employee holding a coffee mug confronts the Boss, blaming his age group for ruining the younger generation's prospects. He points out that the Boss's parents were called the Greatest Generation and wonders what the Boss's generation will be called. As he leaves, he predicts the label will include the word "bag", while the Boss sits at his desk looking unimpressed.
punchline: The young employee implies the Boss's generation will be remembered with an insulting name like "baggers" or a "bag of..." insult, a sarcastic contrast to the flattering "Greatest Generation" label.
summary: A junior worker blames the boss's age group for wrecking his generation's future, then snidely guesses at the unflattering nickname history will give them.

title: Delegating Work Until It Dies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to take care of... um...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...whatever is on the top of my pile.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is a job for marketing, not engineering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give it to the Director of Marketing and ask him to assign it to someone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you're delegating to me to pass this off to someone else, who will delegate it to someone else.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With each handoff, the sense of urgency will diminish until the likelihood of completion approaches zero.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could save the company money by crumpling up this document and throwing it away right now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This feels wrong.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try using more wrist.

situation: The Boss can't remember what task he wants done and hands Dilbert whatever is on top of his pile. Dilbert points out it belongs to marketing and is told to pass it to the Director of Marketing to assign to someone. Dilbert explains that each handoff erodes urgency until nothing gets done, then coaches the Boss to crumple the document and throw it away himself.
punchline: Since delegating a task through layers of management guarantees it will never be completed, Dilbert sarcastically suggests the cheaper option of simply trashing it, and even coaches the Boss on his crumpling technique.
summary: A manager who doesn't even know what he's assigning gets a lesson in how passing work down the chain is just a slow way of throwing it out.

title: CEO Takes Credit for Economy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Consumer confidence is up, and that means more people will buy our products.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm off to make random management changes so I can take credit for the improved economy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's working?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sales are up!

situation: An executive reports to CEO Dogbert that consumer confidence is rising, which should boost sales. Dogbert announces he will make random management changes so he can claim credit for the improving economy. Later, Dilbert asks if the changes are working, and Catbert, dressed in a suit, reports that sales are up.
punchline: The CEO deliberately makes meaningless changes just before an economic upswing so he can take credit for success he did not cause.
summary: A canine chief executive plans pointless shake-ups to claim credit for a recovering economy that was going to lift sales anyway.

title: Boss Delegates to Wrong Person

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you'll be acting manager next week while I'm on vacation

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't. I'll be in a training class all week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, you'll. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be at a customer site all week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol. . .

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll be getting my tubes tied.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok. . .

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm going to my grandmother's funeral in India.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes? Is there something you need me to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Attend a funeral in India. Tell everyone you're Asok and you had a horrible accident.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell them the acid destroyed your hair and your personality.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That took an ugly turn.

situation: The Boss tries to find someone to act as manager while he is on vacation, but Alice, Dilbert, Carol and Asok each have an excuse. Wally, who hasn't been asked and offers to help, is instead sent to impersonate Asok at a funeral in India so Asok can avoid it. The Boss even coaches Wally on a cover story about a horrible accident.
punchline: Wally's offer to help gets him assigned to attend Asok's grandmother's funeral in India while pretending to be Asok with a disfiguring acid accident, and Asok is horrified by how cruel the cover story gets.
summary: After everyone dodges a request to cover for the vacationing manager, the one coworker who volunteers is sent abroad to impersonate a colleague at a funeral.

title: Dilbert's Psychopathic Hobo TV Options

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, we can watch a cooking show and imagine what delicious food tastes like...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or an action movie so we can imagine killing people while cracking jokes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I can reword those choices to make us feel less like psychopathic hobos.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please do.

setting: Dilbert's living room couch at home
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch with Dogbert, holding the remote and deciding what to watch. He lists the options as imagining the taste of food from a cooking show or imagining killing people while joking in an action movie. He then offers to reword the choices to sound less disturbing, and Dogbert urges him to.
punchline: Dilbert's honest description of his TV choices makes them sound pathetic and sinister, and Dogbert dryly agrees he should find a nicer way to phrase them.
summary: A man and his dog size up their television options and realize that describing them honestly makes them sound like unhinged drifters.

title: Salesman's Money Hat Enrages Alice

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Thanks to a new law, every customer in my sales territory needed to upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Now I wear a hat made of money. The funny thing is that I'm not even a good salesman.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Next week, the donuts are on me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Die! Die! Die!

situation: At a meeting, a salesman with a money-bag hat on his head explains that a new law forced all his customers to upgrade, so his big sales numbers had nothing to do with skill. He admits he isn't a good salesman and offers to buy donuts. Alice, seething throughout, finally screams "Die!" at him.
punchline: The salesman's windfall success came from a law rather than talent, and his smug offer of donuts pushes the hard-working, resentful Alice into a murderous rage.
summary: A lucky salesman flaunts his undeserved windfall at a meeting, and his casual generosity sends a furious coworker over the edge.

title: Lock Your Desk Against Coworkers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Welcome to your first day on the job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Always lock your desk at night because many of your coworkers are crooks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the ones that have eyes like this got hired before we did drug testing.

situation: The Boss welcomes a new employee on his first day and shakes his hand. He then warns the newcomer to lock his desk every night because so many coworkers are thieves. He adds that the ones with wild, bloodshot eyes were hired before the company began drug testing.
punchline: The Boss's orientation advice reveals that the company's workforce includes thieves and drug users, and the company's only fix is a drug test it started only after hiring them.
summary: A manager greets a rookie with a warm handshake, then casually cautions him that his colleagues are thieves and that the glassy-eyed ones predate the company's drug screening.

title: Worthlessness Becomes A Lifestyle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm tense because the company is downsizing and I have no project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Being worthless at work is only hard for the first ten years. After that, it's a lifestyle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't say I was worthless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now you're making me nostalgic for my old denial phase.

setting: Office hallway near a cubicle wall
situation: Dilbert tells Wally he is anxious about layoffs because he currently has no project. Wally, holding his coffee mug, cheerfully reassures him that being worthless at work only feels bad for the first decade, after which it becomes a lifestyle. Dilbert protests that he never called himself worthless, and Wally says that makes him miss his own denial phase.
punchline: Wally treats his own long-standing uselessness as a comfortable way of life, and his 'comforting' advice implies Dilbert is worthless too, while mocking Dilbert's denial about it.
summary: A worried colleague gets consoling advice from a veteran slacker who has fully embraced having no useful work to do.

title: Your Skills Will Become Outdated

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: There is a huge disconnect between my enormous technical knowledge and the trivial tasks you assign to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's a temporary situation, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Okay, good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Eventually your technical skills will become outdated

situation: Asok complains to The Boss that his advanced technical knowledge is wasted on trivial assignments. The Boss says the mismatch is only temporary, and Asok is relieved. The Boss then explains that the mismatch will end because Asok's skills will become obsolete.
punchline: The mismatch will indeed end, but only because Asok's technical skills will decay from lack of use, not because he will be given more meaningful work.
summary: A boss promises that an underused engineer's mismatch will end, then reveals the cause will be his expertise going stale.

title: Finance Troll Denies Flight, Prescribes Hitchhiking

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Finance trolls

transcript.speaker: Finance Troll
transcript.text: Your request for airline travel is denied. We don't have the budget for that.

transcript.speaker: Finance Troll
transcript.text: Company policy requires you to hitchhike with alleged killers and not offer to pay for gas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, at least things can't get worse.

transcript.speaker: Finance Troll
transcript.text: Apparently you don't know what "alleged" means.

setting: Finance department troll's desk in a cave-like office
situation: Dilbert asks to travel by airline for work, but a green troll in the finance department denies the request because there is no budget. The troll says company policy instead requires him to hitchhike with alleged killers without offering to pay for gas. When Dilbert says things can't get worse, the troll implies they can.
punchline: Dilbert thinks the situation can't be any worse, but the troll's ominous remark about the word "alleged" implies the killers may very well be real killers.
summary: A cost-cutting troll in finance forces an employee to hitch rides with dangerous strangers rather than approve a plane ticket.

title: If We Had Money Meeting Game

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Welcome to another round of "If we had money."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll go first.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we had money, we could design and test new products.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We could go to training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You forgot to say, "If we had money"!

situation: The Boss opens a meeting with a game called "If we had money," where everyone lists things they could do with funds they don't have. Dilbert goes first, suggesting product design and testing. Asok then suggests training, and Dilbert scolds him for leaving off the required opening phrase.
punchline: The company is so broke that wishing for things it can't afford has become a formal meeting ritual with rules, and Dilbert polices the phrasing rather than the futility.
summary: With no budget for anything real, a team turns daydreaming about spending into a structured group game.

title: Dilbert's Halo Fails Lie Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please ignore my wings and halo. They are side effects from my prescription meds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anyway, my pointy-haired boss asked me to tell you that we will finish the prototype on time and on budget.

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: That is one bad tell you got there.

characters: Woman in green top (client or customer)
situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table with wings and a halo, which he explains away as side effects of his medication. When he then relays his boss's promise that the prototype will be on time and on budget, the wings and halo vanish with a poof. A woman across the table points out that this is a very obvious sign he is lying.
punchline: Dilbert's angelic wings and halo disappear the moment he tells a lie, which gives away that the on-time, on-budget promise is false.
summary: A man sprouting angelic features is exposed as dishonest when they vanish right as he repeats a management promise about project delivery.

title: Catbert Threatens Winged Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My prescription meds caused me to grow wings.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I have a sudden urge to kill you because you're different.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that would be wrong

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "Wrong" is one of those concepts that depends on witnesses.

situation: Dilbert, who has sprouted angel wings as a side effect of his prescription medication, explains this to Catbert, the evil HR director. Catbert announces he suddenly wants to kill Dilbert for being different, and when Dilbert objects that it would be wrong, Catbert points out that morality depends on who is watching.
punchline: Catbert, the evil HR director, treats ethics as purely situational, implying that killing is fine as long as nobody witnesses it, while mocking how HR is supposed to protect employees from discrimination.
summary: A winged employee tells the malevolent personnel chief about his medication's strange side effect and learns that the chief's morality is only as strong as the audience watching.

title: Aspiring to Overpaid Worthlessness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My dream is to someday be like you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope to advance from being totally worthless to being totally worthless and overpaid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's your role model?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Grumpy.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and hallway
situation: Wally stands holding a coffee mug in front of the seated Boss and tells him that his dream is to become like him. He explains that he wants to advance from being worthless to being worthless and overpaid. Afterward Dilbert asks how Wally's role model is doing, and Wally reports that the Boss is grumpy.
punchline: Wally delivers a thinly veiled insult to the Boss by praising him as a role model who is both useless and overpaid, and the Boss reacts by getting grumpy.
summary: A coffee-sipping employee flatters his superior with a backhanded compliment about wanting his useless but well-paid career, and the superior takes it badly.

title: Deliberately Confusing User Interfaces for Profit

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This is Phil, our new vice president of marginally legal activities.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: He'll be leading the effort to make our user interfaces so confusing that people have to pay us for training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We already do that unintentionally.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Sure, but we can't always rely on luck.

situation: At a meeting, a devil-costumed figure introduces Phil as the new vice president of marginally legal activities. Phil explains his job is to make the company's user interfaces so confusing that customers must pay for training. Dilbert points out the company already does this by accident, and Phil replies that they shouldn't depend on luck.
punchline: The company's software is already so badly designed that it confuses users by accident, but Phil wants to make the confusion deliberate and reliable as a revenue stream.
summary: A new executive is hired to turn the company's accidental usability disasters into a planned way of selling training.

title: Therapist Imagined Into Existence Cruelly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worry that the Boltzmann brain hypothesis is true and my reality is entirely imagined.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But if I'm imagining my life, why don't I imagine better things happening to me?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I'll probably regret this practical joke.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Mmmm

situation: Dilbert lies on a therapist's couch and confesses he fears his whole reality is imagined, as in the Boltzmann brain hypothesis. He wonders why, if he were imagining his life, it isn't better. In the last panel the therapist thinks to herself that she will regret this practical joke, as she lies on top of him and he sits there oblivious.
punchline: Dilbert's life is miserable because the therapist is imagining it as a cruel practical joke, so she is the Boltzmann brain, and it is Dilbert who exists only in her mind.
summary: A patient doubting whether his life is real unknowingly gets the unsettling answer that he is merely a prank in his own therapist's imagination.

title: Foodie Pretentiously Describes French Fry

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The foodie with a huge forehead

transcript.speaker: Foodie
transcript.text: Mmmm, a pomme de terre frite with sea salt and just a hint of rosemary.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Punch!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That was a French fry. And much like yourself, it was a salted.

setting: A restaurant table where three colleagues are eating lunch
situation: A bald, big-foreheaded coworker pretentiously describes the French fry he is eating in fancy French terms. Alice, sitting beside him, loses her patience and punches him, sending him sprawling across the table. She then explains that it was just a French fry and puns that he, like the fry, had been 'salted'.
punchline: Alice answers the pompous food description with violence, and her pun on 'salted' (as in assaulted) shows she has no patience for pretension.
summary: A snobby diner waxing lyrical over a plain fry gets knocked flat by an irritated coworker who ends with a groan-worthy pun.

title: Dating a Coworker for Free Meals

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The company cut my pay so I'm going to date a co-worker to make up the difference.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: From now on, one of you will be buying all of my meals and gifts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm oddly aroused by your offer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In that case it's not you.

situation: Alice announces that because the company cut her pay, she will date a co-worker to make up the difference, and demands that one of the men buy all her meals and gifts. Wally, holding his coffee mug, says he is oddly aroused by the offer, and Alice immediately rules him out.
punchline: Wally's eager, creepy enthusiasm disqualifies him, showing that Alice's mercenary scheme still has standards.
summary: After a salary reduction, a woman announces she'll recruit a colleague as a paid-for dating partner, then promptly rejects the one who volunteers.

title: Morgan's Vague Meeting Update

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Morgan: The man with no communication skills

transcript.speaker: Morgan
transcript.text: They decided to do option one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who is "they"? What is option one? And are they testing or implementing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just earned yourself a creepy stare until the topic changes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Okay, moving on...

situation: At a meeting table, Morgan announces that 'they' decided to do 'option one' without explaining who or what he means. Dilbert asks the obvious clarifying questions, but Morgan just sits there. Dilbert then announces he will give Morgan a creepy stare until the topic changes, and another attendee hurriedly moves the meeting on.
punchline: Morgan's useless, context-free update gets no explanation at all, and Dilbert's response is to punish him with an uncomfortable stare rather than get answers, which is enough to make the meeting move on.
summary: A colleague drops a cryptic status update with no context, and Dilbert's follow-up questions go nowhere, so he resorts to staring him down.

title: Bribery Disguised as Access

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO and the Senator

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It wouldn't be legal for me to bribe you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So I hired your wife as a consultant despite the fact that she thinks "present value" is some sort of gift card.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I wrote some legislation for you because you're a lazy thief.

transcript.speaker: Senator
transcript.text: Ha ha! Let's call that "access."

setting: A meeting across a desk in an office
situation: Dogbert, acting as a CEO, meets with a senator and notes that bribing him directly would be illegal. He explains he has instead hired the senator's financially clueless wife as a consultant and has written legislation on the senator's behalf. The senator cheerfully agrees to label it all "access."
punchline: Corporate bribery of politicians is thinly disguised as legal lobbying, with the participants openly acknowledging the corruption while giving it a respectable name.
summary: A scheming executive lays out how he gets around anti-bribery rules by giving a lawmaker's spouse a fake job and ghostwriting his bills.

title: Dilbert's Insolence Safety Zone Dance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My insolence safety zone has expanded.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a measure of how rude I can be without fear of consequences.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have no budget to give me a raise, so I have no potential gain from acting professionally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And it would be inconvenient for you to fire a highly experienced engineer and try to bring a new one up to speed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So from now on, when you ask me to do something stupid, which is most of the time...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll roll my eyes, make a dismissive grunt and do this dance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Phhht!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey walla-walla walla! Boopita boopita boopita!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You finally raised my morale. Good work on that.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that, since there is no raise budget and firing an experienced engineer would be inconvenient, he can now be as rude as he likes without consequences. He announces that whenever given a stupid task he will roll his eyes, grunt dismissively and perform a silly dance, then does so while the Boss glares.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically credits the Boss with raising his morale, since being insolent and dancing is the only 'raise' he is getting.
summary: With no raise on offer and no threat of being replaced, an engineer announces he will mock his boss's dumb orders with a rude little dance.

title: Conversation Hijackers Ignore Social Disorder

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then Ted said he'd...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Ho ho! I've seen that a million times!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: At my old job we used to make cricket noises whenever our manager was approaching.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But that doesn't mean you should cut corners when it comes to quality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're hijacking our conversation!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm adding value.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't even know what we were talking about.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Apparently you have a social disorder that compels you to insert irrelevant stories and trite observations into other people's conversations.

transcript.text: I assume part of the disorder involves not being able to recognize it in yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if he can hear us.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did I tell you about my camping trip?

characters: Coworker with green tie and mug
situation: Dilbert tries to tell a story to a coworker but is repeatedly interrupted by another colleague who injects irrelevant anecdotes and platitudes into the conversation. When Dilbert confronts him, the interrupter claims he is adding value. Dilbert ends up talking about the man's apparent social disorder right in front of him, and the man keeps interrupting anyway.
punchline: The conversation hijacker is so oblivious to his own habit that even a direct diagnosis of his problem doesn't register, and he immediately interrupts again with another irrelevant story.
summary: A man who keeps barging into other people's chats with pointless tales stays completely unaware of his own habit, even as his colleagues spell it out in front of him.

title: Thighs Strong Enough for Escape Velocity

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Topper

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I went for a long walk yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: My thighs are so strong that I'm afraid to jump rope when the sun is directly overhead.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're full of beans.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Exactly. That's how I achieve escape velocity.

characters: Coworker (man in white shirt and tie)
situation: A woman with big curly hair mentions a long walk she took, and a male coworker immediately tries to top her. He claims his thighs are so strong he fears jumping rope when the sun is overhead. When she accuses him of being full of beans, he turns it into a rocket-propulsion joke about escape velocity.
punchline: He takes the insult 'full of beans' literally, claiming the gas from the beans is what propels him to escape velocity, which neatly caps his absurd boast.
summary: A man one-ups a colleague's modest walking story with an outrageous boast about his strength, then turns her accusation of lying into a flatulence joke.

title: Preemptive Guilt Avoids Work

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: According to The Book of Wally, I should use something called "preemptive guilt" to avoid work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Exactly. If you wait until after you get an assignment, it is already too late for guilt.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Stress killed both of my parents. The doctors said they worked too hard.

situation: Asok reads from a book written by Wally and tells him he is applying its advice about "preemptive guilt" to dodge work. Wally, holding his coffee mug, explains that the guilt must be felt before an assignment arrives. He then claims his parents died from stress because they worked too hard, as the Boss sits at his desk in the background.
punchline: Wally justifies his lazy philosophy with a darkly absurd claim that overwork killed his parents, using it as an excuse to avoid working at all.
summary: A coworker seeks slacking tips from a manual by the office's laziest employee, who backs up his advice with a grim family story.

title: Birthday Collection Ends in Punching

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm collecting money for our Pointy-Haired Boss' birthday.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: PUNCH!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How much did we get so far?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Well, nothing you could send by FedEx.

situation: Asok, holding a small envelope, tells Alice he is collecting money for the boss's birthday. Alice punches him so hard that he flies up over the cubicle wall. Later, Asok returns bruised, with a bandaged head and an arm in a sling, and tells the boss the collection has netted almost nothing.
punchline: Asok's meagre collection is so small it would only cover a cheap FedEx envelope, and he took a beating from Alice, who refuses to chip in, to get it.
summary: A coworker who tries to gather birthday cash for the boss gets violently punched and ends up bandaged with nearly nothing to show for it.

title: Dilbert Checks Investments, Considers Warlords

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Maybe some warlords are hiring.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk with a computer
situation: Unemployed Dilbert tells Dogbert he isn't stressed about losing his job because he has investments. He sits down at his computer to check on them. A scream is shown echoing out over a view of Earth from space, and a frazzled Dilbert, hair standing on end, says maybe some warlords are hiring.
punchline: Dilbert's portfolio has collapsed so badly that he panics and is reduced to considering work for warlords, implying the economy is in ruins.
summary: A jobless man confident in his savings looks at his accounts, screams, and then contemplates working for violent warlords.

title: Dogbert Tests Hobos Against CEO Pay

transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't tell if my pay is excessive enough.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So I created a lab to test the reaction of hobos to my different pay scenarios.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's your turn to find the next hobo.

setting: A corporate boardroom, then a laboratory
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, sits at the head of a boardroom table surrounded by executives and explains that he can't tell whether his pay is excessive enough. He built a lab to test how hobos react to his various pay scenarios. In the lab, Dilbert holds up a paper and tells a scientist it's his turn to find the next hobo, while a headless hobo's clothes sit smoking after the previous experiment.
punchline: Dogbert measures how excessive his CEO pay is by seeing whether hobos literally explode with rage, and the lab keeps needing fresh test subjects.
summary: A canine chief executive builds a research facility to gauge outrage at his compensation, and the test subjects keep blowing up.

title: Pigeon Duty to Drive Ted Out

transcript.speaker: Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss

When Ted guesses the Boss is hoping he'll fall out a window, the Boss pointedly tells him to stop guessing.
punchline: The Boss's refusal to deny the window theory implies that he actually hopes Ted will fall out the window, revealing the assignment as a thinly disguised attempt to get rid of him.
summary: A manager hands an employee a ridiculous ledge-patrolling chore, then hints that the dangerous outcome the employee fears is exactly the point.

title: Wally's Free Coffee Cost-Cutting Argument

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bring back free coffee.

transcript.text: That's the opposite of cutting spending.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seems that way if you're short-sighted.

transcript.text: When I buy my own coffee, I don't drink as much.

transcript.speaker: Wally

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zzz

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting
situation: The Boss asks his team for ideas to cut spending, and Wally suggests bringing back free coffee. When Ted objects, Wally argues that paying for his own coffee makes him half as productive, so free coffee would let the company fire Ted and still come out ahead. The Boss buys the logic and apologizes to Ted while Wally dozes off.
punchline: Wally twists his own laziness into a cost-saving argument, and the clueless Boss accepts it, so Ted loses his job while Wally falls asleep at the table.
summary: A manager seeking budget cuts is talked into restoring a perk by an employee who reasons that the savings from firing a coworker outweigh the cost of his caffeine.

title: Productivity Software Reports Meeting Waste

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I used the rest of the week trying to make it interface with our time reporting system.

transcript.text: So far all it can do is tell me how much time I'm wasting in this meeting.

situation: Wally sits at a conference table with Dilbert and the Boss and explains how he spent his whole week installing new productivity software and connecting it to the time reporting system. In the last panel he sips his coffee and reveals the software's only output so far is how much time he is wasting in this very meeting.
punchline: The productivity software consumed an entire week of work and its only result is measuring the time wasted in meetings, making it a perfect example of a productivity tool that destroys productivity.
summary: A worker's elaborate week of setting up efficiency software yields nothing except a tally of the time he squanders sitting in a status meeting.

transcript.text: Did he solve your problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to say yes.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for more resources for his project, and the boss offers to take someone from Alice's project instead. Dilbert points out that this just shifts the shortage to Alice, but the boss says he can only solve one problem at a time. Alice then asks if the boss solved Dilbert's problem, and Dilbert decides to say yes.
punchline: The boss's 'solution' merely moves the problem onto someone else, and Dilbert gives up and calls it solved, since that is the only way to count as success.
summary: A manager fixes one employee's staffing shortage by creating an identical shortage for a colleague, and the first employee shrugs and declares victory.

title: Kitty Litter Beach Staycation

transcript.text: Vacationing in a bad economy
