transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So I bought some kitty litter and a 100-watt bulb. It's exactly like being at the beach.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This could turn ugly.

setting: Office cubicles, then a bare room or office floor
situation: Alice tells a coworker she can't afford a real vacation this year, so she bought kitty litter and a bright bulb to simulate a beach. In the last panel she lies on the floor in sunglasses on a pile of kitty litter under the lamp, while Catbert watches nervously and thinks that this could turn ugly.
punchline: Alice's cheap fake beach is a litter box under a heat lamp, and Catbert, a cat, worries about how she will react when he uses it as a litter box.
summary: A budget-conscious employee builds a pretend seaside holiday out of cat litter and a lamp, much to the concern of the cat who sees what she's lying in.

title: Smuggling Packages with Tranquilizer Darts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found a less expensive delivery service for our overseas packages.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Find someone who is traveling to the same country as the package, shoot him with a tranquilizer dart, and hide the package under his hat.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The first day of any new system is always a problem.

setting: Office cubicle area, with a closing shot in a corridor outside a door
situation: The Boss tells Alice he has found a cheaper delivery service for overseas packages. The delivery method is described over a shot of an office building: tranquilize a traveler heading to the destination country and hide the package under his hat. In the final panel Alice, holding a package, thinks that the first day of any new system is always a problem, while a slumped figure with a dart in him sits against a wall.
punchline: The absurdly dangerous and illegal cut-rate delivery scheme is treated by Alice as a routine teething problem with any new system, with the dart-struck traveler as evidence the plan is working as designed.
summary: A boss touts a bargain shipping method that involves drugging unsuspecting travelers, and his employee shrugs it off as ordinary new-system growing pains.

title: Boss Ruins Drawings, Shares Credit

transcript.text: I made some improvements to your drawings and sent them for fabrication.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But don't worry — I left your name on them so you'll get all of the credit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: WAAAA!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You don't handle good news very well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shoot me! Shoot me! Shoot me!

situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Dilbert that he altered Dilbert's engineering drawings and sent them off for fabrication. Dilbert is horrified, and the Boss adds that Dilbert's name is still on the modified drawings, so he will get all the credit. Dilbert is distraught and begs to be shot while the Boss misreads his despair as a poor reaction to good news.
punchline: The Boss thinks keeping Dilbert's name on his botched redesign is a generous favor, when it actually means Dilbert will take the blame for the Boss's unqualified changes.
summary: A manager meddles with an engineer's blueprints, ships them off, and proudly lets the engineer keep the credit for the likely disaster.

title: Dogbert's Parasitic News Business Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We're going into the internet news business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're hiring reporters?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, we'll summarize stories from other sites and provide links.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... we'll be parasites?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Go buy a vinyl record, Grandpa.

situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, announces the company will enter the internet news business. Dilbert assumes they will hire reporters, but Dogbert explains they will merely summarize other sites' stories and link to them. When Dilbert calls this parasitic, Dogbert mocks him as an old-fashioned relic.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses Dilbert's valid criticism that the business model is parasitic by treating it as an outdated, old-man objection, implying that freeloading on others' content is simply how the modern web works.
summary: A dog in charge plans a news site that does no reporting of its own, and brushes off the accusation of freeloading by calling his employee a relic.

title: Ratbert Beats Salesman With Spoon

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert: VP of Sales

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Humphrey, some might say you're below your sales quota because the economy is soft.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But I say it's because I haven't beaten you enough with this wooden spoon.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You know what I'm tired of hearing? "Not my good eye! Not my good eye!"

situation: Ratbert, the VP of Sales, meets with a salesman named Humphrey who is missing his quota. Ratbert dismisses the soft economy as an excuse and brandishes a wooden spoon, claiming Humphrey just hasn't been beaten enough. Off-panel, he evidently beats Humphrey, who is left cowering with a damaged eye.
punchline: Ratbert's management style is literal physical abuse, and he is more annoyed by the victim's repeated pleas about his good eye than by any ethical concern.
summary: A tiny rodent executive takes a wooden spoon to his underperforming salesman and complains about the whimpering.

title: Skipping Straight to Contract Failure

transcript.text: And during that time there's a 100% chance that we'll change our minds or you'll discontinue the product.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shall we save some time by declaring failure and blaming each other?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: I gave up before I even handed you the contract.

situation: Dilbert sits across from a client and explains that his company's contract negotiations normally take four months. He admits that during that time the deal is certain to fall apart because either side will change course. He proposes skipping ahead to failure and mutual blame, and the client says he already gave up before handing over the contract.
punchline: Both sides are so sure the negotiation will fail that they agree to skip it entirely, which makes the whole process look like a pointless ritual.
summary: Two businessmen cynically agree to jump straight to the inevitable collapse of their deal instead of wasting months negotiating it.

title: Scrubbing the Useless Database

transcript.text: Asok, I want you to scrub the CPS database.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No one uses that data.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But you are incapable of admitting error. So now I must dedicate my time to a thoroughly useless task.

situation: The Boss orders Asok to scrub a database, and Asok points out that nobody uses its data. Asok then reasons that the Boss can't admit a mistake, so he is doomed to do pointless work. While Asok complains, the Boss thinks to himself that management got easier once he stopped listening to employees, and Asok flails in despair.
punchline: The Boss deliberately tunes out his employees' objections, so Asok's accurate protests have no effect and he is left to suffer through meaningless work, which he compares to death without the glamour.
summary: A manager assigns a worthless data cleanup and cheerfully ignores the engineer's reasoned objections while the engineer despairs.

title: Don't Stir the Kettle of Crazy

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm a technical writer. Why don't you explain to the admins that my job is different from theirs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you find a big kettle of crazy, it's best not to stir it.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Tina she can no longer work from home because the administrative staff cannot do so and are jealous. Tina reasonably suggests he explain to the admins that her technical writing job is different from theirs. The Boss refuses, saying it is best not to stir up crazy people.
punchline: The Boss would rather take away a legitimate employee benefit than confront the unreasonable admins, preferring to punish the reasonable person to avoid dealing with the irrational ones.
summary: Rather than confront jealous coworkers, a manager strips a sensible employee of her work-from-home arrangement and justifies it with a folksy metaphor.

title: Lowering Dreams for the Economy

situation: Dilbert stands holding an empty mug and tells a seated coworker that he has lowered his hopes and dreams to match the bad economy. His new goals get more absurdly modest, ending with him claiming to save money by drinking only mugs of stale air. The coworker, holding a coffee mug, reacts with alarm.
punchline: The coworker is so unsettled by Dilbert's bleak, absurd austerity that he says it is scaring his coffee, a deadpan way of saying the gloom is unbearable.
summary: A downbeat employee shrinks his ambitions to fit a bad economy and unnerves a colleague with his grim frugality.

situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, tells the engineers to cold-call ten customers a day to boost lagging sales. punchline: The 'guaranteed' sales script is really a protection-racket threat, and Dilbert unknowingly delivers it to his own mother, casually admitting that sales has become his job.
summary: An animal executive gives reluctant technicians a menacing telephone pitch that turns out to be an extortion racket, which one of them unwittingly recites to his own parent.

summary: A cash-strapped manager buys the cheapest outsourcing package available and ends up with one hostile, clueless worker serving many clients.

Dilbert responds that he trusts encryption far more than he trusts pointy-eared sociopaths, a jab at Mordac's appearance. punchline: Dilbert's valid point about encryption is delivered as a personal insult about Mordac's pointed ears, so it ensures Mordac will never consider the actual argument.
summary: An IT security chief dismisses the cloud over data access fears, and Dilbert's counterargument gets sabotaged by an ear-based insult.

title: Doctor Takes Wingman Literally

setting: Doctor's examination room, then Dilbert's home
situation: A doctor asks Dilbert, who is sitting shirtless on an exam table, to take pills from a pharmaceutical rep so he can impress her. He admits there may be side effects but invokes the guy code that Dilbert must be his wingman. In the last panel Dilbert has grown literal wings, with Dogbert looking on from a chair.
punchline: The pills' side effect gives Dilbert actual wings, so the doctor's request to be his 'wingman' is fulfilled literally, and the doctor's scheme to boost drug sales has put his patient at risk.
summary: A doctor guilt-trips his patient into testing a risky drug to impress a sales rep, and the patient ends up sprouting real wings.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside path
situation: Dilbert walks and sits outside with Dogbert, explaining how he gets blamed both for neglecting tasks he didn't know about and for taking initiative without being asked. He concludes that tomorrow he will do nothing and avoid everyone at his cubicle. Dogbert asks if the unspoken word he's implying rhymes with "bird."
punchline: Since Dilbert is punished whether he acts or doesn't, he resolves to do nothing, and Dogbert crudely guesses the word Dilbert is too polite to say ("turd").
summary: Penalized for both inaction and initiative, an exasperated engineer decides the only safe option is to freeze up and hide, while his dog supplies the crude word he skipped.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that customers cannot figure out the company's user interface. punchline: Rather than address the usability problems, the Boss literally buries his head in the sand, and it still doesn't fit his whole body.
summary: A manager shrugs off a chain of increasingly unhelpful customer-help options and then dodges the issue by wedging his head into a tiny hole.

summary: A sinister HR cat cautions a worker about his soul slipping away, and the worker answers with a mock-polite request to send scouts after it.

The stunned employee says he didn't see it coming, and Wally remarks that no class exists to fix that.
punchline: Admitting a skills gap gets you fired rather than trained, and Wally sarcastically notes that no training can cure the employee's naivety about how management works.
summary: A worker honestly asks for technology training and is promptly dismissed by a boss who only wants staff who already know everything.

punchline: The Boss's hopeful alternatives are both ruled out by a darker reality: the stockbroker is so reviled that even do-gooder celebrities want him dead, implying he has done something terrible with clients' money.

He then reads the script, claiming poisonous spiders are hidden in the debtor's home and offering an antidote in exchange for credit card payment. The debtor reluctantly agrees to pay.
punchline: The debtor is so unmoved by the absurd spider threat that he agrees to pay only grudgingly, then sarcastically tells Dilbert to call him if he feels a tickle on his leg, mocking the implausible scheme.
summary: A debt collector's ridiculous scripted threat about booby-trapped arachnids gets a weary, sarcastic surrender from the person on the other end of the line.

setting: Catbert's office in the Human Resources department
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, sits at his desk across from a stoic employee and tells him he has many career options. He then offers an absurd suggestion: flap his arms and fly to a planet that values morons. Catbert dismisses the rest of the list with 'etcetera' while the employee sits there unreacting.
punchline: Catbert disguises a savage insult about the employee's stupidity as encouraging career counseling, implying his only marketable trait is being a moron.
summary: The cruel HR cat pretends to offer upbeat career guidance while actually mocking an employee's lack of intelligence.

title: Pandemic Planning: Productivity Already Halved

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I'm putting you in charge of pandemic contingency planning.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Calculate the impact on our business if 50% of our employees are unable to be productive.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's twice as good as we're doing now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just make some slides that say it would be bad.

situation: The Boss assigns Asok to lead pandemic contingency planning and asks him to calculate the business impact if half of the employees cannot be productive. Asok points out that this would actually be an improvement over current productivity. The Boss ignores the observation and tells him to just produce slides saying the outcome would be bad.
punchline: Asok's remark that losing half the workforce's productivity would be an improvement implies the company is already only about 25% productive, and the Boss cares only about slides with a predetermined conclusion, not the truth.
summary: Asked to model the damage of a pandemic, a young engineer notes the company is so unproductive that the scenario would be an upgrade, but his manager only wants a deck that looks alarming.

title: Tax-Exempt Heaven Incorporation Scam

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Income Tax Auditor

transcript.speaker: Income Tax Auditor
transcript.text: You claim your company is exempt from taxes because you're incorporated in... heaven?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Income Tax Auditor
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to question that claim because of the separation of church and state.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I am the angel Wally!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hold on, Wally. We're selling past the close.

situation: An income tax auditor questions Dogbert's claim that his company is exempt from taxes because it is incorporated in heaven. Dogbert simply confirms it, and the auditor backs down, saying he cannot question the claim because of the separation of church and state. Wally then appears dressed as an angel, overplaying the part, and Dogbert tells him to stop because they are already making the sale.
punchline: Dogbert's absurd claim of heavenly incorporation works as a tax dodge because the auditor thinks questioning it would violate religious freedom, making Wally's angel costume unnecessary overkill.
summary: A dubious tax-exemption story gets accepted by an auditor on religious grounds, rendering an eager accomplice's angel act superfluous.

title: Alice Punches the Airborne Virus

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pandemic planning

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: In the worst-case scenario, the only survivors would be cockroaches and Alice.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POW! POW! POW!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Airborne virus. It's safe now. I broke its protein coat.

setting: Conference room during a pandemic planning presentation
situation: A presenter in a pandemic planning meeting says that in the worst case only cockroaches and Alice would survive. Alice reacts by furiously punching at something in the air while a coworker falls back in his chair and Dilbert looks on. She then calmly announces that she has neutralized an airborne virus.
punchline: Alice's violent, fist-swinging approach to a microscopic virus confirms the presenter's claim that she is as indestructible as a cockroach, and the absurd explanation that she broke its protein coat is delivered with total seriousness.
summary: Told she would outlast almost everyone in a plague, Alice proves it by brawling with an invisible germ in the middle of the meeting.

title: Younger Worker Threatens Elders With Immortality

transcript.speaker: Young Coworker
transcript.text: Your generation is leaving my generation a dying planet and a crippling debt.

transcript.speaker: Older Coworker
transcript.text: Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Young Coworker
transcript.text: But we shall invent life-extending drugs so you will suffer along with us! Ha!

transcript.speaker: Older Coworker
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Young Coworker
transcript.text: We will connect you to machines and keep you alive until the poor demand to eat you.

transcript.speaker: Older Coworker
transcript.text: Well played.

situation: A younger coworker with a newspaper complains that the older generation is leaving them a dying planet and crippling debt, while the older coworker with a coffee mug laughs. The young worker then retaliates by threatening to invent life-extending drugs to keep the elders alive and suffering, eventually until the poor demand to eat them. The older coworker concedes the point.
punchline: The younger generation's revenge for inherited debt and environmental ruin is to keep the older generation alive on machines so they share the suffering, until a starving underclass turns on them as food.
summary: A young employee fires back at a smug older colleague with a darkly satirical vision of endless life support and cannibalism.

title: Punching Every MBA Holder at Once

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hear you have an MBA, just like the jerks who ruined the economy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm going to punch you so hard that it hurts everyone who has the same degree.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was that hideous noise?

transcript.speaker: Man with MBA
transcript.text: Ow!!!

situation: Alice confronts a male coworker, accusing him of sharing a degree with the people who wrecked the economy, and threatens to punch him so hard that it hurts everyone with an MBA. In the final panel, at a conference table, another man with an MBA cries out in pain while Dilbert wonders about the noise.
punchline: Alice's punch on one MBA holder is so powerful that every other MBA holder, including someone in a different room, feels it, and the strip implies the whole degree class deserves the pain.
summary: A furious coworker's punch at one business graduate is felt by every graduate of the same program, including a distant colleague who yelps in agony.

title: Demon Marketing Director Confuses Pricing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new Director of Marketing is an angry demon of some sort.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's in charge of making our prices impossible for customers to understand.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What the #%!*$ kind of price is "it depends"?

transcript.speaker: Store Clerk
transcript.text: He makes me say these things.

setting: A conference room and a retail checkout counter
situation: The Boss introduces the company's new Director of Marketing, a green horned demon, and explains that his job is to make the prices impossible for customers to understand. At a store counter, an angry elderly customer demands to know what kind of price is "it depends," and the clerk blames the demon for making him say it.
punchline: Deliberately opaque, evasive pricing is so infuriating to customers that it seems to be the work of a literal demon in marketing.
summary: A demonic marketing chief is hired to obscure pricing, and a puzzled shopper and apologetic clerk feel the fallout at the register.

title: Military Loves Self-Harming Software

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Marketing

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: How do we market a product that is known to trigger despondency and self-mutilation?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Employee
transcript.text: So... it has a military application?

transcript.speaker: Soldier
transcript.text: I thought it was just software, but before I knew it I was stabbing myself.

transcript.speaker: General
transcript.text: Get me a trillion of these.

setting: Marketing department conference room, with a cutaway to a military office
situation: In a marketing meeting, a manager asks how to sell a software product known to cause despondency and self-mutilation. A woman at the table suggests it must have a military application. A bandaged soldier testifies that the software made him stab himself, and a general reads the testimonial and eagerly orders a trillion copies.
punchline: The product's harmful side effects are exactly what makes it appealing to the military, which sees a weapon rather than a defect.
summary: A product that drives users to hurt themselves turns out to be the perfect sale for an enthusiastic army general.

title: Economist Hedges Every Possible Forecast

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company Economist

transcript.speaker: Company Economist
transcript.text: The economy will either recover or not.

transcript.speaker: Company Economist
transcript.text: Unless time itself is an illusion, in which case all matter is either stationary or imagined.

transcript.speaker: Company Economist
transcript.text: I'd take questions, but I'm not entirely sure you're real.

situation: A company economist gives a presentation using a projection screen with up and down arrows, offering a forecast that says nothing. He then retreats into philosophical absurdity about time and matter being illusions, and finally declines to take questions because he doubts his audience exists. The audience of employees sits silently at a table.
punchline: The economist's forecast covers every possible outcome so he can never be wrong, and he then dodges accountability entirely by questioning whether his audience is real.
summary: An economist's prediction is so hedged it is meaningless, and he escapes questioning by doubting that anyone is actually there.

title: Refusing Boss's Murderous Sales Scheme

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your boss says you refuse to do your job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He told me to kill a customer, assume her identity, and place a huge order with our company.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'll transfer you to the Collections Department until you're willing to kill.

setting: Catbert's office, with Dilbert seated across the desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Dilbert that his boss has complained he refuses to do his job. Dilbert explains that the boss ordered him to murder a customer, steal her identity, and place a big order with the company. Catbert responds by threatening to transfer Dilbert to Collections until he is willing to kill.
punchline: HR sides with the boss's absurd, criminal demand and treats Dilbert's ethical refusal to commit murder as a performance problem to be punished.
summary: A human resources cat treats an employee's unwillingness to commit a crime for sales numbers as insubordination worthy of demotion.

title: Forensic Analysis of Her Business Card

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Give me a call sometime.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll need to do a complete forensic analysis of your business card.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your home phone is a landline. That must come in handy when someone calls from 1993.

setting: Crowded social gathering or networking mixer
situation: At a party, a woman invites Dilbert to call her sometime and he noncommittally answers 'maybe.' He then studies her business card as though conducting a forensic investigation, and mocks her for listing a landline home phone number.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically insults the woman's outdated landline, implying the only people who would call it are time travelers from 1993, which ruins any chance of romance.
summary: A man at a mixer responds to a woman's phone invitation by scrutinizing her card and ridiculing her old-fashioned home phone.

title: Golf Buddy Consultant's Qualifications

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired my unemployed golf buddy to consult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are his qualifications?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He has two qualifications: He's unemployed and he's a golf buddy.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: I recommend firing the whistleblower and playing nine before it gets dark.

situation: The Boss introduces his unemployed golf buddy, who carries a golf club, as a newly hired consultant. When Dilbert asks about his qualifications, the Boss says his only credentials are being unemployed and being a golf buddy. The consultant's first recommendation is to fire the whistleblower and play nine holes before dark.
punchline: The consultant is hired purely out of cronyism, and his first piece of advice is to retaliate against a whistleblower so he can get back to golfing.
summary: A boss gives a consulting job to his jobless golf friend, whose very first advice is to get rid of the employee who reported wrongdoing so they can hit the links.

title: Anticipating Problems During Performance Review

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You need to get better at anticipating problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I could anticipate problems, I wouldn't have agreed to work for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You seem angry. I did not see that coming.

setting: Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert in his performance review that he needs to get better at anticipating problems. Dilbert replies that if he could anticipate problems he would never have taken a job working for the Boss. When the Boss glares angrily, Dilbert deadpans that he didn't see that reaction coming.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss by implying that working for him is the ultimate problem, then mocks the review criticism by claiming he failed to anticipate the Boss's anger.
summary: An employee turns his manager's criticism of his foresight into a double jab, first insulting the job and then feigning surprise at the boss's temper.

title: Keeping Secrets Is Cost-Benefit Analysis

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to keep this information to yourself. Can you do that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, obviously I'd have to weigh the benefits of sharing it versus the risk of getting caught.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's sort of a dumb question if you think about it.

situation: The Boss holds out a paper and asks Dilbert to keep some information confidential. Dilbert answers that he would have to weigh the benefits of sharing it against the risk of getting caught. He then points out that the Boss's question was a dumb one.
punchline: Dilbert reveals that anyone's promise of secrecy is just a self-interested calculation, so asking 'can you keep a secret?' is a pointless question.
summary: Asked to keep a secret, an employee calmly admits his silence depends on a risk-reward calculation and mocks the question for being naive.

title: Tax Auditor Admits Government Shakedown

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Tax Auditor
transcript.text: I'm here to do a tax audit of your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How's that work?

transcript.speaker: Tax Auditor
transcript.text: I look for reasons to transfer money from small, disreputable entities to a larger one.

transcript.speaker: Tax Auditor
transcript.text: I call my salary vigorish, but it's not as ironic as it once was.

situation: A tax auditor carrying a briefcase arrives at Dogbert's company, which Dogbert runs as CEO. When Dogbert asks how an audit works, the auditor candidly explains that his job is to move money from small, disreputable entities to a larger one. He then compares his own salary to vigorish, the cut taken by a bookie or loan shark.
punchline: The auditor describes the government's tax collection as indistinguishable from a criminal shakedown, and says his salary-as-vigorish joke is less ironic now since the government has become the bigger, more dubious organization taking its cut.
summary: A government inspector cheerfully equates tax auditing with organized-crime extortion while explaining his job to a dog CEO.

title: Click Buttons, You Can't Hurt Anything

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Now what do I do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Click some buttons and see what happens. You can't hurt anything.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Click

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FZZEET!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my defense, that hardly ever happens.

setting: Office cubicle with a computer desk
situation: A coworker sits at a computer and asks Dilbert what to do next. Dilbert casually tells her to click buttons and see what happens, assuring her she can't hurt anything. She clicks and the computer zaps her with an electric shock, leaving her singed, angry and smoking.
punchline: Dilbert's reassurance that you can't hurt anything proves false when the computer electrocutes her, and his only excuse is that it hardly ever happens.
summary: After being told that experimenting with a computer is perfectly safe, a user gets zapped by it and her helper offers a feeble excuse.

title: Asking Vendor About Payroll Data Risk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is there any risk that the new software will erase our payroll data?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you ask the vendor that question?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, no, I...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you can't be sure, can you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We outsource our payroll service. The payroll data isn't even on our servers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Isn't everything connected to everything else by the Internet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to ask our vendor if his software will hunt down our payroll data from across the Internet and try to kill it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you think he might say yes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Better safe than sorry.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that day

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Yes, sometimes it does that. You're the first to ask.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shoot me.

situation: The Boss worries that new software might erase the company's payroll data and insists Dilbert should have asked the vendor. Dilbert points out the payroll data is outsourced and not on their servers, but the Boss argues everything is connected via the Internet. Dilbert reluctantly asks the vendor, who admits the software sometimes does exactly that.
punchline: The Boss's absurd paranoia about software hunting down data across the Internet turns out to be a real, if unlikely, risk, leaving Dilbert wishing he were dead.
summary: A manager's far-fetched fear about a software product destroying remote data gets validated by a vendor who cheerfully confirms it can happen.

title: Asok's Promotion Depends on Deaths

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, the company isn't growing, and no one is quitting in this economy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your only hope for promotion is if a senior engineer dies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I joined a gym!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No-ooo!

setting: Boss's office, then a hallway or break area
situation: The Boss tells Asok that with no company growth and nobody quitting in a bad economy, the only way he'll be promoted is if a senior engineer dies. In the last panel Dilbert cheerfully announces he joined a gym, which means he plans to live longer, and Asok screams in despair.
punchline: Dilbert's healthy new habit is bad news for Asok, whose career advancement depends on senior engineers dying, so he reacts as if his hopes were just destroyed.
summary: A grim promotion outlook leaves a young engineer waiting for his elders to die, until a coworker's fitness plan crushes even that hope.

title: Work for Money, Not Meetings

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You shouldn't come to work just for money.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You should come to work to avoid not having any money.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm only in it for these meetings.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Settle down, Baldy.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the meeting attendees that they shouldn't come to work just for money, then clarifies that they should come to avoid having no money. Wally chimes in that he is only there for the meetings, and Catbert tells him to settle down.
punchline: Catbert's cynical reframing shows that work is really about avoiding poverty, and Wally's claim to love meetings is met with a dismissive insult, since his enthusiasm is really just a way to avoid real work.
summary: An HR cat redefines why employees show up to work in a bleakly negative way, then brushes off a slacker who admits he only enjoys the meetings.

title: Consensus Culture Means Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: It takes an average of five people to approve any action in this company, and at any given time, three are on vacation.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Should I violate our company culture of consensus building, or just sit around and do nothing for lack of buy-in?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you mention flailing around in futility?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I was hoping you forgot that option.

situation: At a conference table, a bald coworker explains that approvals need five people and three are always on vacation. He asks whether to break the consensus-building culture or do nothing. The Boss adds a third option, flailing around in futility, which the coworker had hoped would be forgotten.
punchline: Because the approval process makes real action impossible, the only options left are rule-breaking, idleness, or futile flailing, and even the boss knows the last one is the likeliest.
summary: A frustrated employee weighs his dismal choices when a slow approval process stalls everything, and his boss cheerfully supplies the worst one.

title: Boss Fails the Turing Test

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get us some risk management software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What can risk management software tell you that my common sense and experience can't?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Data.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop failing the Turing test!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to get risk management software. Dilbert asks what it could offer that his own common sense and experience can't, and the Boss answers with a single flat word, 'Data.' Dilbert, exasperated, yells at him to stop failing the Turing test.
punchline: The Boss's curt, robotic answer makes him sound like a poorly functioning computer, so Dilbert accuses him of failing a test meant to distinguish humans from machines.
summary: An engineer questions the need for risk software and gets such a mechanical one-word reply that he accuses his manager of not seeming human.

title: Director of Marketecture Skirts Law

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet our new Director of Marketecture.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's in charge of preventing customers from realizing what they're buying.

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketecture
transcript.text: It's legal because we're only violating the intent of the law.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can do a thousand push-ups when no one is looking.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to the company's new Director of Marketecture, whose job is to keep customers from understanding what they are purchasing. The director defends the practice by saying it only violates the intent of the law, not the letter. Dilbert responds with an unrelated boast about his push-ups.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the director's loophole logic by making an equally empty, unverifiable claim, implying that the company's legal justification is just as unconvincing as saying you can do push-ups when no one is watching.
summary: A new executive whose role is to keep buyers confused justifies it with a legal technicality, and Dilbert answers with a ridiculous boast of his own.

title: Per Diem Grilled Cheese Hotel Iron

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending you on a trip. Remember that our per diem isn't as extravagant as it was in our golden years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need to use the hotel iron to make grilled cheese sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will you pay for the bread and cheese?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll pay for the bread. But cheese and free soap are practically the same thing.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with a hotel exterior shown in the middle panel
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being sent on a business trip but warns that the per diem has been cut. He instructs Dilbert to cook grilled cheese sandwiches with the hotel room iron. Dilbert asks who pays for the ingredients, and the Boss agrees to cover only the bread, claiming cheese is basically a free hotel amenity like soap.
punchline: The Boss's absurd logic that cheese is as free as hotel soap is a transparent excuse to dodge paying for it while cutting travel expenses to ridiculous extremes.
summary: Facing budget cuts, a manager tells his employee to cook his own meals with a hotel iron and then refuses to reimburse the cheese.

title: Donut Meeting With Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks for coming on short notice. I called this meeting because...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...company policy allows me to order donuts for any meeting that includes customers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't work on commission.

setting: Conference room with a plate of donuts on the table
situation: The Boss gathers customers for a meeting called on short notice. He reveals that the meeting exists only because company policy lets him order donuts when customers attend. He then eats a donut and tells the irritated customers he doesn't earn commission, so he has no stake in their business.
punchline: The Boss lures customers to a meeting purely to get free donuts and openly admits he has no incentive to care about their business.
summary: A manager summons clients for a meeting just to justify ordering pastries, then shrugs off their anger by pointing out he earns no sales bonus.

title: Pie Chart Impresses Gullible Audience

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't have anything useful to say so I made this pie chart.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oooh!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oooh!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It must be true because it's pie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That worked too well.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I pledge my life and my fortune to the pie!

situation: Dilbert openly admits he had nothing useful to say and shows a colorful pie chart on a presentation board. His seated colleagues, including the Boss, respond with awe and declare the chart must be true simply because it is a pie. Dilbert is left thinking his ploy worked too well while someone pledges loyalty to the pie.
punchline: People will accept any claim as credible, even when the presenter admits it has no substance, if it comes with a pie chart.
summary: A presenter with nothing to say hides behind a colorful graphic and his audience worships it without question.

title: Dogbert Flaunts Wealth In Bedroom

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does my vast wealth make you feel inadequate and sad?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, not really.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about now?

situation: Dilbert sits up in bed reading while Dogbert stands at the bedside and asks whether his vast wealth makes Dilbert feel inadequate and sad. Dilbert calmly says it doesn't. In the last panel Dogbert has apparently arranged for something to change, and asks if Dilbert feels bad now.
punchline: Dogbert, unfazed by Dilbert's indifference, immediately escalates his flaunting of wealth, implying he can always find a way to make Dilbert feel inadequate.
summary: A rich and smug Dogbert pesters a bedridden Dilbert about his riches, then tries again with a bigger show when the first attempt fails.

title: Overqualified Temp Dismissed as Talker

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Overqualified temp

transcript.speaker: Temp
transcript.text: My last job was ambassador to Brunei. Before that I was undersecretary of commerce.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe the other admins can watch how you make copies and learn something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's a talker.

situation: A temp worker at her desk tells the Boss about her impressive career as an ambassador and undersecretary of commerce. The Boss, taking her for a boastful exaggerator, hands her a document and suggests the other admins watch how she makes copies. As he walks away he thinks that she is just a talker.
punchline: The Boss refuses to believe the temp's genuinely impressive resume and sarcastically dismisses her as a mere braggart, when she is in fact wildly overqualified for the copying job.
summary: A boss shrugs off an assistant's lofty past achievements as idle chatter and sends her off to photocopy papers.

title: Threatening To Become Your Nemesis

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. A truck turned over on the highway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What did I miss?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We don't want to rehash the entire meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about a quick summary?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, if we leave out any details, you'll think we made the wrong decisions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's best for us if we keep you ignorant and angry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you marginalize me, I will become a nemesis to your project!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm cool with that.

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A nemesis is not like a mascot!

situation: Dilbert arrives late to a meeting and asks what he missed. His coworkers refuse to brief him, saying it's better to keep him ignorant and angry. When Dilbert threatens to become a nemesis to their project, they cheerfully compare him to a mascot and suggest a squirrel costume.
punchline: Dilbert's threat to sabotage the project is brushed off so completely that his colleagues reframe it as a harmless mascot role, showing he has no real leverage.
summary: Excluded from a meeting summary, a latecomer's threat to become the project's enemy is mocked as a chance to wear a mascot costume.

title: Signing the Code of Conduct Dodge

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You need to sign the corporate code of conduct.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Wow! You're totally hot.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Um... That's inappropriate, and you need to sign the code of conduct.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I don't have a pen. Can you take it back to your cubicle and sign it for me?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: No. And I think you're lying about not having a pen. But maybe we can find one for you.

punchline: The code of conduct is so meaningless that Carol will threaten violence to get it signed, and she tells him not to bother reading it, just to say he did.
summary: A clerk pushing a conduct pledge ends up threatening a stalling coworker, proving the policy is a formality nobody takes seriously.

summary: A moonlighting employee waves away legality by citing his shady lawyer, whose rubber-stamp opinions are available to anyone with a hundred dollars.

title: Ratbert's Reciprocity Sales Pitch Backfires

situation: Ratbert, now the VP of Sales, brings a trainee named Humphrey to a sales meeting with prospective clients. punchline: Ratbert applies the reciprocity principle of persuasion in the cruelest way possible, sacrificing his trainee as the 'gift' and apparently succeeding since everyone wants to take part.
summary: A sales master demonstrates a persuasion trick by offering his apprentice up for a beating, and the prospects happily accept.

title: Slackers Reduce Raise Competition

situation: The Boss scolds Wally for not giving 100% and making his co-workers pick up his slack. Wally counters that his co-workers probably appreciate having less competition for raises. The Boss reveals there is no raise budget this year, and Wally advises keeping that secret from the others.
punchline: The extra effort employees put in to compensate for Wally's slacking is pointless because there are no raises, and Wally cynically suggests keeping them in the dark so they keep working hard.
summary: A manager lectures a lazy employee about fairness, only to admit that the reward everyone is working toward does not exist.

punchline: Dogbert's honest pitch scares off the client, so he has him knocked on the head and then lies, showing that hedge funds depend on amnesia and false promises.
summary: A hedge fund manager confesses his scam to a would-be investor, then has him bludgeoned into forgetting and swindles him with a wild promise.

situation: Dilbert sits on the floor in his living room and asks Dogbert if he wants to stay up until midnight for New Year's Eve. Dogbert dismisses the idea and declares that his own personal new year starts at 10 PM. When Dilbert notes that it is already 10 PM, Dogbert celebrates by hugging himself.
punchline: Dogbert redefines the new year to suit his own schedule and celebrates by hugging himself, a self-absorbed and slightly sad party that gets him to bed early.
summary: Dogbert declares that his own private new year begins hours before everyone else's and marks it with a solitary self-hug.

title: Rob Someone You Don't Like

situation: Dilbert, working in debt collections, asks his supervisor how to get money from people who have none. She advises telling debtors to rob someone they dislike. Dilbert then follows the advice on a phone call, giving the caller his supervisor's home address as a target.
punchline: Dilbert takes the supervisor's terrible advice literally and points the debtor at the supervisor's own home, urging haste before the loot is gone.
summary: A collections agent gets absurd guidance from his boss on squeezing cash from the broke, and cheerfully sends the burglary suggestion back at her.

punchline: The Boss ignores an explicit safety warning and shows off the dangerous flash, vaporizing the CEO and then obliviously asking the skeleton to pose.
summary: A boss ignores a warning about a lethally bright phone flash and zaps his chief executive into a skeleton while trying to take a photo.

punchline: Dilbert's job leaves him so overworked and stressed that he is already silently screaming all the time, and only politeness keeps him from doing it out loud.
summary: A drama instructor demonstrates a howl of workplace misery and learns his student already feels that way constantly.

punchline: The company demands a useless, instantly outdated inventory that nobody will read, so Dilbert fabricates it, which makes the company an example of worst practices rather than best ones.
summary: Told to catalogue software that no one will ever consult, an employee resigns himself to inventing the numbers and wryly hopes outsiders never study how the firm operates.

punchline: Dilbert sarcastically admits he is dumb enough to work for the company but not dumb enough to invest his retirement savings in it, showing he has no faith in the company's future.
summary: A manager asks staff to lobby for government pet projects, and Dilbert retorts that doing so would just fund executive bonuses with his taxes, then jabs that he would never trust the firm with his savings.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert his project has no funding, but he refuses to lay Dilbert off because he wants to keep his headcount. Instead he hires an acting coach to train Dilbert to look busy and useful. The coach sees Dilbert's blank, listless expression and asks if he is dead or just non-expressive.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan reply that this lifeless look is simply what having a job is like implies that work saps all enthusiasm and expression, and that his lack of acting talent is really just ordinary job misery.
summary: With no money for his work, a manager hires a coach to teach his engineer to fake being busy, only to find the engineer's flat demeanor is simply what employment looks like.

title: Teamwork Award With No Incentive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Great. Now I have no incentive to do a good job on this award thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert, Alice and Wally to create a teamwork award program. When he refuses to let them win it themselves and says keeping their jobs is incentive enough, Dilbert points out that this makes the award pointless. They decide to hastily throw something together and nominate people at random, and a coworker later admits the award made no difference to him.
punchline: If keeping your job is supposed to be motivation enough, an award has no real value, so a randomly handed-out award predictably changes nothing.
summary: A manager orders a recognition program yet denies any reward for building it, so the team makes a sloppy one that leaves its recipient unmoved.

title: Dogbert's Illuminati Stock Bubble Plan

setting: Dogbert's CEO office and a conference table
situation: Dogbert, now a CEO, tells The Boss that the company needs another economic bubble to boost its stock value. He then summons the Illuminati, whose members gather at a table and cheerfully divide up the labor: one creates a media frenzy, Dogbert rigs prices, and an alien vaporizes anyone who blows the whistle.
punchline: Economic bubbles are presented as the routine product of a secret cabal that manipulates markets and eliminates whistle-blowers, implying that corporate stock hype is deliberately engineered and criminal.
summary: A dog in charge of a company calls on a secret society of manipulators to inflate the market again, with disposal of witnesses built right into the plan.

title: Self-Esteem Staked on Slides

characters: Audience member (woman with big curly hair)
setting: Dilbert's cubicle, then a conference room
situation: Dilbert works at his computer, thinking dramatically about how much of his self-worth depends on his PowerPoint presentation. He then presents it to two colleagues seated at a table. One of them asks if the chimp who made the slides has been caught, leaving Dilbert wincing in pain.
punchline: After Dilbert pins his entire self-worth on his presentation, a colleague cruelly insults it by implying a chimp must have made the slides, crushing him.
summary: A man who has staked his whole identity on his slide deck gets it publicly mocked as the work of an escaped primate.

title: Faking Positive Reviews, Ethics Be Damned

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Doesn't that break some sort of law?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Heck no. It only crosses some ethical boundaries and violates the terms of service for the web site.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And depending on your religious views, it might be a hiccup on your way to paradise.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I'm almost positive there won't be any jail time or eternal damnation.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Well... okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And be sure to defame our competitors.

situation: The Boss tells Asok the company is suffering from bad online reviews and orders him to pose as several customers and post glowing ones. Asok asks if that's illegal, and the Boss cheerfully lists the ethical and terms-of-service violations while assuring him there's no jail time or damnation. Asok gives in, and the Boss adds that he should also slander competitors.
punchline: The Boss reassures Asok by listing only the legal consequences he can rule out while casually admitting the scheme is unethical, then escalates by asking for defamation of competitors too.
summary: A manager talks his young employee into inventing fake customer praise by downplaying every wrongdoing except the ones that might land them in trouble, then piles on an even shadier request.

title: Dilbert's Winged Date Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I can turn it sexy by flying you over the city on this moonlit night.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Seriously, how many appetizers did you have?

setting: A restaurant table by a window at night
situation: On a dinner date, Dilbert explains that a side effect of his prescription medication gave him wings, then offers to make it romantic by flying his date over the city. He picks her up and struggles to stay aloft, flapping frantically while she dangles from his arms.
punchline: His date's only concern is that he is too heavy to fly, so she tactlessly asks how many appetizers he ate, implying he is overweight.
summary: A man tries to impress his date with a flight made possible by a bizarre medication side effect, only to labour under her weight and her blunt insult.

title: Salesman's Lowball Quote Called Out

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Your order will only cost about $20,000.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No it won't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We both know you're intentionally underestimating the true cost to get the sale, you lying sack of spit.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You're not supposed to say that out loud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it okay if I imagine a bear attacking you?

setting: Office desk during a sales meeting
situation: A salesman at a desk quotes Dilbert a price of about $20,000 for his order. Dilbert bluntly accuses him of deliberately lowballing the true cost to win the sale. The salesman complains that Dilbert isn't supposed to say that aloud, so Dilbert asks if he may at least imagine a bear attacking him.
punchline: The salesman's only objection is to Dilbert saying the lie out loud, which implicitly admits the deception, and Dilbert responds with a deadpan wish for the salesman to be mauled by a bear.
summary: A customer refuses to play along with a vendor's deliberately low estimate and then politely asks permission to fantasize about violence against him.

title: Committee Approves Framework, Not Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did the executive steering committee approve my project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We agreed on a predecisional draft framework for making the decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that mean anything?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It depends what you mean by "anything."

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether the executive steering committee approved his project. The boss answers with a jargon-heavy statement about a draft framework for making the decision. When Dilbert asks if that means anything, the boss replies with an evasive non-answer.
punchline: The boss's bureaucratic double-talk reveals that the committee did nothing meaningful, and he dodges even admitting that by quibbling over the word 'anything'.
summary: A manager hides the fact that a committee made no decision behind layers of corporate jargon and wordplay.

title: Collecting Money For Own Birthday

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm collecting money for Scott's birthday present.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: So? Is there some sort of rule against collecting money for your own birthday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... no.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm buying myself some paper towels and cereal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop making it worse!

situation: A coworker approaches Dilbert's desk holding an envelope and asks for contributions to Scott's birthday present. Dilbert points out that the coworker is Scott, and Scott brazenly defends collecting money for himself. Dilbert hands over cash anyway while Scott announces he'll buy mundane items like paper towels and cereal.
punchline: The coworker shamelessly solicits gifts for his own birthday and plans to spend them on mundane household items, and Dilbert's pleading shows how awkward and absurd it is.
summary: A man openly shakes down his colleague for money toward his own birthday gift, then cheerfully reveals the gift will be everyday groceries.

title: Hidden Costs Sales Pitch Succeeds

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We have the best hidden costs of any vendor.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our upgrade and maintenance fees won't kick in until you've already received a bonus for reducing costs.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Please, please, please be a sociopath.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Sounds good. I'm not a big fan of our stockholders.

situation: A vendor salesman pitches software to a bald manager, openly bragging about his product's hidden costs. He explains that the upgrade and maintenance fees will not appear until after the manager has collected a bonus for cutting costs. Privately the salesman hopes the manager is unethical, and the manager cheerfully agrees, saying he does not care for the stockholders.
punchline: The manager is happy to take a bonus for cost savings he knows are fake, because he doesn't care that the company's shareholders will foot the real bill.
summary: A vendor's shady proposal to delay fees until after a bonus is paid lands perfectly with a manager who has no loyalty to shareholders.

title: Cheese-Insulated House Tops Stock Losses

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa! My stocks are down 70%!

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.text: Gouda?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Grated.

situation: At a meeting table, Dilbert complains that his stocks have lost 70% of their value. A coworker one-ups him by announcing that his house is insulated with cheese. Dilbert asks if it is the good kind of cheese, and the coworker says it is grated.
punchline: The coworker's cheese-insulated house is a bizarre topper to a stock loss, and the cheap grated cheese makes his misfortune sound even sillier and more pathetic.
summary: Two colleagues try to outdo each other's bad luck, and one wins with a ridiculous cheese-based home insulation problem.

title: Dilbert Insults Customer Over Handshake

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to meet one of our biggest customers. She has some technical questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: No offense, but you look more like a virus incubator than a vigorous hand washer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So why don't you pull that death stick back up your sleeve and we can pretend this ugly incident never happened.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And if it's not too much to ask, could you exhale toward things I'm unlikely to touch?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, now that the pleasantries are out of the way, what can I tell you about our new product line?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We lost a customer, but I survived the meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next time, do it the other way.

setting: Office meeting area and conference room
situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to an important customer with technical questions. Dilbert, a germophobe worried about infection, refuses her handshake and insults her as a disease carrier, then asks her to breathe away from him. Afterward he reports to the Boss that the customer is lost, and the Boss tells him to prioritize the customer next time.
punchline: Dilbert proudly says he avoided catching germs even though he drove away a major customer, and the Boss deadpans that next time he should save the customer and risk the germs instead.
summary: A germ-obsessed engineer rudely rebuffs a client's handshake and loses her business, then gets a mild rebuke from his boss.

title: Shushed Out of Every Question

setting: Meeting at a conference table in an office
situation: Dilbert tells a female coworker that he understood nothing of her half-hour presentation. He points out that she shushed him every time he tried to ask a question. When he complains that the meeting is over and all he remembers is noise coming from her mouth, she responds that his complaining is exactly why she won't let him speak.
punchline: The coworker treats Dilbert's legitimate complaint as proof that he should never be allowed to talk, using the very behavior he's objecting to as her justification for it.
summary: A confused listener protests that he was silenced throughout a baffling meeting, and the speaker answers that his protest is exactly why she silenced him.

title: Watering Plastic Plants Under Contract

situation: Dilbert catches a contractor watering a plastic plant and asks why. The contractor explains that the boss swapped the live plants for fake ones to save money, but nobody cancelled his company's watering contract, so he keeps doing it. He jokes that his career is meaningless but still beats a cubicle, which leaves Dilbert depressed.
punchline: The watering contractor's pointless job is still preferable to Dilbert's own cubicle existence, so Dilbert concludes that talking to people only makes him feel worse.
summary: A man keeps tending fake foliage because his employer's contract was never terminated, and his cheerful acceptance of futility leaves Dilbert gloomy about his own job.

Dilbert asks if it worked, and Wally says he thinks so but will put a donut by the cave entrance just in case.
punchline: Wally treats caring about his work as a dangerous creature or ailment to be drowned in coffee and kept caged with a donut, showing his commitment to doing as little as possible.
summary: A habitually lazy coworker battles a rare flash of conscientiousness by gulping down coffee and planning to bar its return with pastry.

punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that sitting next to the relentless, grating laughter makes every moment drag on so painfully that time now feels very slow.
summary: A boss puts an incessantly cackling new hire right next to Dilbert, whose workday now crawls by in misery.

He then explains that this means complying with all company policies plus every government procurement rule. Dilbert complains of feeling smothered, and the Boss cheerfully insists that this is what victory feels like.
punchline: Winning a government contract is really a prize of overwhelming bureaucracy, and the oblivious Boss presents the suffocating burden as the sensation of success.
summary: A triumphant announcement of a big government deal quickly turns into a pile of extra rules, and the boss insists the suffocation is the reward.

punchline: The customer response is so absurdly insulting that the only way it counts as 'unpredictable' good writing is as sarcastic praise for something terrible.
summary: A colleague's complaint-response letter dismisses an angry customer with a bizarre insult, and her reviewer deadpans that its weirdness makes it flawless.

situation: Alice, wearing a heavy hooded parka at her desk, complains to Dilbert that the office is freezing and asks why he isn't cold. Dilbert replies that his larger brain generates body heat when he thinks. He then notes that Alice's angry reaction to his insult is warming her up as well.
punchline: Dilbert insults Alice's intelligence by claiming her brain is smaller, and her furious reaction generates enough heat to warm her up, proving his point about thinking-induced warmth.
summary: A shivering coworker in a parka learns that insulting her intelligence is a surprisingly effective way of getting her temperature up.

punchline: The scheme is cynically self-serving, and Wally's idea of executive coaching is so inappropriate that it shows how easily the company would get its clients fired.
summary: A company invents its own demand by sabotaging clients with terrible coaching so it can then profit from placing replacements.

summary: A pair of employees talk their vain manager into broadcasting his whereabouts online so they can tell when to look busy.

title: Stock Tip From Self-Proclaimed Expert

transcript.text: Shocker.

situation: A male coworker with a bold pompadour-style haircut offers Alice a stock tip while they both hold coffee. Alice sarcastically questions his credibility, pointing out his ridiculous hair. He responds by adding that he also knows about old cars, and Alice dryly acknowledges how unsurprising that is.
punchline: The coworker's claimed expertise in old cars fits his dated, vintage hairstyle perfectly, so Alice's sarcastic 'Shocker' confirms that his credentials only reinforce her doubts.
summary: Alice shoots down a coworker's unsolicited investment advice by mocking his outdated hairdo, and his follow-up boast about vintage automobiles only proves her point.

The Boss responds only by joking that he will avoid dinner invitations to Asok's house, and Asok angrily shouts back.
punchline: The Boss reacts to an employee's genuine poverty with a callous quip about not wanting to eat at his house, showing zero sympathy for the pay cut he is imposing.
summary: A manager demanding salary reductions answers a hungry employee's hardship story with a heartless joke about his cooking.

situation: Two businessmen sit across a table negotiating a price during a recession. The Boss claims his company needs a 20% price reduction or it will fail, and the other man tops this with an absurd claim about how poor his company is. The Boss offers a compromise of 10%, and the other man keeps escalating with another poverty joke.
punchline: The negotiation turns into a poverty one-upmanship contest, with each side exaggerating its destitution to gain leverage, and the other man refuses to stop even when a deal is offered.
summary: Two executives haggle over a discount by trying to outdo each other with ridiculous claims of corporate poverty.

title: Couch Questions Boss's Great Suggestions

punchline: Dilbert insults the boss by comparing him to an idiot couch, since the only distraction at home would be a couch that questions his good ideas, which is exactly what the boss does.
summary: An employee seeking to telecommute slips in an insult by likening his skeptical manager to a piece of furniture.

As she stands there looking pleased, he directs her to a seat next to the Chief Artificial Coffee Creamer Officer, revealing the title carries no real status.
punchline: By seating the new Chief People Officer next to the Chief Artificial Coffee Creamer Officer, Dogbert shows that the supposedly prestigious title is as trivial as every other made-up C-level role.
summary: A canine CEO hands his HR head a grand executive title, then quietly demotes its meaning by parking her beside the most absurd title imaginable.

title: Fixing Pay By Lowering Average

transcript.text: I will correct this injustice, no matter what it takes!

transcript.text: You would do that for me?

transcript.text: You have my word that I will lower the industry average!

situation: The Boss tells Tina that her salary is 20% below the industry average and dramatically vows to fix the injustice. Tina gratefully asks if he would really do that for her. He reveals his plan is to lower the industry average rather than raise her pay.
punchline: The Boss technically keeps his promise to close the pay gap by dragging down the industry average instead of paying Tina more.
summary: A manager promises to remedy an underpaid employee's salary gap, then reveals he intends to shrink the benchmark rather than increase her wages.

title: Dogbert Buys Bank, Insults Executive

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What do you think of that, you big fiduciary bag?

setting: Executive office with a desk and a high-backed chair
situation: Dogbert, acting as a CEO, sits across a desk from a bank executive. He announces he will buy the failed bank for a single dollar. He then explains that phase two is insulting the executive with ordinary business jargon, and demonstrates by calling him a 'big fiduciary bag'.
punchline: Dogbert mocks the failed banker with business jargon dressed up as an insult, satirizing both the bank collapse bailouts and corporate buzzwords.
summary: A canine chief executive snaps up a wrecked bank for pocket change and then trades blows with the ex-boss using finance-speak as name-calling.

title: Herding Cats Offends Catbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, we're hosting a forum for human resources executives, and I need you to organize it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! That will be like trying to herd cats.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: What did you just say?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm not a racist.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Denial is proof!

situation: The Boss asks Asok to organize a forum for human resources executives. Asok complains that it will be like herding cats, and Catbert, the evil HR director who is a cat, overhears. When Asok protests that he is not a racist, Catbert declares that denial is proof of guilt.
punchline: Catbert, a cat in charge of HR, treats the common idiom 'herding cats' as a racial slur against cats, and twists Asok's defensive denial into evidence of guilt, mocking how HR can punish innocent remarks.
summary: An intern's offhand idiom about cats gets him accused of bigotry by the feline human resources director who refuses to accept his protests.

title: Phased Plan to Deceive Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In phase one, we'll tell our customer that the system failure won't happen again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In phase two, when it happens again, we'll act surprised.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then we'll say a software patch is being installed.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! We're bad people!

situation: The Boss presents a slide showing a man labeled 'Not us!' and lays out a multi-phase plan for handling a customer after a system failure. The plan involves promising it won't recur, feigning surprise when it does, and blaming a software patch. A coworker panics at the dishonesty while Dilbert sits calmly.
punchline: The Boss's carefully staged plan to deceive the customer is so blatantly dishonest that a coworker finally breaks down screaming that they are bad people, while the Boss remains unbothered.
summary: A manager outlines a scripted deception for placating a customer after repeated outages, and one horrified listener realizes how unethical it is.

title: Three Days of Elbonian Starvation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to attend a three-day industry standards meeting in Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why Elbonia?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because Elbonia is the worst place on Earth. The member companies don't want this to look like a boondoggle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess three days won't be so bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not allowed to eat.

situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to attend a three-day industry standards meeting in Elbonia. He explains that the location was chosen because it is the worst place on Earth, so the member companies won't think the trip is a boondoggle. When Dilbert shrugs it off as tolerable, the Boss adds that he isn't allowed to eat.
punchline: To avoid any appearance of a perk-filled junket, the trip is deliberately made miserable, to the point of forbidding Dilbert from eating.
summary: A manager sends an employee to a wretched foreign country on purpose so the business trip can't be mistaken for a vacation, then piles on an extra hardship.

title: Wally Tricks Boss Into Slacking

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you prefer that I spend the day planning, which doesn't look like work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or should I plunge into my project with aggressive randomness?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He told you to not work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He doesn't know it yet.

setting: Office cubicle area and coffee station
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, offers the Boss a choice between spending the day planning, which looks like idle time, or diving into his project in a chaotic, random manner. After the Boss leaves, Dilbert asks if the Boss told Wally not to work, and Wally answers that the Boss hasn't realised it yet.
punchline: Wally frames a false choice so that either answer lets him avoid real work, and the Boss will unknowingly approve his slacking.
summary: Wally offers his manager two equally unproductive ways to spend the day, steering him into accidentally sanctioning laziness.

title: Fake Hearing Aid Dodges Boss's Requests

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I don't do what you ask me to do, it's because my hearing aid fell in the toilet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't know you had a hearing problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eh? What? Eh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could try e-mailing me, but I have my spam filter cranked up to "Taliban."

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells the Boss in advance that if he fails to do what's asked, it's because his hearing aid fell in the toilet. When the Boss says he didn't know about a hearing problem, Dilbert pretends to be deaf. He then adds that e-mail won't work either because of his extreme spam filter setting.
punchline: Dilbert pre-emptively builds excuses to ignore the Boss, claiming fake deafness and a spam filter so aggressive it blocks everything, comparing it to a terrorist group.
summary: An employee invents a bogus disability and an over-aggressive spam filter so he can plausibly ignore every instruction his manager gives him.

title: Unproductive Time Means Your Life

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to write a white paper for an industry trade association.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fine, but that will leave me with less time to work on my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do the trade association stuff during your unproductive time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What exactly is my "unproductive time"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It goes by many names, including sleep, leisure and healthy lifestyle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I do less of those things it will reduce the quality of my life below the point at which good hygiene has any utility.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to make out with you. I just want you to work harder for no extra money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I spend too much time explaining the obvious.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to write a white paper for an industry trade association. When Dilbert says it will cut into his project time, the Boss tells him to do it in his 'unproductive time', which Dilbert learns means sleep, leisure and a healthy lifestyle. Dilbert protests that his quality of life would collapse, and the Boss replies that he just wants more work for no extra pay.
punchline: The Boss treats the employee's sleep and personal life as free, unused capacity, demands unpaid overtime, and then complains that he wastes time explaining things that should be obvious.
summary: A manager dumps an extra writing task on an employee by redefining his rest and personal life as spare time to be exploited without compensation.

title: Hired to Sell Laptops to Idiots

transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.text: Okay. What-ever.

transcript.text: There's no base pay. You only get paid on commission.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can buy it from our company with a 5% employee discount.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're hired.

transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
