transcript.speaker: Job Applicant
transcript.text: By the way, what does the company sell?

setting: Dogbert's office, during a job interview
situation: Dogbert interviews a job applicant with no sales experience and hires him anyway. The terms are commission-only pay and a required special laptop that the applicant must buy from the company. Only after being hired and celebrating does the applicant ask what the company sells.
punchline: The company's real business is selling laptops to gullible people like the new hire, who has just become its latest customer.
summary: A desperate job seeker joyfully accepts a commission-only post and buys his own required laptop, never realizing he is the product being sold.

title: Replaced By A Pile Of Binders

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I want to thank you for your 14 years of loyal service in this fabric-covered box.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On a related note, the company has decided to right-size. And keeping you would be the wrong size.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Clear out your debris in an hour so I can use your cubicle to store my old binders.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Who will do my job?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: So... for all practical purposes I am being replaced by a pile of old binders?

transcript.text: If it makes you feel better, the binders are useless. Everything is online now.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: So... I'm better than old binders?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe this would be a good time to change the subject.

situation: The Boss lays off Ted after 14 years, euphemistically calling it right-sizing and telling him to clear out his cubicle so it can store the Boss's old binders. Ted realizes he is being replaced by a pile of binders, and the Boss admits the binders are useless anyway.
punchline: Ted is being fired to make room for storage of binders the Boss himself admits are useless, so he is worth less than obsolete junk, and the Boss awkwardly tries to end the conversation.
summary: A veteran employee is let go so his cubicle can house obsolete paperwork, and his boss's attempt at comfort only makes it worse.
keywords: no one will do my job

title: Temps Attend Meetings, Fire Contractors

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're paying contractors to do work that I could do if I weren't always in unproductive meetings.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could hire temps to attend the unproductive meetings for me, and fire the more expensive contractors.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why don't I understand what you just said?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because it made sense?

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that he is paying expensive contractors to do work Dilbert could do himself if he weren't stuck in pointless meetings. He proposes hiring cheap temps to sit in the meetings instead and firing the contractors. The Boss is baffled and asks why he doesn't understand the suggestion.
punchline: The Boss can't follow the proposal precisely because it is logical and sensible, which is foreign to his usual way of thinking.
summary: An employee offers a cost-saving fix to wasteful staffing, and his manager is confused only because the idea is so reasonable.

title: Precise Estimate for Undefined Project

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need a budget estimate for my project, but I don't have a scope or a design for it yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, my estimate is $3,583,729.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You don't know anything about my project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That makes two of us.

situation: A coworker in a green sweater asks Dilbert for a budget estimate on a project that has no scope or design. Dilbert responds with an oddly exact dollar figure. When the coworker points out that Dilbert knows nothing about the project, Dilbert replies that neither does the coworker.
punchline: Dilbert's absurdly precise number mocks the request for an estimate on an undefined project, and he points out that the requester knows just as little as he does.
summary: Asked to price a project nobody has defined, Dilbert names a strangely exact figure and observes that the project's owner is just as clueless as he is.

title: CEO Dogbert Silences Questions Violently

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Does anyone have any questions about my strategies?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes, I...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bonk!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This isn't the dotcom era.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: Dogbert, now CEO, asks a boardroom of employees if anyone has questions about his strategies. When an employee raises his hand to ask one, a coffee mug hits him in the head with a bonk. Dogbert then calmly remarks that this isn't the dotcom era.
punchline: Dogbert implies that in a tough economy, employees no longer have the luxury of questioning leadership, so he enforces silence by hurling a mug at anyone who tries.
summary: A dog running the company hurls a mug at the first worker who dares to question his plans, then explains that the days of cushy tolerance are over.

title: Survivors Celebrate, Guilt Workshop Cancelled

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wahoo!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cancel the workshop on survivor guilt.

setting: Office meeting area and the Boss's desk
situation: The Boss announces to the assembled employees that many of their co-workers were laid off but that their own jobs are safe. Instead of mourning, the surviving employees cheer, dance and laugh with glee. Seeing this, the Boss tells an assistant to cancel the planned workshop on survivor guilt.
punchline: The employees feel no guilt at all about their laid-off colleagues, making the company's survivor guilt workshop completely unnecessary.
summary: After a round of layoffs, the remaining staff celebrate wildly, proving that management's planned counseling session was a waste.

title: Halloween Costume Mocks Management Style

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why does it seem so familiar?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table with two coworkers, all wearing Halloween costume horns or hunchback-style headgear. One coworker asks what his costume is supposed to be, and he explains it's a village idiot with a dash of Quasimodo. When the coworker says it seems familiar, Dilbert reveals he is dressed as someone's management style.
punchline: Dilbert's costume of a village idiot and hunchback is actually a dig at a boss's management style, implying that style is foolish and deformed.
summary: A Halloween costume turns out to be a veiled insult aimed at the way a certain boss manages people.

title: Top Secret Director Emails From Gmail

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to hear this from the Director.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'll ask him to e-mail you from his Gmail account.

situation: A bald, bespectacled employee holding a coffee mug tells the seated Boss that the director of a top secret research group wants to borrow him for six months, with no disclosure of his location or work. The Boss insists on hearing it from the director himself. The employee cheerfully offers to have the director email the Boss from a Gmail account.
punchline: A supposedly top secret research group's director would contact the Boss from a free personal Gmail account, which is not credible verification and hints the employee is fabricating the whole arrangement.
summary: A worker tries to vanish from his job for half a year by invoking a secret project, then offers a flimsy email as proof.

title: Overpromising Like a Honeymoon Lie

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our customer is asking for features we can't possibly deliver.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say we can. We'll disappoint them later when it's too late to back out.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Leaders don't like it when you compare things to their honeymoons.

setting: The Boss's office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a customer wants features the company can't possibly deliver. The boss instructs him to simply promise them and let the customer be disappointed later, once it's too late to cancel. In the last panel Dilbert is at home with Dogbert on the couch, who notes that leaders dislike having their approach compared to a honeymoon.
punchline: The boss's plan to lure a customer in with promises and disappoint them after they're committed is exactly how a marriage proposal and honeymoon work, and bosses don't like hearing the comparison.
summary: A manager's plan to lock in a customer with false promises gets likened to the way newlyweds find out too late that reality differs from the honeymoon.

title: Drug Side Effects Slap Meeting Attendee

transcript.text: Maybe you should use a doctor who has less-effective pharmaceutical reps in his territory.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Fist!

situation: At a conference table, a coworker explains that his medication makes him drowsy, so he was given a second drug to keep him awake. That drug causes a phantom hand to slap him at random moments. Alice suggests he should switch to a doctor who is less influenced by pharmaceutical sales reps.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that his doctor prescribes drugs to treat the side effects of other drugs because drug company reps are too persuasive, creating a chain of absurd prescriptions.
summary: A man treats one drug's side effect with another drug whose side effect is worse, prompting a pointed remark about doctors swayed by pharmaceutical salespeople.

title: Anger Management School Insults Customers

situation: An instructor named Eddy welcomes a group of angry attendees to his anger management school, with a flip chart labeled 'You' showing an angry figure. He explains he used to be furious at every idiot in the world, and when a student asks how he overcame it, he reveals his method. The attendees, including Dilbert, glare in irritation.
punchline: Eddy cured his anger by running a business where idiots pay him to be insulted, which is exactly what is making his students angrier.
summary: A self-help guru confesses his anger cure is charging fools money to hear himself insult them.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, announces he is taking up crime and asks Dilbert to be one of his henchmen. Dilbert asks what the job involves, and Wally explains that henchmen get killed in reverse order of importance. When Dilbert asks how important he is, Wally implies he would be killed immediately.
punchline: Wally's advice not to bother packing a lunch tells Dilbert he would be the first henchman shot, so the job would be over before lunchtime.
summary: A coffee-sipping coworker recruits a colleague as a criminal sidekick, then bluntly reveals the position has a very short life expectancy.

title: No Charge Code, No Work

transcript.text: It's another failure of management, but I know you can do better next week.

situation: At a conference table, an employee tells The Boss that he accomplished nothing all week because his project has no charge code. He explains that the chargeback group ignores his e-mails and that ethics rules prevent him from using a fake code. He then blames management for the failure while cheerfully assuring The Boss that next week will be better.
punchline: The employee turns his own week of idleness into a management failure and condescendingly encourages The Boss to do better, using bureaucracy and ethics as a perfect excuse for doing nothing.
summary: A worker blames a missing accounting code and unresponsive bureaucrats for a completely unproductive week, then patronizingly encourages his manager to improve.

title: Moisturizer Explains Crimean War Veteran

situation: At a meeting table, a young coworker says the recession frightens him. An older-seeming colleague one-ups him by claiming he survived the Crimean War with nothing to eat but the stench of death. When the young man points out he does not look old enough, the colleague claims moisturizer is the reason.
punchline: The colleague's absurd claim to have fought in the Crimean War in the 1850s is defended with the ridiculous excuse that he looks young thanks to moisturizer.
summary: A man tries to top his coworker's recession worries with an impossible tale from a nineteenth-century war and blames his youthful skin on skin cream.

Dilbert points out that he lacks the time to evaluate every option, so he is bound to choose poorly. The salesman cheerfully replies that selling only counts if the buyer loses.
punchline: The salesman admits that overwhelming customers with choices is deliberate, since a sale is only real if the buyer ends up worse off.
summary: A vendor buries a customer under thousands of configuration choices and then cheerfully admits the customer's inevitable misstep is the whole point of selling.

title: Debt Collector Meets Very Bad Day

situation: Dilbert, working as a debt collector, phones a customer who is behind on his bills. The man explains his terrible circumstances, and Dilbert asks if that excuses the unpaid bills. The final panel shows the debtor on the phone with a pot on his head, an arrow stuck nearby and rabid badgers clinging to him.
punchline: The debtor insists he isn't making excuses, only noting the call came at a bad time, while he is literally being attacked by badgers and shot at with arrows.
summary: A bill collector's phone call reaches a man whose life is an absurd disaster zone of archery fire and snarling badgers.

situation: Dilbert walks up to a woman at her cubicle and tries to introduce himself, but she stops him and insists she only meets men through online dating sites so she can screen out losers. Dilbert says she is too crazy too fast, and she calmly admits she is aware of the problem and working on it.

summary: A coworker shuts down an in-person introduction by explaining her strict online-only approach to meeting men, then agrees she comes across as a bit much.

A coworker tries to one-up him by claiming he paid a homeless Elbonian family a million dollars to take his house. Dilbert protests that a recession isn't a competition, and the boaster dismisses him as a loser.
punchline: Even in a recession, the one-upper insists on winning the contest of who lost the most, and he mocks anyone who points out it isn't a competition.
summary: Coworkers trade stories of housing-market misery until one boasts of a ridiculous loss and brushes off the objection that suffering isn't a contest.

Dogbert then says he will phone himself to demand ransom for returning the Boss to his own office.

summary: A dog in charge of the company shows his contract lets him abduct staff, then arranges to pay himself for releasing his captive.

title: Buying the Company to Fire You

transcript.text: Thanks for not being totally worthless.

situation: Dogbert stands on the Boss's desk and announces that he bought a majority stake in the company after its stock collapsed to a penny a share. He explains he can double his investment simply by firing the Boss, then thanks him for not being totally worthless. The oblivious Boss replies 'You're welcome', taking the insult as a compliment.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he politely accepts thanks for being 'not totally worthless' while being told he is about to be fired, and the firing itself is what makes the company valuable.
summary: After snapping up most of a collapsing company's shares, Dogbert reveals that dismissing the manager will instantly double his money, and the manager doesn't notice the insult.

title: Filtering Accuracy Through Sales Reps

transcript.text: Our VP of Sales asks that you answer customer questions through the sales reps, not directly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the goal to reduce the timeliness of my answers or just to filter out the accuracy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why are you like this?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I tell you or the sales reps?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert, who is typing at his computer, that the VP of Sales wants customer questions answered through the sales reps rather than directly. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether the aim is to slow his answers or to strip out their accuracy. When the Boss asks why he is like this, Dilbert asks whether he should explain it to the Boss or to the sales reps.
punchline: Dilbert turns the new rule against the Boss by suggesting that routing information through sales reps is how accuracy gets lost, so he'll only answer 'why are you like this' by mocking the same flawed middleman process.
summary: An engineer mocks a mandate to route technical answers through salespeople, implying the detour only delays and distorts the truth.

title: Boss Practices Dismissive Scoffing Sound

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Book some one-on-one meetings for me so I can practice my new dismissive scoffing sound.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and then I think we should...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phhht!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like what you've done with your dismissive scoffing sound.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: 20% more spittle!

situation: The Boss asks his assistant to schedule one-on-one meetings so he can rehearse a new dismissive scoffing sound. In the meeting, Dilbert tries to make a suggestion and the Boss scoffs at him with a spray of spit. Dilbert then flatters the sound, and the Boss proudly says it now has more spittle.
punchline: The Boss treats insulting his employees as a skill to improve, and Dilbert's flattering reply only encourages him, as the Boss takes pride in the extra spit.
summary: A manager rehearses his contempt on his own staff and is delighted to learn his disdain has become messier.

title: Violence Fixes the Network Printer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After you punched that monitor, the broken printer started working.

transcript.speaker: Printer
transcript.text: Humm

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They were on the same network. Word gets around.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And you won't need passwords for a while.

transcript.speaker: Printer
transcript.text: Please don't hurt me.

situation: Dilbert notes that the broken printer began working right after Alice punched a monitor. Alice, still holding the damaged monitor, explains that the devices share a network so news of the violence spread. The printer now pleads not to be hurt, and Alice adds that the threat will also keep the system from demanding passwords.
punchline: Alice's violent outburst intimidated the networked machines into behaving, implying that threatening technology is the only reliable IT support.
summary: After one machine gets smashed, the rest of the office equipment cowers and starts obeying, so even login security gives way to fear.

title: Boss Now Has Reason for Apathy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just forgot what it's like to be one of the little people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's liberating because I have no empathy for your suffering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And how is this different?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I have a reason.

situation: The Boss stands beside Dilbert's desk holding a coffee mug and announces that he has forgotten what it's like to be a lowly employee. He says this frees him from feeling any empathy for Dilbert's suffering. Dilbert, seated at his computer, points out that the Boss never had empathy before.
punchline: The Boss has always been indifferent to his employees' suffering, but now he considers his lack of empathy justified rather than just natural callousness.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits he no longer remembers life at the bottom of the ladder, and his employee notes that his coldness is nothing new.

title: Restraining Order Against Wally's Role

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: Wally, we'd like to transition your role in this project.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: During the first week, you were the lead engineer.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: Going forward, you'll be in more of an advisory role.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: And by that I mean we have a restraining order against you.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: You're not allowed within 100 yards of the conference room.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: We've changed our cell phone numbers and e-mail addresses.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink sweater
transcript.text: And we're all having reconstructive surgery so you won't recognize us in the hallway.

transcript.speaker: Man with pointy hair
transcript.text: Did you accomplish anything this week?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mary, is that you?

setting: Conference room, then an office hallway
situation: A woman in a meeting tells Wally his role in the project is being 'transitioned', then reveals this means a restraining order, banned access to the conference room, changed contact details, and even plastic surgery to avoid him. In the last panel, a pointy-haired man asks Wally if he accomplished anything this week, and Wally fails to recognize the woman as Mary.
punchline: The polite corporate euphemism of an 'advisory role' escalates into a literal restraining order, and the colleagues' surgery works so well that Wally doesn't recognize Mary.
summary: Coworkers escalate from gently reassigning a lazy colleague to legally and surgically avoiding him entirely.

title: Project Risk: Our Own Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The biggest risk to the project is our own thundering incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It is a known fact that every project has at least one irredeemable imbecile.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a vague, uneasy feeling about your clip art.

setting: Conference room during a project presentation
situation: Dilbert gives a presentation to The Boss and a coworker, with a slide showing a cartoon figure labeled 'Duh!'. He bluntly says the project's biggest risk is the team's own incompetence and that every project has an irredeemable imbecile. The Boss, missing the point entirely, responds only with unease about Dilbert's clip art.
punchline: The Boss fails to recognize that the 'irredeemable imbecile' described is himself, and instead criticizes the clip art, proving Dilbert's point.
summary: A candid risk assessment slide goes right over the head of the very manager it describes, who only fusses about the artwork.

title: Streamlining Christmas Gift Exchange Efficiency

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Merry Christmas. Here's a hundred bucks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And here's a hundred bucks for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could save another step by setting up an electronic transfer with an annual recurring option.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Excellent.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Or we could not give gifts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hush your crazy talk.

setting: Dilbert's home kitchen table on Christmas morning
situation: Dilbert in a bathrobe hands Dogbert a hundred dollars as a Christmas gift, and Dogbert hands him a hundred back. Dilbert proposes automating the swap with a recurring electronic transfer, and Dogbert then points out they could simply skip the gifts, which Dilbert dismisses.
punchline: The two optimize a pointless cash swap into an automated process but reject the obvious solution of not exchanging gifts at all.
summary: Two friends trade identical cash gifts and then try to make the ritual more efficient instead of dropping it.

title: Asok's Many Side Jobs

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Asok, we need to cut your pay again. But maybe you could get a second job.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Second???

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I am already doing freelance I.T. support... and donating blood... and working as a male escort.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I don't need the details.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Running guns... robbing graves... starting a hedge fund...

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Asok his pay is being cut yet again and suggests he take a second job. Asok nervously reveals he already has several side gigs, starting with freelance IT support and blood donation and escalating to male escorting. Catbert cuts him off, but Asok keeps listing increasingly illegal and shady jobs.
punchline: Asok's list of side jobs escalates from desperate to criminal, ending with starting a hedge fund as the worst of all, implying that the finance industry is as morally dubious as grave robbing and gun running.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel slashes an underling's salary and is then treated to a growing catalogue of the shady ways the employee already scrapes by.

title: Shirtless Employees Shield the Servers

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The employees are scared shirtless about losing their jobs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This is a good time to cut their benefits and roll out some draconian corporate policies.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "In the event of a bomb threat, the employees are expected to shield the servers with their bodies."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I miss my shirt.

setting: The Boss's office and the office cubicle area
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that employees are so frightened of layoffs that it's the perfect moment to cut benefits and impose harsh new policies. In the cubicles, a new policy requires employees to shield servers with their bodies during a bomb threat, while a shirtless Dilbert and Wally stand by.
punchline: The employees were literally scared shirtless, and now Wally wistfully misses his shirt while management exploits their fear to impose absurdly harsh policies.
summary: Taking advantage of job-loss panic, the HR cat slashes perks and invents ridiculous rules, leaving the staff both figuratively and literally stripped down.

title: Stress Tests Without Yes-No Answers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Morgan: The man with no communication skills.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you get the results from the stress tests yet?

transcript.speaker: Morgan
transcript.text: Stress tests have to be performed under controlled conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Has anyone ever explained to you the yes-no form of questions?

transcript.speaker: Morgan
transcript.text: Is it my turn to talk?

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker named Morgan, who is labeled as having no communication skills, a simple question about whether the stress test results are in. Morgan responds with an irrelevant statement about controlled conditions instead of answering. When Dilbert asks if anyone has explained yes-no questions, Morgan asks whether it is his turn to talk.
punchline: Morgan's complete inability to communicate extends even to recognizing a conversation, as he doesn't realize he has already been talking and just gave a non-answer.
summary: A coworker famous for being unable to communicate dodges a straightforward question with a tangent, then reveals he doesn't even grasp how conversational turns work.

title: Wally's Dream Job: Fake Inventory

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to do an inventory in our warehouses. It should take about a month.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hypothetically, would anyone know the difference if I just made up the numbers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, no. . .

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Dream job!

situation: The Boss assigns Wally a month-long inventory of the company warehouses. Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks whether anyone would notice if he simply invented the figures. The Boss admits nobody would, and Wally cheers and dances with delight.
punchline: The Boss inadvertently confirms that nobody checks the inventory numbers, giving the perpetually lazy Wally a month of paid time doing nothing.
summary: Offered a tedious warehouse count, a slacker discovers that fabricating the results would go unnoticed and celebrates his good fortune.

title: Procedures for Policies for Procedures

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to develop a procedure for creating policies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do we have a policy on how to develop procedures?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think someone wrote a white paper on that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the procedure for finding white papers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could ask around.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that night

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: So, what do you do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I ask around to see if anyone knows about a white paper that talks about a policy for developing procedures to create policies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You find that sexy.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Stop doing the Jedi mind trick!

setting: Office meeting room, then an evening party
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to create a procedure for creating policies, and Dilbert's questions lead him into a circular chain of needing white papers, procedures and policies. Later at a party, a woman asks what he does for a living, and he describes his convoluted task in the same recursive way.
punchline: Dilbert's job description is so tediously circular that he treats it as an alluring pickup line, and the woman accuses him of a Jedi mind trick for making her feel attracted.
summary: A boss assigns a self-referential bureaucratic task, and the same dull circularity later gets Dilbert unexpected romantic interest at a party.

title: Risk Software Rejects Honesty Input

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our risk management software says your idea is too risky.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try reducing one of the inputs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which one?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Honesty.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I just threw up in my mouth.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with an office building exterior in the final panel
situation: Dilbert tells the group that the risk management software has flagged an idea as too risky. The Boss, seated at the table, suggests tweaking the software's inputs to get a better result. When Dilbert asks which input, the Boss says honesty, and Alice reacts with disgust.
punchline: The Boss's fix for a failing risk assessment is to feed the software dishonest data so it approves the idea, a suggestion so unethical that Alice is physically sickened.
summary: Faced with software that calls his plan too dangerous, the boss recommends fudging the numbers by lowering the truthfulness of the data.

title: Dead Cat Transfer Request Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's an opening in my old department. Is it okay if I apply?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure. I'd be happy to toss that dead cat in someone else's backyard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was worried that I might be too valuable...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why are you still here?

situation: Dilbert asks Alice, who is holding a coffee mug, for permission to apply for an opening in his old department. Alice cheerfully agrees because she would be getting rid of an unwanted employee. Dilbert says he feared he was too valuable to be released, and Alice angrily asks why he is still around.
punchline: Dilbert assumes he is too valuable to lose, but Alice makes clear she considers him a worthless burden she is eager to pass on to someone else.
summary: An employee seeking a transfer discovers his supervisor views him as an unwanted problem she is delighted to offload.

title: Doing Nothing Versus Useless Designs

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I did no work this week because I judged the user's specifications to be inadequate.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Should I continue to do nothing or do you prefer I use incomplete specs to produce useless designs?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The next thing you hear is something called leadership.

setting: Conference room meeting around a table
situation: At a meeting, a bald coworker with glasses admits he did no work all week because the user's specifications were inadequate. He offers his boss a choice between continuing to do nothing or producing useless designs from incomplete specs. The boss, visibly angry and steaming, threatens to show him 'leadership'.
punchline: The coworker's false dilemma exposes that the project's problem is poor requirements, but the boss responds with an angry threat of 'leadership' instead of fixing the specs.
summary: An employee justifies a week of idleness by blaming bad requirements, and his fuming manager answers with a menacing promise of leadership.

title: Injuring Yourself to Avoid Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't understand why...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did you suddenly stop talking?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh no... This can't be good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!!! Now you're not making eye contact with me!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Layoffs are coming! I must be on the list!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My only hope is to injure myself and go on disability so he can't legally fire me.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, as I was saying, I can't figure out why so many employees are injured.

situation: The Boss is chatting with Dilbert and abruptly stops talking and looks away. Dilbert misreads the lack of eye contact as a sign that layoffs are coming and that he is on the list. He decides to injure himself to qualify for disability, and the Boss then wonders aloud why so many employees are getting hurt.
punchline: The Boss's innocent pause causes Dilbert to panic and hurt himself, and the Boss is baffled that fear of layoffs is behind the rash of employee injuries.
summary: A manager's awkward silence convinces a worried employee that his job is doomed, so he harms himself to dodge the axe while the manager puzzles over the injury statistics.

title: Honesty Impedes Sales, Oops

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hey, engineer, can I ask you a question?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to talk to customers. We believe that honesty impedes sales.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I think you just impeded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops.

situation: A customer approaches Dilbert, an engineer, to ask a question. Dilbert explains that engineers are forbidden from speaking with customers because the company believes honesty hurts sales. The customer points out that Dilbert has just let the truth slip, and Dilbert realizes his mistake.
punchline: By explaining the company's policy of keeping engineers away from customers, Dilbert accidentally reveals the very honesty the policy is meant to prevent, damaging sales on the spot.
summary: An engineer blurts out the real reason he is barred from customer contact and so proves the rule right in the act of citing it.
keywords: not allowed to talk to customers

title: Wally Explains Getting Paid for Nothing

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I didn't do any work this week because my project will probably be cancelled in the next budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I don't pay you to do nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure you do.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But I understand your confusion.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I too was surprised by the first few years of getting paid for doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In time, doing nothing became its own sort of challenge.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm like a ninja with no hopes and dreams.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, set up a meeting with me later.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll get right on that.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally cheerfully admits he did no work all week because his project will likely be cancelled in upcoming budget cuts. The Boss objects that he doesn't pay Wally to do nothing, and Wally calmly replies that he does. Wally then philosophizes about how doing nothing has become a challenge over the years, and the Boss, unfazed, asks him to schedule a meeting.
punchline: Wally exposes that the company has been paying him for doing nothing for years, and the oblivious Boss responds by assigning him a meeting, which Wally will treat as just another way to avoid real work.
summary: A slacking engineer openly admits to idleness and turns his years of paid inactivity into a mock-heroic art form while his clueless manager misses the point entirely.

title: Industry Standards: Success or Failure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How did the industry standards meeting go?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you convince 83 companies to adopt standards that benefit only us while dooming the entire industry in the long run?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or are you a complete failure?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I hear those choices again?

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Dilbert how the industry standards meeting went. He then offers only two possible outcomes: Dilbert tricked 83 companies into adopting self-serving standards that will ruin the industry, or he is a complete failure. Dilbert, unimpressed by the options, asks to hear them again.
punchline: The Boss presents a choice between unethical, industry-destroying success and total failure, and Dilbert's request to hear the choices again suggests he finds both options unappealing, or that he is weighing which is the lesser evil.
summary: A manager frames a meeting's outcome as either a sneaky triumph that sabotages everyone or personal disgrace, leaving his employee asking for a second look at the menu.

title: Venture Capitalist's Dollar Sign Hair

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Vijay, the world's worst venture capitalist

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A hundred million people need this type of service.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already built the web site and people are signing up.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Foop!

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: When we negotiate my equity stake, focus on my poker face and not my optimistic hair.

transcript.speaker: Vijay
transcript.text: Yee-ha!!!

setting: A meeting table in an office
situation: Dilbert pitches his web service to Vijay, a venture capitalist, explaining that a hundred million people need it and that users are already signing up. As Dilbert makes his case, a large dollar sign pops up in Vijay's hair, revealing his excitement. Vijay then tells Dilbert to ignore the hair and watch his poker face during negotiations.
punchline: Vijay is a terrible negotiator because his hair involuntarily sprouts a giant dollar sign when he gets excited, undermining his poker face and giving away how much he wants the deal.
summary: An investor's hair betrays his greed with a giant money symbol while he insists he is hiding his enthusiasm during a startup pitch.

title: Servile Executive Compensation Committee Members

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You two are my executive compensation committee.

transcript.speaker: Orange creature
transcript.text: I live to serve you, my lord and master!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dial it back just a little.

transcript.speaker: Green dinosaur
transcript.text: Are we allowed to kneel?

situation: Dogbert, as CEO, appoints two subordinates to be his executive compensation committee. One gushes with exaggerated servility and calls him lord and master. Dogbert asks him to tone it down, and the other member asks if they may kneel.
punchline: The people supposed to set the CEO's pay are so obsequious that they cannot be independent, and they are still eager to grovel even after being told to dial it back.
summary: A newly crowned CEO stacks his pay-setting committee with fawning underlings who can barely contain their groveling.

title: Prototype Camera Flash Vaporizes Tester

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss just told me that he changed my drawings for the smart phone before he sent them to you for prototyping.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was wondering if you're having any problems with it?

transcript.speaker: Prototyping Engineer
transcript.text: The camera's flash is a bit aggressive.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and a prototyping lab, connected by a phone call
situation: Dilbert phones the prototyping engineer to check on his smart phone design after learning his boss altered the drawings. The engineer, holding the prototype, calmly says the camera flash is a bit aggressive, while behind him a colleague has been reduced to a smoking skeleton.
punchline: The engineer's mild understatement about an 'aggressive' flash hides the fact that the boss's design changes turned the phone into a weapon that incinerated a coworker.
summary: After the boss secretly tampers with a phone design, the prototype's camera flash turns out to be lethal enough to leave a technician as a smoldering skeleton.

title: Choosing Between Two Layoff Candidates

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you want to lay off the highly skilled, whiny jerk who is toxic to the workplace or. . .

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: . . . the pleasant but incompetent guy who will lead us to ruination?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: This got harder after we fired all of the unskilled, whiny jerks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one is uglier?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, presents the Boss with a layoff decision between a talented but toxic employee and a likeable but incompetent one. He notes the choice is harder now that the unskilled, whiny employees are already gone. The Boss ignores the substance and asks which of the two is uglier.
punchline: The Boss decides who loses their job based on appearance rather than skill, behavior or any business reasoning.
summary: Faced with a hard downsizing choice, the boss settles it by picking the less attractive person.

title: Fixing Only Some Bugs Means Failure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can only afford to fix the high-priority bugs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we don't fix 100% of the bugs, the software will be 100% useless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So our plan is to fail?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: More slowly.

situation: The Boss reads from a paper and tells Dilbert that the budget only allows fixing the high-priority bugs. Dilbert objects that unfixed bugs will make the software completely useless and asks if the plan is to fail. The Boss calmly confirms it, adding only that the failure will be slower.
punchline: The Boss admits the plan is to fail, treating a slower failure as an acceptable improvement, which mocks management's short-sighted budget-driven decisions.
summary: A manager cites limited funds to justify leaving most software defects unrepaired, then happily admits the result will simply be a gradual collapse.

title: Background Check Ends in Beating

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, I just got the results of your security clearance background check.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Homeland Security ordered me to beat you to death with our emergency preparedness binder.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: But... I haven't done anything wrong!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I might have said some things about your new beard.

setting: Office cubicle, with an exterior shot of the office building in the last panel
situation: The Boss stands at Ted's cubicle and announces he has the results of Ted's security clearance background check. He then claims Homeland Security has ordered him to beat Ted to death with the emergency preparedness binder. When Ted protests his innocence, the final panel (shown outside the building) reveals the Boss may have given the agency negative information about Ted's new beard.
punchline: The Boss let his personal dislike of Ted's new beard influence the background check, so the supposed government order to kill Ted is really a petty grudge.
summary: A manager reports a grim verdict from a security screening, then casually admits he may have slandered his employee's facial hair to the investigators.

title: Faxing Requirements Back to 1995

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Can I send our requirements to your fax?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Absolutely.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'll just travel back in time to 1995, when faxing was a good way to handle this sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You realize I'm a customer, right?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Until you spend all of your money on new fax machines.

setting: Office desk during a business meeting
situation: A customer asks Dilbert if he can send the project requirements to Dilbert's fax machine. Dilbert enthusiastically agrees, then mocks the idea by saying he will travel back to 1995 when faxing made sense. The customer points out that he is a customer and Dilbert threatens that he will only remain one until he wastes his money on new fax machines.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically mocks the customer's outdated fax habit, then threatens the customer's business with the claim that the customer's spending will be wasted on obsolete fax machines.
summary: A client's request to fax over specifications prompts a sarcastic jab about outdated technology and a pointed reminder of who is paying whom.

title: Check Your Spam Folder Excuse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you didn't e-mail me your project status.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you check your spam folder?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you should check there before you besmirch my good name with your baseless accusations.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you send it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I see how you're trying to turn this all around.

situation: The Boss tells Wally he never received his project status e-mail. Wally responds by suggesting the Boss check his spam folder. When the Boss is then asked whether he actually sent it, he claims Wally is turning the accusation back on him.
punchline: The Boss, who never sent the status e-mail himself, indignantly accuses Wally of deflecting blame while doing exactly that, so the strip pokes fun at the endless blame-shifting and 'check your spam folder' excuses that pass for accountability.
summary: A missing status report triggers a round of mutual blame in which each person insists the other should have checked or sent something first.

title: Late Because of Serial Killer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry I'm late. My company cut the travel budget so I had to hitch a ride with a serial killer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He took me to an abandoned slaughterhouse. I knocked him out with a hambone, stole his truck and drove directly here.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: All I heard was "Blah, blah, blah, I'm late."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't make me get my hambone.

situation: Dilbert arrives late to a meeting and explains that budget cuts forced him to hitch a ride with a serial killer, whom he then knocked out with a hambone before stealing his truck. A coworker dismisses the whole story as just another excuse for being late. Dilbert responds by threatening him with the hambone.
punchline: Dilbert's genuinely harrowing excuse is brushed off by a coworker as a routine lateness excuse, so he threatens violence with the same hambone he used on the killer.
summary: A tardy employee blames a slashed travel budget for a near-death ordeal, but his indifferent colleague tunes it out, earning a menacing warning.

title: Dogbert Propositions CEOs to Collude

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO Summit

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you collude?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Sometimes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you colluding with anyone now, because I'd sure like to collude with you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What are you into? Maybe a little price-fixing?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: This is all happening so fast.

situation: At a CEO summit, Dogbert stands on a stool holding a drink and asks a nearby executive whether he colludes. After the exec admits he sometimes does, Dogbert eagerly pitches himself as a collusion partner and suggests price-fixing. The flustered CEO says it is all happening too fast.
punchline: Dogbert hits on a CEO with the pushy tone of a romantic pick-up line, but for illegal price-fixing, and the exec responds like a nervous date.
summary: A scheming dog works the room at an executive mixer, chatting up a businessman as if propositioning him for an illicit price-fixing arrangement.

title: CEO Dogbert Punishes Consumers for Pay Cap

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We need to make our pricing plan more confusing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And change our packaging to that hard plastic that always cuts the consumers' hands.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been in a bad mood since everyone started talking about capping my excessive pay.

situation: Dogbert, serving as CEO, sits behind a desk and gives orders to the Pointy-Haired Boss, who stands by. He first demands a more confusing pricing plan, then orders packaging in hard plastic that cuts customers' hands. He finally explains that these cruel ideas stem from his bad mood over talk of limiting his pay.
punchline: The CEO takes out his anger over proposed executive pay caps by deliberately inflicting misery on his own customers.
summary: An irritable chief executive makes his products worse for shoppers as petty revenge for people criticizing his huge salary.

title: Become Patent Trolls, Skip Innovation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to my analysis, all future ideas are already covered by over-general patents.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our best strategy is to get out of this business and become trademark infringement lawyers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how to be a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That only matters if you take cases on a contingency basis.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his analysis shows every future idea is already covered by overly broad patents, so the company should quit its business and become trademark infringement lawyers. The Boss objects that he has no legal training. Catbert, perched on the desk, points out that lack of skill only matters if lawyers are paid on contingency.
punchline: Catbert implies that lawyers who work on contingency get paid only when they win, so incompetence is a handicap only in that case, which cynically suggests that lawyers otherwise get paid regardless of skill.
summary: Faced with a world where broad patents block all new ideas, Dilbert proposes switching to litigation, and Catbert cynically notes that incompetent lawyers only suffer when they work for a share of the winnings.

title: Showing Pictures of Unwanted Products

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Someone borrowed the unit you asked to see, so I'll show you pictures of models you aren't interested in.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: There's one you don't want... and you sure don't want that one...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And how does this help?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Would you like a CD of products we no longer carry?

setting: A sales office or showroom, with Dilbert seated across a desk from a salesman at a computer
situation: Dilbert has come to see a particular product, but the salesman says someone else borrowed it. Instead he scrolls through pictures of models Dilbert doesn't want. When Dilbert asks how this helps, the salesman offers him a CD of discontinued products.
punchline: The salesman's attempt at helpfulness is completely useless, and he escalates it by offering Dilbert a CD of products the company doesn't even sell anymore.
summary: A salesman who can't produce the requested item fills the time by showing irrelevant photos and then offers a disc of discontinued merchandise.

title: Recession Makes Dilbert Attractive

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're not my type. Why am I attracted to you? How did you do this, you monster!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In troubling economic times, my financial stability appeals to your survival instincts. It's basic evolution.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! That made me bored and aroused at the same time!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Science!

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with a woman who is upset that she finds herself attracted to him even though he isn't her type. Dilbert calmly explains that in a bad economy, his financial stability triggers her survival instincts. She reacts with distress at feeling both bored and aroused, and Dilbert proudly credits science.
punchline: Dilbert's dull but stable finances make him irresistible to a woman's evolutionary instincts in a recession, leaving her simultaneously bored and aroused.
summary: A woman is horrified to discover that a shaky economy has made a steady, unexciting engineer strangely appealing.

title: Dilbert Insults Coworker's Crazy Eyes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'd actually be attractive if you didn't have crazy eyes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The eyes are the mirror of the soul. Your soul appears to be mostly spiders and bad news.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any minute now . . .

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You cause the rain!

situation: Dilbert tells a female coworker she would be attractive if she didn't have crazy eyes, then insults her further by saying her soul is full of spiders and bad news. He then calmly waits for the inevitable reaction, and she screams a bizarre accusation at him.
punchline: Dilbert's tactless insults provoke exactly the unhinged outburst that he predicted, seemingly confirming her crazy eyes while proving he deserved it.
summary: After a blunt comment about a coworker's unsettling gaze escalates into a spider-themed insult, Dilbert simply stands by and awaits her explosive meltdown.

title: Egg Carton Office Vibe Mandate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, remove the toys from your cubicle. It sends the wrong message.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You mean the message that says this company is a creative environment that values the individual?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly. We're going for more of an egg carton vibe.

situation: The Boss stands beside Alice's desk and orders her to remove the toys from her cubicle because they send the wrong message. Alice, seated at her computer, asks if he means the message that the company values creativity and individuals. The Boss confirms and says management wants a uniform, egg carton look instead.
punchline: The Boss openly admits that the company wants identical, interchangeable workers rather than the creative, individual-valuing culture it claims to promote.
summary: A manager forces an employee to strip her desk of playthings, cheerfully conceding that he prefers a bland, uniform workplace to the one the company advertises.

title: Alice Calls Colleagues Mediocre Minds

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We haven't heard from engineering yet. What do you think, Alice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think several mediocre minds concocted an impractical plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Could you be more specific?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sure. You're one of them. And this guy is another. . .

situation: In a meeting, the Boss asks Alice for engineering's opinion on a plan. Alice bluntly says the plan was devised by mediocre minds. When the Boss asks her to be more specific, she points out that he is one of them, along with another man at the table.
punchline: Alice's blunt insult is made worse when she happily names the people at the table, including the Boss, as the mediocre minds behind the plan.
summary: Asked for her opinion, an engineer responds to a vague critique request by pointing straight at the people responsible for the flawed plan.

title: Story Hater Seeks Real Expert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And that was the last time I yanked a cable just to find out what would happen.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: How many inane stories do I have to hear before I can speak to someone who knows something?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: She's a story hater.

situation: The Boss tells a rambling story about yanking a cable to see what would happen while a dark-haired woman sits across the table. She snaps that she is tired of hearing pointless stories and wants to talk to someone who actually knows something. The Boss then complains to Dilbert in the hallway that she is a 'story hater'.
punchline: The Boss treats a reasonable complaint about his useless, rambling stories as a character flaw in the woman, missing the fact that he is the one who knows nothing.
summary: A manager's pointless anecdote exhausts a visitor, and he dismisses her impatience as an odd dislike of storytelling.

title: Automated Questions Fool The Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I programmed my instant-messaging software to send random questions to our boss every hour.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They're all yes or no questions so he'll have the illusion of managing me.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Should I rotate the domain protocols so they wear out evenly?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes

setting: Office cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Wally explains to Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, that he has set up his instant-messaging software to send random yes-or-no questions to the boss every hour. In the last panel the boss sits at his computer, receives a nonsensical technical question about rotating domain protocols, and confidently answers yes.
punchline: The boss is so eager to feel like he is managing that he approves nonsense technical questions without understanding them, and Wally exploits this to keep him satisfied while doing no real work himself.
summary: A lazy employee automates fake questions so his clueless supervisor can feel in control while he is left alone.

title: Brutally Honest Strategy Meeting Presentation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Strategy meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The weak economy is limiting our strategic options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I won't sugarcoat anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Option one is a long slide to oblivion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Option two is a death spiral.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our new company logo is a man getting sucked into a toilet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our revised mission statement is "Forage during daylight. Hide at night."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll pass out clubs, and you can decide among yourselves how to downsize by fifty percent.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is it just me or was it better when they sugar-coated?

setting: Conference room during a strategy meeting
situation: During a strategy meeting, Dilbert gives a presentation that deliberately refuses to sugarcoat the company's grim prospects in a weak economy. He shows slides of a slide to oblivion, a death spiral, and a toilet logo, then hands out clubs so the attendees can decide how to cut the workforce in half. The coworkers start beating each other, and one wishes for the sugarcoated version.
punchline: After hearing a brutally honest presentation that ends with a literal fight to the death over layoffs, a coworker concludes that corporate sugarcoating was preferable to the truth.
summary: A presenter delivers a relentlessly bleak company outlook and arms his colleagues with bats to settle layoffs among themselves, leaving one of them nostalgic for comforting spin.

title: Visitor Named Gom Axfon Arrested

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Tom Jackson. I have a meeting with your boss.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: He has no one by that name on his calendar.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The only people he's meeting today are Fob Meterfon, Gom Axfon, and Dabe Aggams.

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Maybe when your boss said he was meeting with "Tom Jackson" you heard it as "Gom Axfon."

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Is that how you want to play this? Really?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Security, come arrest this man!!!

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: I'm Gom Axfon! I'm Gom Axfon!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's Tom Jackson?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Don't you start with me.

situation: A visitor named Tom Jackson arrives for a meeting with the boss, but the receptionist insists nobody by that name is on the calendar, only people with bizarre names like Gom Axfon. When the visitor suggests she misheard the name, she takes offense and has security arrest him. As he is dragged away claiming to be Gom Axfon, the boss arrives asking where Tom Jackson is.
punchline: The receptionist's rigid, hostile refusal to admit she misheard the name gets an innocent visitor arrested, and she snaps at the boss when he asks the obvious question.
summary: A receptionist who mangled a guest's name responds to the suggestion of her mistake by having him hauled away by guards.

title: One Word Per Day Tweets

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I decided to Twitter because everything that pops into my head is fascinating.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't have time to write entire sentences, so I'll just send out one word per day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Riboflavin.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the arm of the couch next to Dilbert and explains that he has started using Twitter because he finds all of his own thoughts fascinating. He says he will post only one word per day, then sends out a single random word on his phone: riboflavin.
punchline: Dogbert's supposedly fascinating thoughts turn out to be a meaningless random word, mocking the self-importance and banality of social media posts.
summary: A smug Dogbert joins Twitter convinced his every thought is brilliant, and his first one-word post is a vitamin.

title: Capitalism Ends Over Mutual Distrust

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we lease a machine from you, how can we be sure you'll stay in business to service it?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: How can we be sure you'll have enough money to pay the lease?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You could check our financials.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure your financials are as fraudulent as ours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good point. Maybe we could ask trusted third parties to vouch for us.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Do you trust any third parties?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not since my financial advisor put my retirement savings in a Ponzi scheme and had an affair with my wife.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And thus ended capitalism

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, we tried.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Maybe I could grow food in my car.

setting: Conference room during a business negotiation
situation: Dilbert and a prospective customer discuss leasing a machine, but each doubts the other company will survive long enough to honor the deal. Both admit their financials are fraudulent and that they can't trust any third parties to vouch for them. The negotiation collapses, and the narrator declares that capitalism has ended.
punchline: When neither party in a deal can trust the other's finances or any outside verifier, commerce becomes impossible, and the strip humorously declares the collapse of capitalism itself.
summary: Two businessmen realize that mutual fraud and betrayal leave no basis for trust, so their deal falls apart and takes the whole economic system with it.

title: Carol's Murderous Career Goal

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, I'd like to talk to you about your career goals.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: My career goal is to take over the department by tricking you into a fatal accident, then telling everyone you're just working from home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not right.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: So you're saying I should set my goals low?

situation: The Boss approaches Carol's cubicle to discuss her career goals. Carol calmly states that her goal is to replace him by murdering him in a staged accident and covering it up by claiming he is working from home. When he objects, she deadpans that he must want her to set lower goals.
punchline: Carol treats the boss's objection to her homicidal plan as criticism that her career ambitions are too high, deliberately misreading him with deadpan sarcasm.
summary: An employee cheerfully admits she plans to kill her manager and take his job, then interprets his protest as advice to be less ambitious.

title: Dogbert Considers Somali Piracy Career

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking of becoming a Somalian pirate.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd still get to steal from stockholders, but my booty wouldn't be taxed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And who doesn't like grenade launchers?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ka-pow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mom? Cancel your cruise.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hill, with Dogbert sitting on a rock
situation: Dogbert, in his CEO role, muses to Dilbert about quitting to become a Somalian pirate. He points out that he could keep stealing from stockholders while avoiding taxes on his loot, and adds that he likes grenade launchers. Dilbert, alarmed, phones his mother and tells her to cancel her cruise.
punchline: Dogbert's switch from corporate CEO to pirate is barely a career change, since both involve plundering people, and Dilbert is so convinced he'll follow through that he warns his mom off her cruise.
summary: A CEO dog fantasizes about trading the boardroom for high-seas piracy, and his friend responds by urgently protecting his mother from the threat.

title: Rebaterus and the Impossible Rebate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I bought a new phone. It was only $50 after rebate.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see what the terms of the rebate. . .

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FOOM!

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: I am Rebaterus.

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: You must pass five tests before your rebate will be authorized.

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: You must wait 30 days without losing or accidentally discarding the rebate forms, the receipt, and the box.

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: You must figure out which of the several unlabeled codes on the box is the real rebate code.

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: You must write that code into a space designed for a code half as long.

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: Some numbers look like letters.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just keep my money!!!

transcript.speaker: Rebaterus
transcript.text: Dude, we spent it before you left the store.

situation: Dilbert buys a phone advertised as $50 after rebate and opens the box to read the rebate terms. A three-headed green monster named Rebaterus bursts out in a puff of smoke and lays out a series of absurd tests Dilbert must pass to receive the rebate. Dilbert gives up and tells the monster to keep his money.
punchline: The rebate process is deliberately so convoluted that nobody can claim it, and the company has already spent the money, so it never intended to pay out.
summary: A monster guarding a phone rebate piles on ridiculous hurdles until the buyer surrenders, revealing the refund was never really meant to be paid.

title: Ratbert Becomes Sadistic Sales VP

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, you're my new VP of Sales.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your job is to set impossible goals for the salespeople and punish them for failing.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Yay! I always wanted to be a sadist!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dreams do come true.

situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, promotes Ratbert to VP of Sales from behind his desk. He explains that the role consists of setting impossible sales targets and punishing the salespeople when they fail. Ratbert cheerfully celebrates, since he has always wanted to be a sadist.
punchline: The VP of Sales job is described as pure cruelty, which Ratbert sees as a dream come true, satirizing how sales management often relies on unreachable quotas and punishment.
summary: A pet-turned-executive hands his tiny underling a promotion whose entire purpose is to torment the sales team, and the underling is thrilled.

title: Bonus Tied to Strangers' Losses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a bonus because another division had huge losses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remind me again why my bonus is tied to the performance of strangers?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I shouldn't tell you this, but we model our employee compensation program after practical jokes.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss about his bonus and is told he won't get one because a different division lost a lot of money. Dilbert questions why his pay depends on the results of people he doesn't know. The boss admits the compensation program is modeled on practical jokes.
punchline: The boss's admission that the pay system is modeled on practical jokes implies that the bonus program is designed to be unfair and to mock employees rather than reward them.
summary: A manager denies an employee's bonus over another division's failures and then casually confesses the pay system is basically a prank.

title: MBA Versus the Crazy Old Witch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The MBA versus the crazy old witch

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know who to believe.

transcript.speaker: Witch
transcript.text: Spreadsheets don't lie, but neither does bat excrement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remind me again who ruined the economy. Was it witches?

situation: The Boss sits at his desk comparing the analysis of a young MBA and a pointy-hatted witch holding a broom, unsure whose advice to trust. The witch fires back that spreadsheets and bat excrement are equally truthful. The Boss then asks who actually ruined the economy, implying the MBA's side is the discredited one.
punchline: The Boss's sarcastic question implies that MBAs, not witches, wrecked the economy, so the witch's superstition looks more trustworthy than the MBA's spreadsheets.
summary: A confused manager weighs a business-school graduate's data against a witch's mystical claims and decides the graduate's track record is the worse one.

title: Dilbert Meets His Smarter Look-Alike

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: Look-alike
transcript.text: Don't be surprised.

transcript.speaker: Look-alike
transcript.text: In any large company there is at least one employee who is your exact replica and has the same assignment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why didn't I know that?

transcript.speaker: Look-alike
transcript.text: I'm not your replica. I'm a look-alike that is much smarter.

setting: Office, apparently a break area where both hold coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert is startled to come face to face with a man who looks exactly like him. The look-alike calmly explains that every large company has an exact replica of each employee doing the same job. When Dilbert asks why he never knew, the look-alike corrects him, saying he is not a replica but a much smarter look-alike.
punchline: The look-alike insults Dilbert by claiming to be much smarter, which also implies Dilbert is the dumber one and explains why he never noticed the duplicate.
summary: A man who looks just like Dilbert reveals that big companies secretly employ duplicate workers, then boasts that he is the brainier version.

title: Dilbert's Darwinian Pickup Line

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have an actual job and I don't live at home.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My offspring would probably be smart.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My palms are getting sweaty and my heart is pounding. What is going on?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a Darwinian thing.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Make it stop!

setting: A cocktail party or social mixer with wine glasses and a bartender
situation: Dilbert tries to impress a woman at a party by listing his practical qualifications as a mate: he has a job, lives on his own, and would father smart children. She reacts with sweaty palms and a pounding heart, and he coolly explains it's evolutionary instinct. She is horrified and begs for the feeling to stop, spilling her wine.
punchline: Dilbert's clinical, evolution-based pitch accidentally triggers real attraction in the woman, and she is so appalled at being attracted to such an unromantic approach that she begs him to make it stop.
summary: A man's coldly logical mating pitch works on a woman's body but horrifies her mind.

title: Faxing Bids Blank Side Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll be shutting down our aerospace division because it hasn't won any contracts in two years.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Rumor has it that the admin assistant was faxing all of our bids with the blank side facing up.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The blank side isn't supposed to face up?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

situation: The Boss announces that the aerospace division will be shut down because it has won no contracts in two years. A caption reveals the rumored cause: the admin assistant faxed every bid with the blank side facing up. A meeting attendee asks if that's wrong, and the Boss realizes the mistake.
punchline: The division's two-year failure to win contracts, and the decision to shut it down, came from a trivial faxing error that nobody noticed, which makes the shutdown decision look reckless and the Boss's 'Uh-oh' an admission of blame.
summary: A company kills an entire division over lost contracts, only for it to emerge that every bid was sent blank.

title: Unsafe Product Fuels War Marketing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our product is so unsafe that the military wants to use it as a weapon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now the only way to satisfy our fiduciary duty to stockholders is to foment war to boost our sales.

transcript.speaker: Man in Hat
transcript.text: Hey, why'd you punch a hole in my hat?!!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That's a little thing we call marketing.

setting: Boss's office, then a desert-like war zone with huts
situation: The Boss tells Dogbert that the company's product is so unsafe the military wants to use it as a weapon. He concludes that the company's duty to stockholders now requires stirring up a war to boost sales. In the final panel, a bearded man with a bullet hole in his hat confronts a woman who casually calls the violence marketing.
punchline: The company literally manufactures conflict, with the shooting of a local's hat treated as just a routine marketing tactic to drive demand for its dangerous product.
summary: A manager reasons that profit obligations justify starting a war to sell a hazardous product, and the resulting gunfire is shrugged off as promotion.

title: Stapler Haunted By Coworkers' Misery

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Please order a new stapler for me.

transcript.speaker: Admin
transcript.text: Did your old one break?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Only in spirit.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Every person who came into my cubicle picked it up and fiddled with it.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: At first I would wipe off the cooties and try to forget.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: In time, my stapler became imbued with the sorrow and desperation of every dead-ender that fondled it.

transcript.speaker: Tina
