transcript.text: I covered it with a plastic bowl and taped it to the desk so no fumes can escape.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: If you're wondering why your chair is warm, it's because I borrowed it for a meeting.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: What's the biggest bowl you can order?

setting: Office cubicle area and an administrator's desk
situation: Tina asks the office administrator to order her a new stapler, explaining that her old one has been contaminated by every coworker who handled it. She says she sealed it under a plastic bowl and taped it to her desk. She then asks for the biggest bowl available.
punchline: Tina's germ phobia and gloomy imagination escalate until she wants an enormous bowl to quarantine something far bigger than a stapler, presumably the whole office or her own chair.
summary: A germ-obsessed employee requests a replacement stapler because the old one soaked up the misery of everyone who touched it, then asks for a giant containment bowl.

title: Approval Request Vanishes Into Vapor

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you approve this change?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'll have to run it by my corporate office.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: And we're in merger talks, so they'll need to clear it with our future owners.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: No one will know who should make the decision or what the right decision is.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When do you think you'll have an answer?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Sometime between next week and whenever the Earth is devoured by a gravitational singularity.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Meanwhile I will avoid your calls and e-mails by becoming a vapor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You forgot the approval form.

situation: Dilbert asks a manager to approve a change. She explains that it must go to her corporate office and then to the future owners in a pending merger, so nobody will know who can decide. She says the answer may take until the Earth is destroyed, then turns into vapor to dodge his follow-ups, leaving Dilbert to note the approval form is still unsigned.
punchline: The manager is so determined to avoid making a decision that she literally vaporizes, leaving Dilbert with an unsigned form.
summary: A manager buried in merger-driven uncertainty dodges a simple sign-off so thoroughly that she dissolves into mist before signing.

title: Mocking Managers Without Anyone Noticing

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Moving forward, we'll go after the low-hanging fruit at the end of the day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I like the way you used humor to mock the vacuous way managers speak.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Which part was humor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll just be quiet now.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Snork

situation: At a meeting, a manager speaks in buzzwords about going after low-hanging fruit at the end of the day, and Dilbert laughs. A coworker compliments Dilbert for using humor to mock managers' empty speech, but the manager sincerely asks which part was humor, so Dilbert falls silent.
punchline: The manager was genuinely speaking in empty jargon and cannot tell it from parody, which shows how indistinguishable real management-speak is from satire.
summary: A manager's sincere corporate jargon gets laughed at as a joke, and he is too oblivious to realize he was the target.

title: Revenge Cry, Then Mitten Bump

transcript.speaker: Tall Hat Man
transcript.text: The Imperialists punched a hole in my hat!!! Revenge will be ours!

transcript.speaker: Tall Hat Man
transcript.text: Walla-walla walla-walla walla!!!

transcript.speaker: Tall Hat Man
transcript.text: We don't do that.

transcript.speaker: Tall Hat Man
transcript.text: Mitten bump?

setting: A reddish-walled room with a small window, where three men in tall hats stand in shallow water
situation: Three identical men in tall dark hats and beards stand in murky water. One declares that Imperialists punched a hole in his hat and rallies the group with a loud war cry. A companion then rejects the cry as something they don't do and suggests a mitten bump instead.
punchline: A fierce revenge chant is undercut when a companion declines the war cry and offers a gentle, friendly mitten bump instead.
summary: A hat-wearing warrior rallies his comrades with a battle chant, only for a peaceful companion to politely refuse and propose a cuddly gesture.

title: Hand-Holding Trip to Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to go to Elbonia and do some hand-holding while they cut over to the new system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because they're incompetent?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And lonely.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not comfortable with this.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Mud wine?

setting: Dilbert's office, then a muddy hut in Elbonia
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to travel to Elbonia to support the locals during a switch to a new system. When Dilbert guesses it's because they're incompetent, the Boss adds that they're also lonely. In Elbonia, an Elbonian grips Dilbert's hand and offers him mud wine while Dilbert looks uneasy.
punchline: Literal hand-holding turns the business support job into awkward physical contact, and the Boss's 'and lonely' hints that the Elbonians want companionship more than technical help.
summary: A manager sends an engineer abroad to support a system cutover, only for the job to become literal, uncomfortable hand-holding with a very lonely local.

title: Panicking Employee Becomes Street Mime

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job tension is running high

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I... I... forgot to total the cost estimates.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!!! You're going to fire me! I'm the next casualty of the frail economy!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we could finish this by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Must improve street-mime skills!!!

situation: At a meeting, a nervous employee admits he forgot to total the cost estimates, then spirals into a panic convinced he'll be fired as a victim of the weak economy. Dilbert suggests finishing the work by e-mail while the employee, already planning for unemployment, starts practicing mime moves.
punchline: The employee is so certain he'll lose his job in the recession that he skips straight to rehearsing a street-mime career, absurdly overreacting to a small oversight.
summary: A worker's tiny mistake sends him into such a panic about layoffs that he starts training for a new life as a street performer.

title: Employee Predicts Boss's Review Comment

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's funny that you're evaluating me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Because I understand how to do your job, but you have no idea how to do my job.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: For example, right now you're going to say something that doesn't help the stockholders.

setting: Manager's office during a performance review
situation: Alice sits across a desk from the Boss during her performance evaluation. She points out that she understands his job while he has no idea how to do hers. She then predicts he is about to say something unhelpful to the stockholders, and the Boss visibly sweats and grimaces.
punchline: Alice demonstrates her superior understanding of management by correctly predicting the Boss's useless remark, leaving him nervous because he was about to do exactly that.
summary: During her review, an employee boasts that she could do her boss's job, then proves it by forecasting his next foolish comment.

title: Helpful Idea Ruins Coworker's Year

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In my spare time I came up with an idea for your project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your idea is so good that it makes all the work I did for the past year a miserable mistake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't let you leave this cubicle alive.

setting: Office cubicle, with an exterior view of the office building in the final panel
situation: Dilbert offers a coworker an idea he came up with for the coworker's project. The coworker realizes the idea is so good that it renders a whole year of his own work pointless. Dilbert takes the remark as a compliment, and the coworker responds with a murderous threat.
punchline: Dilbert's helpful contribution exposes the coworker's wasted year of effort, so the coworker's thanks turns into a threat to kill him, with the office building shown calmly outside as the threat is made.
summary: A well-meaning engineer's brilliant suggestion makes a colleague's year of labor obsolete, provoking a homicidal reaction.

title: Catbert's Ejector Seat Firing Policy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: My old policy was to have security immediately escort out anyone I fired.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sproing!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But that left too much time for weeping.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains his old firing policy of having security escort fired employees out. In the next panel, an employee is catapulted out of the frame by a giant spring, with only his feet visible. Catbert then explains that the old method left too much time for the fired person to weep.
punchline: Catbert's new firing method is to launch employees away instantly on a spring, a cruel way of denying them even the dignity of a tearful walk out.
summary: Catbert reveals a faster and crueler way to dismiss staff, replacing the security escort with a spring that flings them out of sight.

title: Dogbert's Trapdoor Raise Denial

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You want a raise? I have one word for you.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Goink!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I love having a new favorite word.

situation: Dilbert asks CEO Dogbert for a raise. Dogbert says he has one word for him, then presses a button on his desk that opens a trapdoor and drops Dilbert through the floor with a 'goink'. Dogbert, pleased with himself, muses that he loves having a new favorite word.
punchline: Dogbert's 'one word' answer is not a spoken word at all but a sound effect from the trapdoor he uses to dispose of employees who ask for raises, which he then adopts as his new favorite word.
summary: A CEO dog answers a pay request by dropping the petitioner through a hidden floor hatch and delights in the noise it makes.

title: Survived Interview, Offered Sales Position

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: You survived the rigorous interview process, but there are no openings in engineering.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: However, I am prepared to offer you a position in sales.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean a job?

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: No, just a position.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This took an ugly turn.

setting: A manager's office during a job interview
situation: A bruised, bandaged, nearly undressed Dilbert stands in front of a desk after enduring a grueling interview process. The interviewer tells him there are no engineering openings but offers a position in sales. When Dilbert asks if that means a job, the interviewer clarifies that it is only a position, which Dilbert finds alarming.
punchline: The word 'position' is played on with innocent-sounding but suggestive double meaning, implying the sales offer is something far less respectable than employment, and Dilbert's worn-out state makes the ugly turn even funnier.
summary: After a brutal hiring gauntlet leaves him bandaged and in his underwear, a candidate is offered something that may not even be a real job.

title: Economist Predicts Cannibals and Darkness

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Company Economist

transcript.speaker: Company Economist
transcript.text: In 2010 the economy will collapse and the world will plunge into darkness.

transcript.speaker: Company Economist
transcript.text: You will all be eaten by cannibals who will, in turn, die from the diseases that riddle your bodies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please never talk again.

transcript.speaker: Company Economist
transcript.text: I get that a lot lately.

situation: A company economist addresses a meeting and delivers an absurdly apocalyptic forecast of economic collapse, cannibalism and disease. The Boss, sitting at the table, begs him never to speak again. The economist admits people say that to him often these days.
punchline: The economist's gloomy, over-the-top predictions are so horrifying that everyone wants him to stop talking, and he is used to hearing it.
summary: A grim forecaster's doomsday speech about collapse and cannibals leaves his audience begging him to be quiet.

title: Dilbert Loves His Phone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've fallen in love with my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It entertains me. It knows where I am. It responds to my touch. It never judges me.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: So, it's like a woman to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Way better. Are you even listening?

situation: Dilbert lies on a therapist's couch and confesses he has fallen in love with his phone, listing its virtues: it entertains him, tracks his location, responds to his touch and never judges him. The therapist sums it up as being like a woman to him, and Dilbert replies it is far better, then complains that she isn't listening.
punchline: Dilbert praises his phone for never judging him, then criticizes the therapist for not listening, which shows the phone really does beat the human company he has had.
summary: A man reclining in therapy raves about his smartphone's devotion, then scolds his counselor for not paying attention.

title: Anger Is Healthy, Just Not Here

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm sending you to an anger management class because of your recent outburst against your boss.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When one is being abused by a figure of authority, anger is a healthy and appropriate response.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Right. We want less of that.

situation: Catbert, the evil human resources director, tells Dilbert he is being sent to anger management class for yelling at his boss. Dilbert replies that anger is a reasonable reaction to abuse by an authority figure. Catbert agrees, but says the company wants less of that reaction.
punchline: Catbert concedes that Dilbert's anger is justified, yet management still wants to suppress it, because the problem is the employee complaining rather than the abuse.
summary: An HR cat admits that an employee's fury at mistreatment is perfectly reasonable, then punishes him for it anyway.

title: Hitchhiker Asks About Slaughterhouse Stop

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for the ride. My company cut back on the travel budget.

transcript.speaker: Driver
transcript.text: Do you mind if we stop at an abandoned slaughterhouse that's miles from civilization?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A little.

transcript.speaker: Driver
transcript.text: Are you trying to make me angry?

setting: Inside a car on a rural road
situation: Dilbert is riding in a stranger's car because his company cut the travel budget. The driver casually asks whether Dilbert minds stopping at a remote abandoned slaughterhouse. When Dilbert honestly admits he minds a little, the driver menacingly asks if he's trying to make him angry.
punchline: Dilbert's travel budget cuts have forced him to accept rides from a sinister stranger, and his honest answer provokes the driver's threatening reaction.
summary: A business traveler without a travel allowance catches a ride with a creepy driver whose proposed detour turns threatening when Dilbert dares to object.

title: Adopt a Toilet Program

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: To all staff:

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: We had to let our cleaning crew go for budget reasons.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In a separate e-mail, I will explain our new "adopt a toilet" program.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to be honest, Timmy. I don't see college in your future.

setting: Office cubicle and a restroom stall
situation: Dilbert reads a company-wide e-mail announcing that the cleaning crew has been laid off for budget reasons. A second e-mail introduces an "adopt a toilet" program. In the final panel Dilbert is in a restroom stall, inspecting the toilet with a magnifying glass and talking to it as if it were a child he has adopted.
punchline: Employees are expected to personally take over cleaning the toilets, and Dilbert treats his adopted toilet like a child, with a parental assessment that it won't be going to college.
summary: After the janitors are cut to save money, staff are told to take responsibility for individual toilets, and Dilbert dutifully scolds his like a disappointed parent.

title: Side Business Gets Dilbert Fired

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My side business, dilbertfiles.com, is getting lots of attention.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a feeling I will soon be leaving my cubicle behind.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yep.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All in favor of firing this idiot for using company resources...

setting: Dilbert's kitchen at home, then a company conference room
situation: Dilbert sits at his kitchen table with Dogbert and tells him his side business website is getting lots of attention, predicting he will soon leave his cubicle behind. Dogbert agrees, but the final panel shows Catbert, the evil HR director, leading a management meeting where everyone raises their hands to fire Dilbert for using company resources.
punchline: Dilbert means he will quit to run his successful side business, but the company reads his prediction as an opening to fire him for misusing company resources on it.
summary: A hopeful entrepreneur expects his website's popularity to free him from office life, but human resources has a very different exit planned.

title: Elbonia Data Center Identity Thieves

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're moving our data center to Elbonia to save money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That seems a bit dangerous since every Elbonian is an identity thief.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It seemed like an exaggeration, but it wasn't.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 1
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Old Man Podemkin.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian 2
transcript.text: I was him this morning!

setting: Office, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: The Boss announces that the company is moving its data center to Elbonia to cut costs. Dilbert warns that every Elbonian is an identity thief, which the Boss seems not to have known. A caption then shows two muddy Elbonians where one introduces himself with a name and the other claims to have been that same person earlier.
punchline: Dilbert's claim that every Elbonian steals identities sounds like hyperbole, but the Elbonians literally swap identities, confirming that the cost-saving move is a security disaster.
summary: A cheap offshore relocation plan runs into a country whose residents casually trade each other's identities.

title: Dogbert's One Dollar Stock Windfall

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My base pay will be one dollar per year. The rest will be stock incentives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That guarantees you will reap obscene profits when the overall stock market improves, no matter what you do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pretend you don't know that.

situation: Dogbert, as CEO, tells the board that his base salary will be just one dollar a year, with the remainder of his pay coming from stock incentives. Dilbert points out that this arrangement guarantees him huge profits whenever the market rises, regardless of his performance. Dogbert simply tells him to pretend he doesn't know that.
punchline: The CEO's seemingly modest pay proposal is a scam, since rising markets alone will make him rich, and he brazenly asks the board to ignore the obvious flaw.
summary: A canine chief executive pitches a token salary paired with stock rewards, and when it's noted the deal pays off no matter what he does, he asks everyone to feign ignorance.

title: The Customer Is Always An Idiot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, answer this customer complaint. And remember, the customer is always an idiot.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I think you mean the customer is always... um... oh my...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quick! Pop your ears so your head doesn't explode!

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Gurk!

situation: The Boss hands Tina a customer complaint to answer and tells her the customer is always an idiot. Tina corrects him that the saying is different, but she stalls as she realizes the implication of what she's saying. The Boss then panics and tells her to pop her ears so her head doesn't explode.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he treats Tina's realization that customers are not actually always right as a medical emergency, implying his contempt for customers is genuine and her brain is overloading from the truth.
summary: A manager's garbled customer-service slogan leaves his employee struggling and him fretting over her imagined exploding head.

title: Interviewer Rejects Sweaty Desperate Candidate

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I detect the flop sweat of desperation.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: I base my hiring decisions on who would make a good mate, and I would never want to give life to your sweaty baby.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see what I'm saying?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I try again when I'm dehydrated?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Crumple

setting: A job interview in an office, with the interviewer seated across a desk from Dilbert
situation: Dilbert, visibly nervous and sweating, is interviewed by a woman who says she can smell his desperation. She explains that she hires based on who would make a good mate and that she would never want to have a baby with him. Dilbert, instead of protesting, asks if he can try again when he is dehydrated.
punchline: Dilbert accepts the absurd, insulting hiring criterion and only worries about his sweating, asking for a second chance when he has less sweat to give.
summary: A candidate gets turned down by an interviewer who treats hiring like choosing a breeding partner, and he meekly asks for a do-over with less perspiration.

title: Layoff Notice Lost In Spam

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You still work here? I thought I downsized you last week.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Um... I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Check your spam folder after the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First recession?

situation: At a meeting, The Boss is surprised that an employee is still at the company because he believes he already laid him off. When the employee says he doesn't think he was fired, The Boss tells him to check his spam folder after the meeting, implying the layoff notice was emailed. The employee looks panicked while Dilbert wryly asks if it's his first recession.
punchline: Layoffs are now delivered by email that may land in your spam folder, and Dilbert's deadpan question implies that this kind of cold, sloppy termination is just normal during a recession.
summary: A manager casually reveals that a worker was supposedly fired by an email that probably got filtered as junk, leaving the worker terrified while a veteran colleague shrugs it off.

title: Idiot-Proofing the Prototype Again

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The prototype is done. Come take a look at the user interface.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It works great, but make sure this thing is totally idiot-proof.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Again?

situation: Alice announces that the prototype is finished and calls the Boss over to see the user interface. The Boss sits at the computer, says it works great, and tells them to make it totally idiot-proof. Dilbert, standing beside Alice, responds with a weary 'Again?'
punchline: Dilbert's 'Again?' implies the Boss has made this same request on every previous project, and that the Boss himself is the idiot the product must be proofed against.
summary: After a finished prototype impresses the boss, he issues the same stale demand for foolproofing, prompting a world-weary response from the engineer.

title: Constructive Feedback While Laying Off Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ted, business is slow, and I have to let you go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I already did your performance review so I thought you might benefit from constructive feedback.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: "You're like a blister on a skunk's colon."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A tiny one.

situation: The Boss tells Ted he is being laid off because business is slow. He then explains that since Ted's performance review was already written, he may as well share it as constructive feedback. Ted reads the review aloud, and it compares him to a blister on a skunk's colon, which the Boss adds was a tiny one.
punchline: The Boss delivers a layoff and then piles on a gratuitously insulting performance review, calling it constructive feedback when it is just cruel.
summary: A manager fires an employee and then, for good measure, hands him a savagely insulting review under the pretense of helping him improve.

title: Employees Steal the Entire Office

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employee theft is on the rise because of the economy.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FOOP!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FOOP!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They finally figured out how to work as a team.

situation: The Boss stands holding a coffee mug, remarking that employee theft is increasing because of the economy while Catbert sits on a desk beside him. In the next panel there are quick 'FOOP' sounds as the desk and furniture vanish and Catbert tumbles through the air. In the last panel the room is stripped bare, with Catbert on the floor and the Boss noting that employees have finally learned teamwork.
punchline: The one thing employees have managed to do cooperatively is steal everything in the office, including the furniture, with the Boss sarcastically crediting the theft as successful teamwork.
summary: A manager laments rising workplace theft until thieves silently strip his whole office bare, leaving him to praise their newfound collaboration.

title: Renaming Staffing to Talent Acquisition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're changing the name of our staffing group to "Talent Acquisition."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This reflects our new focus on hiring only highly talented people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't that imply that your current employees are inferior to the ones you plan to hire?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sort of.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And since you routinely fire the worst performing employees. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have just sealed our doom while expecting us to remain loyal to the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now all I can think about are ways to vandalize the servers before I become homeless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I over-communicated again.

setting: Conference room, then the Boss's office
situation: The Boss announces to a meeting that the staffing group is being renamed 'Talent Acquisition' to reflect a focus on hiring only talented people. Dilbert points out this implies current employees are inferior and, since the worst performers are routinely fired, everyone's job is now at risk. After Dilbert says he is thinking of vandalizing servers, the Boss later admits to Catbert that he over-communicated again.
punchline: The Boss was so tactlessly honest about the implications of the rebrand that he accidentally told his staff they were about to be replaced, and he only regrets saying too much rather than the plan itself.
summary: A cheerful corporate rebranding announcement unintentionally tells the staff they are being replaced by better people, and the manager's only regret is sharing too much.

title: Winning the Debt Collector Misery Contest

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert works in collections.

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: My wife left me, my truck caught on fire, and all of my organs are failing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work in a collections department.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You win.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Winning isn't what it used to be.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Your five-minute break is over!

situation: Dilbert, wearing a headset, is on the phone as a debt collector with a debtor who lists a string of personal disasters to excuse not paying. Dilbert replies that he works in collections and concedes that the caller wins the misery contest. Later, on a break in the hallway, he muses that winning isn't what it used to be until a coworker tells him his break is over.
punchline: Dilbert's job is so miserable that he concedes the contest of who has it worse to a dying, divorced caller, and even then gets no break from the drudgery.
summary: A debt collector hears a caller's litany of woes and cheerfully concedes that his own job is the more wretched, only to be herded back to work.

title: Beta Testers Driven To Despair

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The results of our beta testing are in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our user interface triggered widespread despondency and self-mutilation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously we'll need to delay our launch for the public good.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: When did you become a communist?

situation: Dilbert presents beta testing results using a projector screen showing a screaming, distressed user, then one stabbing himself in the eye with a pen. He concludes that the product launch must be delayed to protect the public. A horned manager at the table responds by accusing him of being a communist.
punchline: Delaying a harmful product to protect users is treated by management as a radical, anti-capitalist idea rather than basic responsibility.
summary: A product so badly designed that test users are driven to self-harm still gets defended by managers who think caring about public welfare is subversive.

title: Seeming Good Beats Being Good

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Director of Marketecture

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketecture
transcript.text: It is better to seem good than to be good.

transcript.speaker: Slide
transcript.text: Being good (overrated)

transcript.speaker: Director of Marketecture
transcript.text: A misleading benchmark test can accomplish in minutes what years of good engineering can never do.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it our maturity that makes that concept sound okay?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope so.

situation: A Director of Marketecture presents a slide arguing that being good is overrated and that seeming good is better. He adds that a misleading benchmark can achieve in minutes what years of real engineering cannot. Afterwards Alice and Dilbert, standing with Wally, wonder whether their own maturity is why the idea sounds acceptable.
punchline: The engineers realize the cynical, deceptive marketing advice sounds reasonable to them, and they hope that's just because they've grown mature rather than morally corrupted.
summary: A marketing executive praises appearances and rigged benchmarks over real quality, leaving the engineers unsettled that it sounds sensible.

title: Sabotage Product to Hide Bad Reviews

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sales are tanking because our online reviews are awful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cripple a feature and change the model number so the online reviews look stale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. That was a lot of evil packed into one sentence.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

situation: Dilbert stands before the Boss's desk and reports that sales are falling because online reviews of the product are terrible. The Boss responds by instructing him to deliberately cripple a feature and change the model number so the old negative reviews no longer apply. Dilbert is stunned by the ruthlessness of the idea, and the Boss takes it as a compliment.
punchline: The Boss proudly accepts "thank you" for a plan that is blatantly deceptive and evil, treating Dilbert's horrified observation as praise.
summary: A manager's scheme to dodge bad reviews by degrading the product and renaming it earns him pride rather than shame.

title: Not Allowed to Talk to Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you tell a customer that you're not allowed to talk to customers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You fool! That makes us look lame!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What was I supposed to do when she asked me a question?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you have access to scissors?

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert for telling a customer that he is forbidden from talking to customers. Dilbert asks what else he could have done when she asked him a question. The Boss responds by asking whether Dilbert had scissors on hand.
punchline: The Boss implies Dilbert should have cut his own tongue out or otherwise silenced himself rather than admit the company's policy, showing absurd management logic that prioritizes appearances over sensible behavior.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for honestly revealing a gag rule about customer contact, then suggests a drastic and absurd way he could have avoided answering.

title: Rehired Dilbert Makes Everyone Expendable

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I rehired Dilbert for a salary much lower than his previous pay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That makes the rest of you overpaid and expendable. Please welcome him back.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How about a hug?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Today you learned that hugging has a dark side.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow.

situation: The Boss announces at a meeting that he has rehired Dilbert at a much lower salary, implying the rest of the team are now overpaid and expendable. Alice responds to the welcome by offering Dilbert a hug, which turns into her violently attacking him and pinning him down on the table.
punchline: The hug is really a thinly veiled assault, as Alice takes out her anger and fear of losing her job on Dilbert, teaching him that a friendly gesture can have a violent side.
summary: A boss brings back a cheaper Dilbert and threatens his colleagues' jobs, so Alice's welcome hug becomes a vicious tackle.

title: Gallstone Became Labor Secretary Boast

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: My first baby weighed 12 pounds. I gave birth in the cab of a stolen backhoe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's nothing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I once passed a gallstone so big that it became Secretary of Labor in the Clinton administration.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I find that hard to believe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me ten minutes and then check Wikipedia.

situation: A coworker boasts about giving birth to a 12-pound baby in the cab of a stolen backhoe, and a man in a white shirt and tie tries to top her with an absurd story about passing a gallstone that became a Clinton-era Secretary of Labor. When a woman says she finds it hard to believe, he tells her to wait ten minutes and then check Wikipedia.
punchline: He implies he will edit Wikipedia to make his ridiculous lie appear true, mocking the site's open-edit unreliability.
summary: Two coworkers trade outrageous tall tales, and the second guarantees his false claim will be verifiable online once he alters the encyclopedia entry himself.

title: Dogbert Pockets the Bailout Bonus

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm happy to announce that the government gave us a bailout loan of $25 billion.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm even happier to announce that I kept the entire amount for my bonus.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who wants to see a picture of my island fortress?

setting: Corporate boardroom, with an exterior shot of the office building
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, addresses a conference table of employees and announces the company received a $25 billion government bailout loan. He then reveals he kept the whole sum as his personal bonus, and cheerfully offers to show off the island fortress he bought with it.
punchline: The CEO openly pockets an entire taxpayer-funded bailout as a personal bonus and brags about it, satirizing executive greed during the financial crisis.
summary: A canine chief executive gleefully reveals that a massive government rescue fund went straight into his own pocket and paid for a private stronghold.

title: Sacrifice Your Health for Testing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to do product testing for our new release.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could I possibly have time for all the work you keep giving me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you tried sacrificing your health?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I look like I can run marathons?

situation: The Boss holding a coffee mug asks Dilbert to take on product testing for a new release. Dilbert protests that he has no time for all the work he's already been given. The Boss helpfully suggests he sacrifice his health, and Dilbert angrily replies that he doesn't look like someone who can run marathons.
punchline: The Boss casually suggests destroying one's health as a time-management strategy, and Dilbert's reply shows he is so out of shape that he assumes he'd never survive the extra effort needed to take on more work.
summary: A manager responds to a time-strapped employee's complaint by recommending he give up his wellbeing to fit in more work.

title: Problems Renamed Opportunities, House Burns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, we will refer to all of our problems as opportunities.

transcript.speaker: Boss's Wife
transcript.text: One of your idiot spawn was playing with the oven and burned down your house.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Camping opportunity?

situation: The Boss announces to the meeting that all problems must now be called opportunities. His wife interrupts the meeting to tell him their house burned down because one of their children played with the oven. The Boss tries to apply his new rule by asking if it's a 'camping opportunity.'
punchline: The Boss absurdly applies his euphemistic jargon to a real disaster, calling his burned-down house a camping opportunity, which shows how meaningless relabeling problems is.
summary: A manager's new vocabulary policy gets tested when his wife delivers news of a house fire and he spins it with his own corporate euphemism.

title: Sneaking Office Supplies Past Guard

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You can have your old job back, but your compensation will reflect the new market reality.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You'll get a small base salary plus anything you can sneak past the guard in the lobby.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These aren't the droids you're looking for.

setting: Catbert's office and the company lobby
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, offers Dilbert his old job back at a reduced pay level. The compensation is a tiny base salary plus whatever he can smuggle out past the lobby guard. Dilbert then walks past the guard with stolen items stuffed in his clothes, thinking a Star Wars mind-trick line.
punchline: With salaries slashed, employees are expected to make up their pay by stealing company property, and Dilbert tries to get away with it using a Jedi mind trick.
summary: After a pay cut, Dilbert's re-hiring package depends on how much office loot he can smuggle past security.

title: Date Ends Over Pirate Insult App

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I judge potential mates by their cell phone apps. Hand it over.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: You have an app that does nothing but hurl pirate insults. That is so stupid. This date is over.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's phone
transcript.text: Don't let the door hit you in the booty. Aaaargh!

setting: Restaurant table with a view of rolling hills
situation: Dilbert is on a date at a restaurant when the woman announces she judges potential mates by their phone apps and demands to see his phone. She finds an app that only hurls pirate insults, declares it stupid and ends the date. After she leaves, Dilbert's phone app taunts her departure with a pirate insult.
punchline: The very app she condemned as pointless gets the last word, insulting her on her way out while Dilbert sits alone and the date is lost.
summary: A woman who vets dates by their phone apps storms off after finding a silly insult app, which then mocks her as she goes.

title: Be Less Pitchforkable, Humphrey

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert: VP of Sales

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Humphrey, you're scaring all of our customers.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Try to be less pitchforkable.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Seriously. Can you do that?

transcript.speaker: Humphrey
transcript.text: Who wants a hug?!

setting: Office of the VP of Sales, with a view of an office building
situation: Ratbert, now VP of Sales, tells his employee Humphrey that he is frightening customers and should try to seem less likely to be chased by an angry mob. A panel of an office building separates the exchange. Humphrey responds by jumping up and enthusiastically offering hugs, which is clearly not an improvement.
punchline: Humphrey's attempt to seem friendlier by loudly offering hugs is just as unsettling, so he remains exactly as pitchforkable as before.
summary: A rodent sales boss asks a frightening employee to become less menacing to clients, and the employee's cheerful overcorrection is even creepier.

title: Finishing Early Means Becoming Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have no project. Do you need any help with yours?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No. If I finish my project too soon, I might become like you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you make a different face when you imagine being like me?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'm trying, but I can't.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, tells Asok he has no project and offers to help with Asok's. Asok refuses, explaining that finishing his work too quickly could leave him idle like Dilbert. Dilbert asks him to at least look less horrified at the thought, but Asok says he can't.
punchline: Asok sees Dilbert's lack of work as a cautionary tale, and he is so horrified by the idea of ending up like him that he can't even fake a neutral expression.
summary: A jobless Dilbert offers help, but a young coworker would rather work slowly than risk turning into him.

title: Catbert Misses Meaningful Evil

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Being evil used to mean something.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: These days I can cut salaries by 10% and people will thank me for not firing them!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Do you want to help me eat employee lunches from the break room fridge?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like that.

setting: Catbert's office, with the Boss sitting across the desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, complains to the Boss that evil just isn't what it used to be. He notes that employees now thank him for a 10% pay cut as long as they aren't fired. He then invites the Boss to join him in petty theft, eating employees' lunches from the break room fridge, and the Boss happily agrees.
punchline: Employees are so cowed by layoff fears that they gratefully accept pay cuts, so Catbert has to settle for stealing lunches to feel properly evil, and the Boss cheerfully joins in.
summary: A bored evil HR cat laments that frightened workers now thank him for pay cuts, so he turns to snacking on their fridge lunches with his willing boss.

title: Call Me Next Week, Yesterday

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have time to talk today?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. Call me next week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have a minute to hear about my day?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure. Call me yesterday.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss if he has time to talk, and the boss cheerfully tells him to call next week, then walks off humming. Later Dilbert arrives home and asks Dogbert if he has a minute to hear about his day, and Dogbert gives the same brush-off by telling him to call yesterday.
punchline: Dogbert mocks Dilbert with an impossible deferral, telling him to call in the past, which makes clear that Dilbert gets brushed off by everyone, even at home.
summary: A man seeking a listener gets fobbed off first by his superior with a future date and then by his dog with a past one.

title: Wally's Unfunded, Coffee-Fueled Project

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My project is unfunded, just the way I like it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I spend my entire day forwarding funny e-mails and lubricating my bowels with coffee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Allow me to explain something...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Better make it fast!

situation: At a meeting, Wally cheerfully announces that his project has no funding, which suits him fine. He admits he spends all day forwarding jokes by e-mail and drinking coffee. When the Boss starts to explain something, Wally gulps his coffee and tells him to hurry up.
punchline: Wally openly brags about doing no real work thanks to having no funding, and the Boss's attempt to lecture him is brushed off because Wally is too busy with his coffee break.
summary: A proudly idle employee tells a meeting that a lack of money means he can goof off all day, then rushes his boss along.

title: Torturous Courtesy Interview Never Disclosed

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: In your first round of interviews we tested your reaction to humiliation and small arms fire.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: In round two I will test your ability to keep company secrets.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: When are you going to tell him this is a courtesy interview?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: What?

setting: Office interview room with a desk
situation: A strange egg-shaped interviewer lists the ordeals a job candidate has endured, including humiliation and gunfire, and announces a second round testing secret-keeping. Ratbert then asks when the candidate will be told the whole thing is only a courtesy interview. The candidate, hanging upside down and tied up over a barrel, can only say 'What?'
punchline: The candidate has been subjected to absurd torture-like interview rounds for a job he was never going to get, since it was only a courtesy interview.
summary: A job seeker dangles bound and upside down after brutal interview tests, unaware that the company never intended to hire him.

title: Dogbert's Pork Barrel Factory Scheme

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the CEO

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll build a factory in every state.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Politicians will vote to throw huge pork projects our way to benefit their home states.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: You're turning capitalism against democracy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You say weiner, I say winner.

setting: Dogbert's CEO office, with an exterior view of a factory building
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, tells a pointy-haired subordinate his plan to build a factory in every state. He explains that politicians will then vote to send huge pork-barrel projects his company's way to benefit their home states. The subordinate objects that this turns capitalism against democracy, and Dogbert shrugs it off with a wordplay.
punchline: Dogbert cheerfully exploits government pork-barrel spending as a business strategy, and when accused of corrupting the system he dismisses the ethical objection with a flippant pun on 'weiner' and 'winner'.
summary: A scheming canine executive plans to spread facilities across the country so lawmakers will funnel government money to his company, and he brushes off a warning about the ethics.
